quiz.q: Using the digits 3 and 5 once each in the form aᵇ, what is the largest number you can make?
quiz.explain: 3⁵ = 243 and 5³ = 125, so 3⁵ is larger.
quiz.mistake: Puts the bigger digit as the base

quiz.q: Which is the largest?
quiz.explain: 100² = 10⁴, 10¹⁰, and 100¹⁰ = 10²⁰, while 2¹⁰⁰ = (2¹⁰)¹⁰ > (10³)¹⁰ = 10³⁰. So 2¹⁰⁰ is largest.
quiz.mistake: Judges by the size of the base

quiz.q: What is 2⁵ − 5²?
quiz.explain: 2⁵ = 32 and 5² = 25, so the difference is 7.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 2⁵ and 5² are equal

teach.ask: Gappu bets that 5³ is bigger than 3⁵ because 5 is bigger. Will he win the bet?
teach.praise: Oops, I lose! 3⁵ = 243 beats 5³ = 125 — the exponent matters a lot.
teach.nudge: Did you work out both numbers? Which part of a power makes it grow fastest?

topics.title: Why and how people first counted

learn.hook: A shepherd long ago could not count to 50 — yet she always knew if a goat went missing. How?
points: Early people counted to keep track of their animals, food stores and trade, and to follow days and seasons (when to sow, when to harvest).
Counting is one-to-one matching: put one pebble aside for each goat in the morning. In the evening, take one pebble back for each goat. Pebbles left over mean goats are missing.
People counted with sticks or pebbles, with spoken sounds (say a, b, c, ... as number names) and with written marks. Each has limits: big numbers need too many pebbles, and 26 letters soon run out.
A numeral is a symbol (or group of symbols) that stands for a number, like 7 or VII. A number system is a set of numerals with rules for writing and reading every number.
You can design your own system: if ★ means 10 and • means 1, then ★★•••• is 24.

example.q: Leela puts aside one pebble for each of her 23 goats in the morning. In the evening each returning goat takes away one pebble, and 2 pebbles are left. How many goats returned?
steps: 2 pebbles left → 2 goats did not return

learn.reallife: A school bus conductor ticking each child's name on a list is doing one-to-one matching too.

games.title: Why count?
pairs: Know how long the grain will last
Know when to sow and harvest

games.title: Counting ideas
items: One-to-one matching needs no number names at all.
You only pair each object with one counter.
'VII' and '7' are two numerals for the same number.
Both are symbols for seven.
Counting with the 26 letters a to z works for any number.
After z = 26 you need new names.
A number system is just one symbol.
It is a whole set of numerals plus rules for writing every number.

quiz.q: A herder puts one pebble aside for each of 35 goats in the morning. In the evening, each returning goat removes one pebble and 4 pebbles are left. How many goats came back?
quiz.explain: 4 pebbles left means 4 goats are still out, so 35 − 4 = 31 came back.
quiz.mistake: Adds the leftover pebbles instead of subtracting

quiz.q: What is one-to-one matching?
options: Writing the number 1 again and again
Pairing each object with exactly one counter
Matching each object with two pebbles
quiz.explain: Each goat gets exactly one pebble, so the pile of pebbles is as big as the herd.
quiz.mistake: Thinks matching means counting in ones aloud

quiz.q: If a = 1, b = 2, c = 3, ..., which letter stands for 8?
quiz.explain: a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h — h is the 8th letter.
steps: Count: a1 b2 c3 d4 e5 f6 g7 h8
quiz.mistake: Miscounts the letters by one

quiz.q: What is the biggest problem with counting using the letters a to z?
options: Letters are too small to write
quiz.explain: With 26 letters you can name only 26 numbers; you need new names after that.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the limit of a fixed set of names

quiz.q: Which of these is a numeral (a written symbol) rather than a number name?
quiz.explain: 19 is a symbol for the number. 'nineteen' and 'unnis' are spoken names in English and Hindi.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up a number's name with its symbol

quiz.q: Why did farmers long ago count days?
options: To count stars for fun only
To know when to sow and harvest
quiz.explain: Keeping track of days and seasons told farmers when the rains would come and when to plant.
quiz.mistake: Does not link counting to real needs

quiz.q: Meena has 3 bundles of 10 sticks and 7 loose sticks. She gets 5 more loose sticks. How many sticks does she have now?
quiz.explain: 30 + 7 + 5 = 42. (12 loose sticks can be bundled into 1 more ten and 2 loose.)
quiz.mistake: Counts the bundles as single sticks

quiz.q: In Ravi's own number system, ★ means 10 and • means 1. What number is ★★★••?
quiz.explain: Three ★ make 30 and two • make 2, so the total is 32.
quiz.mistake: Counts the symbols instead of their values

teach.ask: Gappu has 40 seeds but cannot count past 10. How could he check that none are lost tomorrow?
teach.praise: Brilliant! One pebble for each seed — if a pebble is left over, a seed is missing!
teach.nudge: How can you keep one counter for each seed?

topics.title: How Indian numerals reached the world

learn.hook: The digits 0 to 9 on every phone in the world began their journey in India. Why do some people still call them 'Arabic'?
points: The Yajurveda lists names for powers of ten: eka (1), dasha (10), shata (100), sahasra (1000), ayuta (10⁴), niyuta (10⁵), prayuta (10⁶), arbuda (10⁷), ... up to parardha (10¹²).

The ten digits 0–9 with place value grew in India. The Bakhshali manuscript, found in 1881 in a village now in Pakistan, uses a dot for zero. Aryabhata (499 CE) explained that each place is ten times the one before.
In the 9th century CE, Al-Khwarizmi and Al-Kindi in Baghdad wrote books on calculating with Indian numerals. In 1202 CE Fibonacci's book Liber Abaci spread them across Europe.

So the name 'Arabic numerals' is misleading: they began in India and travelled through the Arab world. 'Hindu-Arabic numerals' or 'Indian numerals' is more accurate — Arab scholars themselves called them Indian numbers.

example.q: How many sahasra make one ayuta?

learn.reallife: Every price tag, cricket score and phone number you read uses this Indian invention.

games.title: Timeline
items: Yajurveda names for powers of 10
Aryabhata's place-value work (499 CE)
Al-Khwarizmi writes on Indian numerals (9th century CE)
Fibonacci's Liber Abaci (1202 CE)

quiz.q: What number is sahasra?
quiz.explain: In the Yajurveda list, sahasra means one thousand.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up shata (100) and sahasra (1000)

quiz.q: What number is shata?
quiz.explain: shata means one hundred (as in 'shatak', a century).
quiz.mistake: Confuses shata with dasha

quiz.q: Which power of ten is ayuta?
quiz.explain: ayuta comes right after sahasra (1000), so it is 10⁴ = 10,000.
quiz.mistake: Skips or repeats a step in the list

quiz.q: Which old Indian manuscript uses a dot as a sign for zero?
quiz.explain: The Bakhshali manuscript, found in 1881, writes zero as a dot.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Indian manuscripts with European books or ancient bones

quiz.q: Whose book Liber Abaci (1202 CE) spread Indian numerals across Europe?
quiz.explain: Fibonacci learnt the numerals from Arab traders and wrote Liber Abaci for Europe.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the people who carried the numerals with those who created them

quiz.q: Which name for 0–9 best shows where they come from?
quiz.explain: They were created in India and carried by Arab scholars, so 'Hindu-Arabic' or 'Indian' numerals is more accurate than 'Arabic'.
steps: Passed on through the Arab world
quiz.mistake: Thinks the people who passed on an idea invented it

quiz.q: What did Aryabhata explain about places in a number?
options: Each place is 60 times the one before
Each place is ten times the place before it
quiz.explain: Aryabhata described the base-10 place value idea: from place to place, ten times.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up base 10 with the Babylonian base 60

quiz.q: How many dasha make one shata?
quiz.explain: dasha = 10 and shata = 100, so 10 dasha make one shata.
quiz.mistake: Uses the value of shata itself as the answer

teach.ask: Gappu read 'Arabic numerals' in a book. Is that the right name? Tell me the story!
teach.praise: So the digits were born in India, travelled with Arab scholars, and reached Europe through Fibonacci. What a journey!
teach.nudge: Where were the digits 0–9 first made? Who carried them to Europe?

topics.title: Early counting: bones, body parts and twos

learn.hook: One of the oldest maths objects ever found is a baboon bone with 29 scratches — over 40,000 years old!
points: Some communities in Papua New Guinea count by touching body parts in a fixed order — fingers, then wrist, elbow, shoulder, ear, eye and so on. Each body part stands for a number.

Tally marks on bones: the Lebombo bone from the Lebombo mountains of southern Africa (more than 40,000 years old) has 29 notches. The Ishango bone from Congo in Africa (more than 20,000 years old) has groups of notches.
The Gumulgal people of Australia counted in twos with just two words: urapon (1) and ukasar (2). So 3 = ukasar-urapon, 4 = ukasar-ukasar, 5 = ukasar-ukasar-urapon.
Most people can see how many things there are at a glance only up to about 4 or 5. Beyond that we must count or group — which is why tallies are bundled in fives.

example.q: In a made-up body-count: little finger 1, ring finger 2, middle 3, index 4, thumb 5, wrist 6, elbow 7, shoulder 8. Which body part means 7?

learn.reallife: When a cricket umpire counts balls in an over on his fingers, he is using body parts to count.

games.title: Old counting facts
items: The Lebombo bone has 29 notches.
It is a very old tally with 29 notches.
The Ishango bone was found in India.
It was found in Congo, in Africa.
Most people can instantly see up to about 4 or 5 objects without counting.
Beyond that we need to count or group.
Body-part counting can go in any order you like.
It works only if everyone uses the same fixed order.

quiz.q: About how many notches does the Lebombo bone have?
quiz.explain: The Lebombo bone, a baboon bone more than 40,000 years old, has 29 notches.
quiz.mistake: Guesses without remembering the famous count

quiz.q: In which continent were the Ishango and Lebombo bones found?
quiz.explain: Ishango is in Congo and Lebombo is in southern Africa — both in Africa.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all old maths objects come from one place

quiz.q: In Gumulgal counting, what number is ukasar-ukasar-ukasar?
quiz.explain: ukasar means 2, so three ukasars make 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.
quiz.mistake: Counts the words instead of adding their values

quiz.q: How would the Gumulgal say 5?
quiz.explain: 5 = 2 + 2 + 1, so it is ukasar-ukasar-urapon.
quiz.mistake: Uses only ones, or stops at 4

quiz.q: Up to about how many objects can most people see at a glance without counting?
quiz.explain: Our eyes can instantly judge only small groups, about 4 or 5. For more, we count or group.
steps: Try it with 3 dots, then 9 dots
quiz.mistake: Overestimates what the eye can judge in a flash

quiz.q: A made-up body-count goes: 5 fingers (1–5), then wrist 6, elbow 7, shoulder 8, ear 9, eye 10. Which number is 'shoulder'?
quiz.explain: After the five fingers come wrist (6), elbow (7) and shoulder (8).
quiz.mistake: Loses track of the fixed order

quiz.q: Why are tally marks usually bundled in fives?
options: Because we cannot see more than about 4–5 marks at a glance
quiz.explain: Bundles of five are easy to see at once, so we count bundles instead of single marks.
quiz.mistake: Does not link grouping with the limits of our eyes

quiz.q: In Gumulgal counting, how is 4 said?
quiz.explain: 4 = 2 + 2, so it is ukasar-ukasar.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up 3 and 4

teach.ask: Gappu found a bone with scratches in a museum. What could people have used it for?
teach.praise: A counting bone! Each scratch is one thing counted — maths is older than writing!
teach.nudge: What could each scratch on the bone stand for?

topics.title: Counting long ago: tallies, Egyptian and Roman numerals

learn.hook: Long before anyone wrote the digit 7, a shepherd tied a knot in a rope or scratched a mark on a bone for every sheep that went out to graze.
points: The first counting was one-to-one matching: one pebble, knot or tally mark for each object.
Grouping makes counting faster. Tally marks are bundled in fives, so 3 bundles and 2 marks means 17.
Egyptian numerals used a picture for each power of ten: a stroke for 1, a heel bone for 10, a coiled rope for 100 and a lotus flower for 1000. You repeat the pictures and add.
Roman numerals use I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100, D = 500, M = 1000. A smaller symbol written before a bigger one is subtracted: IV = 4, XL = 40, XC = 90, CM = 900.
These systems have no place value and no zero, so big numbers need many symbols and sums like 347 × 26 become very hard.

example.q: Write 1984 in Roman numerals.

learn.reallife: Clock towers, chapter numbers in old books and 'Class VIII' written on your notebook all use Roman numerals.

games.title: Ancient number facts
items: In Roman numerals, IX means 11.
I before X is subtracted: IX = 10 − 1 = 9. Eleven is XI.
The Roman system has a symbol for zero.
Roman numerals have no zero at all.
In Egyptian numerals, changing the order of the symbols does not change the value.
Egyptian values are simply added, so order does not matter.
The Egyptian lotus flower stands for 1000.
Stroke = 1, heel bone = 10, coiled rope = 100, lotus = 1000.
CL means 150.
The bigger symbol comes first, so add: C + L = 100 + 50 = 150.
XXXX is the standard Roman way to write 40.
Forty is written XL, which means 50 − 10.

quiz.q: What number is MCMXLVII?
quiz.explain: M = 1000, CM = 900, XL = 40 and VII = 7. Together that is 1947, the year India became independent.
quiz.mistake: Adds C and M (1100) instead of subtracting C from M

quiz.q: How is 49 written in Roman numerals?
quiz.explain: 49 = 40 + 9. Forty is XL and nine is IX, so 49 = XLIX.
quiz.mistake: Writes IL by subtracting 1 from 50 in one jump, which the standard rules do not allow

quiz.q: An Egyptian scribe draws 3 lotus flowers, 2 coiled ropes, 4 heel bones and 5 strokes. What number is this?
quiz.explain: Lotus = 1000, rope = 100, heel bone = 10, stroke = 1. So 3000 + 200 + 40 + 5 = 3245.
quiz.mistake: Just counts the pictures (14) or mixes up which picture means what

quiz.q: How many Egyptian symbols are needed to write 999?
quiz.explain: There is no place value, so 999 needs 9 coiled ropes, 9 heel bones and 9 strokes: 27 symbols.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Egyptian numerals use one symbol per digit like our system

quiz.q: Kabir's cricket scorecard shows three bundles of five tally marks and 3 single marks. How many runs is that?
quiz.explain: Each bundle is 5 runs, so 3 bundles = 15. Add the 3 single marks: 15 + 3 = 18.
quiz.mistake: Counts each bundle as 1 mark instead of 5

quiz.q: Why is it hard to multiply big numbers using Roman numerals?
options: Roman numerals cannot show numbers above 1000
Roman numerals cannot show even numbers
There is no place value or zero, so digits cannot be lined up in columns
Letters are not allowed in maths
quiz.explain: Our column method works because each place has a fixed value. Roman numerals have no place value and no zero, so there are no columns to line up.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the problem is the size of numbers rather than the missing place value

quiz.q: Which of these Roman numerals has the largest value?
quiz.explain: DC = 500 + 100 = 600, CD = 500 − 100 = 400, CX = 110 and XC = 90. So DC is the largest.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that a smaller symbol in front means subtract

quiz.q: Riya sees 'Chapter XIX' in an old storybook. Which chapter is it?
quiz.explain: X = 10 and IX = 9, so XIX = 10 + 9 = 19.
quiz.mistake: Adds every symbol (10 + 1 + 10 = 21) instead of subtracting the I before X

teach.ask: Gappu grumbles: Why does 888 need so many symbols in Roman numerals (DCCCLXXXVIII) but only three digits in our numbers?
teach.praise: Yes! Roman numerals only add and repeat symbols, but our digits get their value from their place, with zero holding empty places. Clever!
teach.nudge: In 888, do all three 8s mean the same thing? What gives each 8 a different value?

topics.title: Roman sums, the abacus and Egyptian limits

learn.hook: Try multiplying CCCXLVII by XXVI. Hard? The Romans thought so too — that is why they used counting boards!
points: Adding Roman numerals means putting the symbols together and regrouping: XXVII + XIV = 27 + 14 = 41 = XLI.
Multiplying Roman numerals is very clumsy, because there is no place value and the symbols do not line up in columns.
Roman numerals can be long: 3888 = MMMDCCCLXXXVIII uses 15 symbols, but our system needs only 4 digits. Our system is far more efficient.
A decimal abacus has lines for 1, 10, 100, 1000, ... and counters on them. When a line gets 10 counters, remove them and put 1 counter on the next line up.
The Egyptian system needs a brand-new symbol for every new power of ten, so bigger and bigger numbers need ever more symbols.

example.q: Add 386 and 247 on an abacus.
steps: Ones: 6 + 7 = 13 → leave 3, carry 1 counter to tens

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers in many countries used abacus-like counting boards for centuries; children still learn abacus maths today.

games.title: Which system is easier?
items: 3888 needs more Roman symbols than Hindu-Arabic digits.
MMMDCCCLXXXVIII has 15 symbols; 3888 has 4 digits.
On an abacus, 10 counters on the tens line become 1 counter on the hundreds line.
10 tens = 1 hundred.
The Egyptian system can write any number with its first four symbols.
It needs a new symbol for each new power of ten.
Roman numerals are easy to multiply in columns.
Without place value the symbols do not line up.

quiz.q: What is XXVII + XIV?
quiz.explain: 27 + 14 = 41, which is XL (40) + I (1) = XLI.
quiz.mistake: Writes four X's instead of using XL for 40

quiz.q: How many Roman symbols are used to write 3888 (MMMDCCCLXXXVIII)?
quiz.explain: MMM (3) + D (1) + CCC (3) + L (1) + XXX (3) + V (1) + III (3) = 15 symbols.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the different symbols

quiz.q: An abacus shows 4 counters on the hundreds line, none on the tens line and 7 on the ones line. What number is it?
quiz.explain: 4 hundreds + 0 tens + 7 ones = 407.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the empty tens line

quiz.q: The ones line of an abacus has 6 counters. You add 7 more and regroup. How many counters stay on the ones line?
quiz.explain: 6 + 7 = 13 counters. 10 of them become 1 counter on the tens line, leaving 3.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to regroup ten counters

quiz.q: Why does the Egyptian system run into trouble with very large numbers?
options: Its symbols change meaning by position
It needs a new symbol for every new power of ten
quiz.explain: Egyptians had separate pictures for 1, 10, 100, ... Every higher power needs one more new picture.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the Egyptian system had place value

quiz.q: What is XX × V in Roman numerals?
quiz.explain: 20 × 5 = 100, which is C. Romans had to work this out without columns.
quiz.mistake: Adds the numerals instead of multiplying

quiz.q: 888 is DCCCLXXXVIII in Roman numerals. How many more symbols is that than our 3 digits?
quiz.explain: DCCCLXXXVIII has 12 symbols. 12 − 3 = 9 more symbols.
steps: D 1 + CCC 3 + L 1 + XXX 3 + V 1 + III 3 = 12
quiz.mistake: Gives the total symbols instead of the difference

quiz.q: An abacus has 3 lines (hundreds, tens, ones) and at most 9 counters on each line. What is the largest number it can show?
quiz.explain: 9 on each line gives 9 × 100 + 9 × 10 + 9 = 999. A 10th counter would need regrouping onto a new line.
quiz.mistake: Adds up the counters instead of using place values

teach.ask: Gappu wants to add CCXLVI and CLXXX. Why might an abacus help him more than Roman numerals?
teach.praise: Yes! On the abacus each line is a place, and 10 counters jump to the next line. So much easier!
teach.nudge: What does each line of an abacus stand for? What happens when a line gets 10 counters?

learn.hook: Imagine a world where people have only 4 fingers. They would write 16 as '100'! Let's visit some other bases.
points: In a base-5 landmark system, the landmarks are 1, 5, 25, 125, 625, ... — each 5 times the one before. In base n, the landmarks are 1, n, n², n³, ...
Adding with regrouping: in base 5, five of one landmark make one of the next. 4 ones + 3 ones = 7 ones = 1 five and 2 ones.
Multiplying landmarks gives a landmark: 25 × 125 = 5² × 5³ = 5⁵ = 3125. Multiplying by the base moves every symbol up one landmark — like putting a 0 at the end.
Base 8 uses digits 0–7 and places 1, 8, 64, 512. So 100 = 1 × 64 + 4 × 8 + 4 = 144 in base 8.

example.q: Add 34 (base 5) and 23 (base 5).

learn.reallife: Computers use base 2, and programmers often write numbers in base 8 or base 16 to make long binary strings shorter.

quiz.q: In a base-5 system, which landmark comes after 125?
quiz.explain: Each landmark is 5 times the one before: 125 × 5 = 625.
quiz.mistake: Adds 5 or doubles instead of multiplying by 5

quiz.q: In base 7, the landmarks are 1, 7, 49, ... What is the next landmark?
quiz.mistake: Adds 7 to 49 or doubles it

quiz.q: In base 5, what is 44 + 1?
quiz.explain: 4 + 1 = 5 ones = 1 five, carry. 4 + 1 = 5 fives = 1 twenty-five, carry. So 100 (base 5). Check: 24 + 1 = 25.
quiz.mistake: Writes the digit 5, which base 5 does not have

quiz.q: 25 × 125 is the landmark 5 to the power of what?
quiz.explain: 25 = 5² and 125 = 5³, so the product is 5²⁺³ = 5⁵ = 3125.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the exponents instead of adding

quiz.q: In base 5, what is 23 (base 5) × 5, written in base 5?
quiz.explain: Multiplying by the base moves every symbol up one landmark, so a 0 appears at the end. Check: 13 × 5 = 65 = 2 × 25 + 3 × 5.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the digits by 5 as if in base 10

quiz.q: How is 16 written in base 4?
quiz.explain: 16 = 4², which is one of the third landmark: 1 × 16 + 0 × 4 + 0 = 100 (base 4).
quiz.mistake: Writes a 4 or a 6, which base 4 does not allow

quiz.q: How is 100 written in base 8?
quiz.mistake: Keeps the base-10 digits unchanged

quiz.q: What is 10110 (base 2) in base 10?
quiz.mistake: Reads the binary digits as an ordinary base-10 number, or uses the wrong place values

teach.ask: Gappu lives in Base-4 Land. He counted to 3 and got stuck. What comes next, and why?
teach.praise: 10! Four ones make one group of four, so I move to the next place. Base-4 Land is fun!
teach.nudge: Which digits can you use in base 4? What happens when you have 4 ones?

learn.hook: Computers count with only two digits, 0 and 1. To a computer, 1010 means ten!
points: The base tells how many make one group before you move to the next place. Base 10 groups in tens, base 5 in fives and base 2 in twos.
In base 2 (binary) the place values are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ... So 1011 in base 2 = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11.
In base 5 the place values are 1, 5, 25, 125, ... and only the digits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 are used.
To write a number in base 2, break it into place values: 13 = 8 + 4 + 1, so 13 = 1101 in base 2.
Base 10 probably comes from our ten fingers, and base 60 still lives on in hours, minutes and seconds.

example.q: Write 13 in base 2.

learn.reallife: Every photo, song and game on a phone is stored as long strings of 0s and 1s. That is binary, base 2.

quiz.q: What is 1101 (base 2) in our base 10?
quiz.explain: The places are 8, 4, 2, 1. 1101 means 8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 13.
quiz.mistake: Just adds the digits (3) or reads it as a base-10 number

quiz.q: How is 6 written in base 2?
quiz.explain: 6 = 4 + 2. Places 4, 2, 1 get 1, 1, 0, so 6 = 110 in base 2.
quiz.mistake: Writes the digits in the wrong order or uses the place values wrongly

quiz.q: Which digits are used in base 5?
quiz.explain: In base 5, as soon as you reach 5 you make a new group, so only 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 are needed.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the base number itself is one of the digits

quiz.q: What is 32 (base 5) in base 10?
quiz.explain: 3 fives and 2 ones: 3 × 5 + 2 = 17.
quiz.mistake: Reads the number as base 10, or swaps the digits (2 × 5 + 3 = 13)

quiz.q: What are the first four place values in base 2, starting from the right?
quiz.explain: Each place is 2 times the one on its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ...
quiz.mistake: Adds 2 each time instead of multiplying by 2

quiz.q: Harpreet packs 19 laddoos in boxes of 5. How is 19 written in base 5?
quiz.explain: 19 = 3 boxes of 5 + 4 loose laddoos, so 19 = 34 in base 5. Check: 3 × 5 + 4 = 19.
quiz.mistake: Writes the remainder first, or uses the digit 9 which base 5 does not have

quiz.q: A movie lasts 150 minutes. How many hours and minutes is that?
quiz.explain: 150 = 2 × 60 + 30, so it is 2 hours and 30 minutes. Time works in base 60, not base 100.
quiz.mistake: Treats an hour as 100 minutes and reads 150 as 1 hour 50 minutes

quiz.q: What is the largest number (in base 10) that can be written using only 4 digits in base 2?
quiz.explain: The largest 4-digit binary number is 1111 = 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15. The next number, 16, needs 5 digits (10000).
quiz.mistake: Thinks 2⁴ = 16 itself fits in 4 binary digits

teach.ask: Gappu asks: How can a computer write the number 5 if it only knows 0 and 1?
teach.praise: Wow, 5 = 4 + 1, so in binary it is 101. Places go 1, 2, 4, 8! Computers are smart and so are you!
teach.nudge: What are the place values in base 2? Which of them add up to 5?

learn.hook: Why does an hour have 60 minutes and not 100? Blame (or thank!) the Mesopotamians of 4000 years ago.
points: The Mesopotamians (Babylonians) pressed wedge marks into clay: a thin wedge for 1 and a corner wedge for 10. Each place could hold any amount up to 59.
Their places stand for 1, 60, 60² = 3600, ... So '2 | 15' means 2 × 60 + 15 = 135.

Why 60? One idea: 60 has many factors (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, 30, 60), so halves, thirds, quarters and fifths are easy. Another: count the 12 finger segments of one hand with the thumb, and keep track on the 5 fingers of the other hand: 12 × 5 = 60.
Regroup at 60: 60 ones make one 60, and 60 sixties make one 3600.
At first they left a blank space for an empty place, which was confusing — '1  1' could be 61 or 3601. Later scribes used a special placeholder sign.

example.q: Write 4000 in the base-60 system.

learn.reallife: Clocks, angles (360°) and minutes of arc in astronomy still follow this base-60 idea.

quiz.q: What is 3 | 20 in the base-60 system?
quiz.explain: 3 sixties + 20 ones = 180 + 20 = 200.
quiz.mistake: Reads the places as base 10

quiz.q: What is 1 | 0 | 5 in the base-60 system?
quiz.mistake: Treats the third place as 100 instead of 3600

quiz.q: How is 150 written in the base-60 system?
quiz.mistake: Splits the number by base-10 digits

quiz.q: How many factors does 60 have?
quiz.explain: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, 30, 60 — twelve factors. That is one reason base 60 is handy.
quiz.mistake: Misses some factor pairs

quiz.q: Which finger-counting idea could explain base 60?
options: 12 finger segments on one hand × 5 fingers on the other
quiz.explain: Using the thumb to count the 3 segments of each of 4 fingers gives 12; the other hand's 5 fingers count dozens: 12 × 5 = 60.
quiz.mistake: Picks a product that does not make 60

quiz.q: Without a placeholder, '1  1' (with a gap) could mean 61 or which other number?
quiz.explain: The gap might be an empty 60s place: 1 × 3600 + 0 × 60 + 1 = 3601.
quiz.mistake: Reads the gap as a base-10 zero

quiz.q: A scribe adds 45 ones and 30 ones. After regrouping, what does he write?
quiz.explain: 45 + 30 = 75 ones = 1 sixty and 15 ones.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to regroup at 60

quiz.q: What is the largest amount a single place can hold in the base-60 system?
quiz.explain: Once a place reaches 60, it is regrouped into one of the next place, so a place holds 0 to 59.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the base itself can sit in one place

teach.ask: Gappu wonders why one hour has 60 minutes. Can you tell him the story?
teach.praise: So 60 was chosen long ago because it splits nicely into many parts. I'll never look at a clock the same way!
teach.nudge: Which old civilisation counted in 60s, and why is 60 such a handy number?

topics.title: Maya numbers, Chinese rods and the road to zero

learn.hook: The Maya drew a shell for zero, and Chinese scholars counted with bamboo rods. Each idea was a step towards our 0–9 system.
points: Maya numbers use a dot for 1, a bar for 5 and a shell for 0. So 3 bars and 4 dots = 15 + 4 = 19.
Maya places are stacked from the bottom up and stand for 1, 20, 360 (= 18 × 20, linked to their calendar), 7200, ...

Chinese rod numerals are base 10 with place value. Ones, hundreds and ten-thousands use vertical rods (zong); tens and thousands use horizontal rods (heng). Alternating stops neighbouring digits from running together; an empty place was left blank.

The big story: one-to-one tallies → grouping → special symbols for groups (landmarks) → landmarks as powers of a base → place value → zero as a digit and as a number. The Indian system has every step.

example.q: A Maya number has 1 dot in the 360s place, a shell in the 20s place and 2 bars in the ones place. What is it?

learn.reallife: Ruins of Maya cities in Central America still have carved numbers in dots and bars for dates.

games.title: Steps towards our number system
items: One-to-one tally marks
Grouping in bundles
Landmark symbols for groups
Landmarks as powers of a base
Place value with a zero

quiz.q: What is the Maya digit made of 3 bars and 2 dots?
quiz.explain: Each bar is 5 and each dot is 1: 15 + 2 = 17.
quiz.mistake: Counts the marks instead of their values

quiz.q: Maya places go 1, 20, ... What is the third place?
quiz.explain: The Maya third place is 18 × 20 = 360, linked to their calendar, not 20 × 20.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every place is 20 times the one before

quiz.q: A Maya number has 1 dot in the 360s place, a shell in the 20s place and 2 bars in the ones place. What is it?
quiz.mistake: Treats the shell as 1 or reads the bars as 2

quiz.q: A Maya number has 2 dots in the 20s place and 1 bar and 1 dot in the ones place. What is it?
quiz.mistake: Uses 10 for the second place instead of 20

quiz.q: Which symbol did the Maya use for zero?
quiz.explain: The Maya drew a shell to show an empty place — an early zero.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the zero sign with the 1 and 5 signs

quiz.q: In Chinese rod numerals, how is the tens digit written?
quiz.explain: Ones use vertical rods, tens use horizontal rods, hundreds vertical again, and so on.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the Chinese and Maya systems

quiz.q: Why did Chinese rod numerals switch between vertical and horizontal rods?
options: So that neighbouring digits do not run together
quiz.explain: Alternating the rod direction from place to place keeps the digits apart and readable.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the direction changes the value of the digit

quiz.q: Which step came last in the story of number systems?
options: Place value with zero as a digit
quiz.explain: Tallies and grouping came first, then landmark symbols, then bases, and finally place value with zero.
steps: tally → group → landmark → base → place value → zero
quiz.mistake: Thinks zero was invented early

teach.ask: Gappu thinks every old number system was just like ours. Tell me how the Maya and Chinese systems were different!
teach.praise: Wow — dots, bars and shells, and rods turned two ways! Every culture found its own clever path.
teach.nudge: What symbols did the Maya use? How did Chinese rods show different places?

topics.title: Place value and the story of zero

learn.hook: With just ten symbols, 0 to 9, you can write any number you can imagine. The secret? Place value, and a humble little zero.
points: In a place value system, a digit's value depends on its position. In 555 the three 5s mean 500, 50 and 5.
Our system is base 10: each place is worth 10 times the place on its right (ones, tens, hundreds, thousands...).
Zero is a placeholder: 205 and 25 are different numbers because the 0 keeps the tens place empty.
About 4000 years ago the Babylonians used place value with base 60. The Maya of Central America used base 20 and drew a shell for zero.
Indian mathematicians built the base-10 system with zero as a number. Brahmagupta (7th century CE) wrote rules like a + 0 = a and a − a = 0. These numerals travelled through the Arab world to Europe.

example.q: Write 40,305 in expanded form using powers of 10.
steps: Zeros add nothing, but they keep the other digits in their places

learn.reallife: Every price tag, PIN code and cricket score uses place value. One extra zero turns a ₹500 note into ₹5000!

quiz.q: What is the value of the digit 6 in 4,60,213?
quiz.explain: Reading the places of 4,60,213 from the left: lakh, ten-thousand, thousand, hundred, ten, one. The 6 is in the ten-thousands place, so it is worth 60,000.
quiz.mistake: Reads the place of the digit wrongly because of the Indian commas

quiz.q: Which number is 3 × 10³ + 5 × 10 + 2?
quiz.explain: 3 × 1000 = 3000, 5 × 10 = 50 and 2 more. 3000 + 50 + 2 = 3052. The hundreds place is empty, so it gets a 0.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the zero in the empty hundreds place

quiz.q: Why does a place value system need a zero?
options: To show an empty place, like the tens place in 405
To make every number look bigger
To stand for the number ten
quiz.explain: Without 0, 405 and 45 would look the same. Zero holds an empty place so the other digits stay in the right positions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks zero is just 'nothing' and has no job to do

quiz.q: The Babylonians counted in base 60. A number shows 2 in the 'sixties' place and 5 in the ones place. What is it in our numbers?
quiz.explain: 2 sixties and 5 ones = 2 × 60 + 5 = 125. It is just like 2 minutes 5 seconds = 125 seconds.
quiz.mistake: Reads the digits as if they were in base 10

quiz.q: Which Indian mathematician wrote rules for working with zero, such as a − a = 0, in the 7th century CE?
quiz.explain: Brahmagupta wrote rules for adding, subtracting and multiplying with zero in 628 CE, treating zero as a number.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Indian mathematicians with Greek ones

quiz.q: The Maya counted in base 20. A Maya number has 3 in the 'twenties' place and 4 in the ones place. What is it in our numbers?
quiz.explain: 3 twenties and 4 ones = 3 × 20 + 4 = 64.
quiz.mistake: Reads the digits as base 10 and gets 34

quiz.q: We still use the Babylonian base 60 for time. How many seconds are there in 1 hour?
quiz.explain: 1 hour = 60 minutes and each minute has 60 seconds, so 60 × 60 = 3600 seconds.
quiz.mistake: Adds 60 + 60 or multiplies by 10 instead of 60

quiz.q: Meena writes 'five thousand and seven' as 57. What did she forget?
options: Zeros to hold the empty hundreds and tens places
That place value works only for small numbers
quiz.explain: Five thousand and seven is 5007. The hundreds and tens places are empty, so they need zeros.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that empty places must be filled with zero

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: 205 and 25 use the same digits 2 and 5. Why are they different numbers?
teach.praise: I see! In 205 the 0 holds the tens place empty, so the 2 moves to the hundreds place. Place value is powerful!
teach.nudge: Where does the 2 sit in 205, and where does it sit in 25? What is the 0 doing?

learn.hook: The blackboard, your maths notebook, a door, and the paper kite you fly on Makar Sankranti are all quadrilaterals. But they are not all the same kind!
points: A quadrilateral is a closed figure with 4 straight sides, 4 vertices, 4 angles and 2 diagonals.
A trapezium has a pair of parallel sides. A parallelogram has both pairs of opposite sides parallel.
A rectangle is a parallelogram with all four angles 90°. A rhombus is a parallelogram with all four sides equal.
A square has all sides equal and all angles 90°, so every square is a rectangle and also a rhombus.
A kite has two pairs of equal sides, and each pair sits next to each other (adjacent).

example.q: A quadrilateral has all four sides 5 cm, and one of its angles is 90°. Which quadrilateral is it?
steps: All sides equal, so it is a rhombus, which is a parallelogram
In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal and neighbouring angles add to 180°
So one 90° angle makes all four angles 90°
All sides equal and all angles 90° means a square

learn.reallife: Carpenters check that a door frame is a true rectangle, and rangoli makers love rhombus and kite patterns.

A square has all four sides equal.
A quadrilateral has 3 diagonals.
A quadrilateral has exactly 2 diagonals.

quiz.q: Which quadrilateral has all four sides equal and all four angles equal to 90°?
quiz.explain: A square has equal sides like a rhombus and right angles like a rectangle.
quiz.mistake: Picks rhombus, forgetting that a rhombus need not have right angles

quiz.q: How many diagonals does a quadrilateral have?
quiz.explain: Each vertex joins only the opposite vertex by a diagonal. That gives 2 diagonals, like AC and BD.
steps: From A: only AC is a diagonal
AC and BD are counted once each: 2
quiz.mistake: Counts each diagonal twice or confuses diagonals with sides

quiz.q: Arjun's paper kite has sides 30 cm, 30 cm, 45 cm and 45 cm. What is its perimeter?
quiz.explain: Perimeter is the sum of all four sides: 30 + 30 + 45 + 45 = 150 cm.
quiz.mistake: Adds only two sides (75 cm)

quiz.q: A quadrilateral has opposite sides parallel and all angles 90°. Its neighbouring sides are 4 cm and 7 cm. What is it?
quiz.explain: Four right angles with unequal neighbouring sides make a rectangle, not a square.
quiz.mistake: Calls every shape with right angles a square

quiz.q: Which statement is true?
quiz.explain: A square has all four sides equal, so it is always a rhombus. A rhombus need not have right angles, so it is not always a square.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the 'special case' relationship between square and rhombus

quiz.q: One side of a rhombus is 6 cm. What is its perimeter?
quiz.explain: All four sides of a rhombus are equal, so the perimeter is 4 × 6 = 24 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses only two sides, or squares the side (36)

quiz.q: Which quadrilateral can have exactly one pair of parallel sides?
quiz.explain: Parallelograms, rhombuses and rectangles always have two pairs of parallel sides. A trapezium can have just one pair.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a rhombus or rectangle has only one pair of parallel sides

quiz.q: Three angles of a quadrilateral are 80°, 95° and 110°. What is the fourth angle?
quiz.explain: The angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360°. 80 + 95 + 110 = 285, and 360 − 285 = 75°.
quiz.mistake: Uses 180° (the triangle angle sum) or makes an adding slip

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: My friend says a square is a rectangle. That sounds wrong! Is it?
teach.praise: Yes! A square has four right angles and equal opposite sides, so it is a special kind of rectangle. Thanks!
teach.nudge: What does a shape need to be a rectangle? Does a square have those things?

learn.hook: Start with just one rule — 'all four angles are right angles' — and you can prove everything else about a rectangle. Like a detective!
points: Definition: a rectangle is a quadrilateral with four right angles. Everything else is deduced from this.
Opposite sides are parallel: the two angles on one side add to 90° + 90° = 180°, and when co-interior angles add to 180°, the lines are parallel.
Opposite sides are equal: the diagonal AC splits rectangle ABCD into triangles ABC and CDA, which are congruent (AC is common and the alternate angles are equal). So AB = CD and BC = DA.
If a quadrilateral has three right angles, the fourth is 360° − 270° = 90°, so it must be a rectangle.
The diagonals are equal and bisect each other, so OA = OB = OC = OD. That makes triangles like AOB isosceles — handy for finding angles.

example.q: In rectangle ABCD the diagonals meet at O and ∠OAB = 30°. Find ∠OBA and ∠AOB.

learn.reallife: Carpenters check a door frame is a true rectangle by measuring both diagonals — if they are equal, the corners are right angles.

items.text: Three angles are 90°, so the fourth is ___

games.title: Prove it!
items: A rectangle's opposite sides are parallel because co-interior angles add to 180°.
The diagonal of a rectangle makes two congruent triangles.
ΔABC ≅ ΔCDA.
A quadrilateral with three right angles might have a fourth angle of 100°.
In a rectangle, the triangles formed by the diagonals at O are always equilateral.
They are isosceles; equilateral only when the angle at O is 60°.

quiz.q: A quadrilateral has three right angles. What is its fourth angle?
quiz.explain: The angles add to 360°, so the fourth is 360° − 3 × 90° = 90°.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the angle sum of a quadrilateral is 360°

quiz.q: Why are the opposite sides of a rectangle parallel?
options: Because all four sides are equal
The two angles on the same side add up to 180°
quiz.explain: Each pair of neighbouring angles is 90° + 90° = 180°. Co-interior angles adding to 180° means the lines are parallel.
quiz.mistake: Uses a property that has not yet been proved

quiz.q: In rectangle ABCD the diagonals meet at O and ∠OAB = 35°. What is ∠OBA?
quiz.explain: OA = OB, so triangle OAB is isosceles and its base angles are equal: ∠OBA = 35°.
quiz.mistake: Takes the complement 90° − 35° instead

quiz.q: In rectangle ABCD the diagonals meet at O and ∠OAB = 35°. What is ∠AOB?
quiz.mistake: Assumes the diagonals of a rectangle meet at 90°

quiz.q: In rectangle ABCD the diagonals meet at O and ∠OAB = 35°. What is ∠OAD?
quiz.mistake: Thinks the diagonal bisects the right angle

quiz.q: In rectangle ABCD, diagonal AC = 10 cm. The diagonals meet at O. How long is OB?
quiz.explain: The diagonals are equal (BD = 10 cm) and bisect each other, so OB = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the diagonals bisect each other

quiz.q: To show that opposite sides of rectangle ABCD are equal, which triangles do we prove congruent?
options: ΔABC and ΔCDA, made by diagonal AC
quiz.explain: Diagonal AC splits the rectangle into ΔABC and ΔCDA. They are congruent, so AB = CD and BC = DA.
quiz.mistake: Uses triangles that do not contain both pairs of sides

quiz.q: In rectangle ABCD the diagonals meet at O and ∠AOB = 60°. If AB = 4 cm, how long is diagonal AC?
quiz.explain: OA = OB and ∠AOB = 60°, so the base angles are 60° too: triangle AOB is equilateral. OA = AB = 4 cm, and AC = 2 × OA = 8 cm.
quiz.mistake: Stops at OA instead of doubling to get the full diagonal

teach.ask: Gappu says: 'A rectangle has opposite sides equal — everyone just knows that.' How can you PROVE it?
teach.praise: Ooh, a proof! The diagonal makes two congruent triangles, so the matching sides must be equal.
teach.nudge: What could you draw inside the rectangle to make two triangles?

learn.hook: Cross two sticks, join their ends with a thread — and you have made a quadrilateral. Which one? It depends on how you cross the sticks!
points: Two equal lines that bisect each other (at any angle) give a rectangle when their ends are joined. Two equal sticks tied at their midpoints with a thread around the ends make a right angle at every corner.
Draw two perpendicular diameters of a circle and join their ends: you get a square, because the diagonals are equal, bisect each other and meet at 90°.
Any two lines that bisect each other give a parallelogram. If they bisect each other at right angles (but are unequal), you get a rhombus.
Kite from its diagonals: make one diagonal the perpendicular bisector of the other, but do not cut the first one in half.
Square from one diagonal, without a protractor: draw diagonal AC, construct its perpendicular bisector with a compass, then mark B and D on it at a distance of half of AC from the centre.

example.q: Diagonals of 8 cm and 8 cm bisect each other at 50°. Which quadrilateral do you get?
steps: So it is a rectangle (not a square)

learn.reallife: Kite makers tie two sticks in a cross before pasting the paper — how they cross them decides the shape of the kite!

games.title: Diagonals decide the shape
pairs: Equal, bisect each other, not at 90°

One is the perpendicular bisector of the other only

Construct the perpendicular bisector of AC with a compass

quiz.q: Diagonals of 6 cm and 10 cm bisect each other at right angles. Which quadrilateral is formed?
quiz.explain: Diagonals that bisect each other at 90° give a rhombus; they are unequal, so it is not a square.
quiz.mistake: Thinks perpendicular diagonals always make a square

quiz.q: Diagonals of 7 cm and 7 cm bisect each other at right angles. Which quadrilateral is formed?
options: Rhombus that is not a square
Rectangle that is not a square
Kite that is not a rhombus
quiz.explain: Equal diagonals give a rectangle; perpendicular bisecting diagonals give a rhombus. Both together: a square.
quiz.mistake: Notices only one of the two properties

quiz.q: Diagonals of 5 cm and 9 cm bisect each other at 70°. Which quadrilateral is formed?
quiz.explain: Diagonals that only bisect each other (unequal, not perpendicular) give a general parallelogram.
steps: Not equal, not 90° → nothing more special
quiz.mistake: Assumes any crossing diagonals make a rhombus

quiz.q: Two perpendicular diameters of a circle with radius 5 cm are joined at their ends. How long is each diagonal of the square formed?
quiz.explain: Each diagonal is a diameter: 2 × 5 = 10 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses the radius as the diagonal

quiz.q: To build a square from a 6 cm diagonal AC, how far from the centre O should B and D be marked?
quiz.explain: A square's diagonals are equal and bisect each other, so OB = OD = OA = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 cm.
quiz.mistake: Marks B and D at the full diagonal length

quiz.q: Diagonal BD is cut into two equal parts of 4 cm by diagonal AC at right angles, but AC is split into 3 cm and 7 cm. What shape is ABCD?
quiz.explain: AC is the perpendicular bisector of BD, but BD does not bisect AC. That is a kite.
steps: AC itself is not bisected → kite
quiz.mistake: Thinks the shape must be a rhombus because the diagonals are perpendicular

quiz.q: Ravi crosses two equal sticks at their midpoints and stretches a thread around their ends. What angle does the thread make at each corner?
quiz.explain: Equal diagonals that bisect each other give a rectangle, so every corner is a right angle.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the corner angle depends on how the sticks are crossed

quiz.q: Which pair of diagonals can NEVER make a rectangle?
options: Diagonals of 6 cm and 6 cm crossing at their midpoints
Diagonals of 9 cm and 9 cm crossing at their midpoints at 30°
Diagonals of 4 cm and 4 cm crossing at their midpoints at 90°
quiz.explain: A rectangle's diagonals must be equal. 5 cm and 8 cm are unequal, so they can never form a rectangle.
steps: Rectangle needs equal diagonals that bisect each other
quiz.mistake: Forgets that a square is also a rectangle

teach.ask: Gappu has two equal straws and some string. How can he make a rectangle without a protractor?
teach.praise: Cross them at their middles and tie the ends! Equal diagonals that bisect each other make a rectangle.
teach.nudge: Where should the two straws cross each other?

learn.hook: Draw any quadrilateral at all, even a wonky one. Tear off its four corners and put them together: they always make a full turn of 360°!
points: The angles of every quadrilateral add up to 360°, because a diagonal splits it into two triangles: 180° + 180°.
Rectangle: the diagonals are equal and bisect each other.
Rhombus: the diagonals bisect each other at right angles (they are perpendicular), and each diagonal bisects the angles at its ends.
Square: the diagonals are equal, perpendicular and bisect each other. It has every property of a rectangle and a rhombus.
Kite: the diagonals are perpendicular, and one diagonal cuts the other in half.

example.q: The angles of a quadrilateral are x, 2x, 3x and 4x. Find each angle.

learn.reallife: Tile makers and architects use the 360° rule to check that floor tiles and window frames fit together with no gaps.

games.title: From general to special
games.prompt: Each shape is a special kind of the one before it. Start with the most general.
items: Quadrilateral
Parallelogram
Rhombus

quiz.q: Three angles of a quadrilateral are 90°, 90° and 120°. What is the fourth angle?
quiz.explain: The four angles add up to 360°. 90 + 90 + 120 = 300, so the fourth angle is 360 − 300 = 60°.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the missing angle must also be 90°

quiz.q: The angles of a quadrilateral are x, 2x, 3x and 4x. What is the largest angle?
quiz.explain: 10x = 360°, so x = 36° and the largest angle is 4x = 144°.
quiz.mistake: Stops at x = 36° and forgets to find 4x

quiz.q: In rectangle ABCD, diagonal AC is 13 cm. How long is diagonal BD?
quiz.explain: The diagonals of a rectangle are equal, so BD = AC = 13 cm.
quiz.mistake: Halves the diagonal, mixing up 'equal' with 'bisect each other'

quiz.q: At what angle do the diagonals of a rhombus cross each other?
quiz.explain: The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular, so they always cross at 90°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the angle depends on the side length

quiz.q: Which quadrilateral always has diagonals that are equal AND perpendicular?
quiz.explain: A rectangle has equal diagonals and a rhombus has perpendicular ones. Only a square always has both.
quiz.mistake: Remembers only one of the two diagonal properties

quiz.q: Why do the angles of any quadrilateral add up to 360°?
options: It always has four right angles
A diagonal splits it into two triangles, and 180° + 180° = 360°
Every quadrilateral fits exactly inside a circle
Its four sides add up to 360
quiz.explain: Each triangle has an angle sum of 180°. A diagonal cuts any quadrilateral into two triangles, so the total is 360°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the rule only works because squares have four 90° angles

quiz.q: In rhombus PQRS, ∠P = 120°. The diagonal PR bisects ∠P. What angle does PR make with side PQ?
quiz.explain: A diagonal of a rhombus bisects the angle at its end, so it splits 120° into two angles of 60°.
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'bisects the angle' with 'is perpendicular'

quiz.q: Aisha draws a quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect each other at right angles but are NOT equal. What shape is it?
quiz.explain: Diagonals that bisect each other at 90° make a rhombus. Since they are not equal, it cannot be a square.
quiz.mistake: Picks kite, but in a kite only one diagonal is cut in half

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: My quadrilateral is all crooked. How can its angles still add up to 360°?
teach.praise: Cut it with a diagonal into two triangles, each with 180°, so 360° in total. It works for any shape!
teach.nudge: What happens if you draw a line from one corner to the opposite corner? What shapes do you get?

learn.hook: Push a rectangular photo frame from one corner and it leans over, but its opposite sides stay parallel. You have made a parallelogram!
points: In a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal and parallel.
Opposite angles are equal.
Neighbouring (adjacent) angles add up to 180°.
The diagonals bisect each other: they cut each other exactly in half. They are not always equal.
Why? A diagonal splits a parallelogram into two identical (congruent) triangles.

example.q: In parallelogram PQRS, ∠P = 70°. Find ∠Q, ∠R and ∠S.

learn.reallife: Folding stools, car jacks and the scissor-lift used to fix street lights all use parallelograms that change shape but keep opposite sides parallel.

items.text: If one angle of a parallelogram is 65°, its neighbouring angle is ___
Opposite angles of a parallelogram are ___
The diagonals of a parallelogram ___ each other

items.q: Diagonal is 14 cm. Length from end to centre?
Neighbouring angles are x and 3x. Find x.

quiz.q: In parallelogram ABCD, ∠A = 65°. What is ∠C?
quiz.explain: ∠A and ∠C are opposite angles, and opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal.
quiz.mistake: Thinks opposite angles add to 180° instead of being equal

quiz.q: In parallelogram ABCD, ∠A = 65°. What is ∠B?
quiz.explain: ∠A and ∠B are neighbouring angles, so they add up to 180°. ∠B = 180° − 65° = 115°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all angles of a parallelogram are equal, or subtracts from 90°

quiz.q: The diagonals of parallelogram PQRS meet at O. If PR = 16 cm, how long is PO?
quiz.explain: The diagonals bisect each other, so O is the midpoint of PR. PO = 16 ÷ 2 = 8 cm.
steps: O is the midpoint of PR
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the diagonals cut each other in half

quiz.q: Two neighbouring angles of a parallelogram are in the ratio 2 : 3. What is the smaller angle?
quiz.explain: Neighbouring angles add to 180°. Split 180° in the ratio 2 : 3: 180 ÷ 5 = 36, so the angles are 72° and 108°.
quiz.mistake: Uses 360° instead of 180° for neighbouring angles (gets 144°)

quiz.q: Joseph's garden gate is a parallelogram with sides 120 cm and 80 cm. What is its perimeter?
quiz.explain: Opposite sides are equal, so the perimeter is 2 × (120 + 80) = 400 cm.
quiz.mistake: Adds only two sides, or multiplies the sides like an area

quiz.q: Which property is NOT always true for a parallelogram?
quiz.explain: In a leaning parallelogram one diagonal is clearly longer than the other. Equal diagonals happen only when it is a rectangle.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up 'diagonals bisect each other' with 'diagonals are equal'

quiz.q: One angle of a parallelogram is 90°. What can you say about its other angles?
quiz.explain: The opposite angle is also 90°, and each neighbouring angle is 180° − 90° = 90°. So all four are right angles: it is a rectangle.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that neighbouring angles must add up to 180°

quiz.q: Two neighbouring angles of a parallelogram are (x + 20)° and (2x + 10)°. What is x?
quiz.explain: Neighbouring angles add to 180°: 3x + 30 = 180, so 3x = 150 and x = 50. The angles are 70° and 110°.
quiz.mistake: Sets the two angles equal to each other instead of adding them to 180°

teach.ask: Gappu asks: In a parallelogram, if I know one angle is 70°, how can I find all the other angles?
teach.praise: Opposite angles are equal and neighbouring ones add to 180°, so 70°, 110°, 70°, 110°. Super!
teach.nudge: What do you know about the angle opposite to 70°? And about the angles next to it?

learn.hook: Take two identical paper triangles and slide them together. You can make a rectangle, a kite or a parallelogram — depending on how you join them!
points: On a geoboard (pins in a square grid), rubber bands make squares, rectangles, parallelograms, kites and trapeziums. Tilted squares can be made too.
To find the area of a tilted shape on a geoboard, draw a box around it and subtract the corner triangles.
Two congruent right triangles joined along the longest side: turned half-way round, they make a rectangle; as mirror images, they make a kite.
Two congruent triangles joined along any side, one turned half-way round, always make a parallelogram.
Joining the midpoints of the sides of a square gives a smaller, tilted square with exactly half the area.

example.q: A square has side 10 cm. Its side midpoints are joined. What is the area of the new square?
steps: The four corner triangles together make half of it

learn.reallife: Tile and rangoli designs often use squares inside squares made by joining midpoints.

games.title: Join two congruent triangles
pairs: Right triangles on the long side, one turned round
Right triangles on the long side, mirror images
Any triangles on a side, one turned round
Midpoints of a square's sides joined

games.title: Geoboard games
items: You can make a tilted square on a geoboard.
For example, with corners (0,0), (2,1), (1,3), (−1,2).
Joining midpoints of a square's sides gives a rectangle that is not a square.
It gives a square, tilted by 45°.
Two congruent triangles can always be joined to make a parallelogram.
Turn one half-way round and join along a side.
The midpoint square has one quarter of the area of the big square.
It has half the area.

quiz.q: Two congruent right triangles are joined along their longest side, with one turned half-way round. What shape forms?
quiz.explain: The two right angles end up at opposite corners and all four angles become 90°, giving a rectangle.
steps: Turning one triangle puts the two right angles at opposite corners
Each other corner gets the two acute angles, which add to 90°
quiz.mistake: Mixes up turning with flipping (mirror image)

quiz.q: Two congruent right triangles are joined along their longest side as mirror images. What shape forms?
quiz.explain: Mirror images put equal sides next to each other: sides a, a, b, b — that is a kite.
steps: Equal sides meet at the same corner
Two pairs of equal neighbouring sides → kite
quiz.mistake: Assumes every join gives a rectangle

quiz.q: Two congruent triangles are joined along a side, with one turned half-way round. What shape always forms?
quiz.explain: Turning one triangle makes the opposite sides equal, so the shape is a parallelogram.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the shape must have equal sides all round

quiz.q: A square has side 10 cm. Joining the midpoints of its sides makes a new square. What is its area?
quiz.explain: The four corner triangles fill exactly half of the big square, so the new square is 100 ÷ 2 = 50 cm².
quiz.mistake: Thinks the new square has half the side, so a quarter of the area

quiz.q: Joining the midpoints of a square with side 6 cm makes a new square. What is its area?
quiz.explain: Big square = 36 cm², and the midpoint square has half of it: 18 cm².
quiz.mistake: Takes a quarter of the area

quiz.q: On a geoboard, a rectangle is 3 units long and 2 units wide. What is its area?
quiz.explain: Area = 3 × 2 = 6 square units.
quiz.mistake: Adds the sides or finds the perimeter

quiz.q: What shape do you get by joining the midpoints of the sides of a square?
options: A rectangle that is not a square
A kite that is not a rhombus
quiz.explain: All four new sides are equal and all angles are 90°, so it is a square standing on a corner.
steps: Each new side is the long side of a corner triangle
quiz.mistake: Thinks tilting changes the type of shape

quiz.q: On a geoboard, a tilted square has corners at (0,0), (2,1), (1,3) and (−1,2). What is its area?
quiz.explain: A 3 × 3 box around it has area 9. The 4 corner triangles each have area 1. So the square is 9 − 4 = 5.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the whole unit squares inside

teach.ask: Gappu cut two identical triangles from paper. How many different quadrilaterals can he make?
teach.praise: So turning gives a parallelogram (or rectangle), and flipping gives a kite. Paper magic!
teach.nudge: What happens if you turn one triangle round? What if you flip it like a mirror?

learn.hook: The kite you fly at Makar Sankranti and the trapezium-shaped dhol stand both have their own special rules. Let's discover them!
points: A kite ABCD has two pairs of equal neighbouring sides: AB = AD and CB = CD.
In a kite, the diagonal AC (joining the corners where equal sides meet) is the perpendicular bisector of the other diagonal BD. Also ∠B = ∠D.
A trapezium has at least one pair of parallel sides. If AB ∥ DC, the two angles on each slanting side add to 180°: ∠A + ∠D = 180° and ∠B + ∠C = 180°.
An isosceles trapezium has its non-parallel sides equal. Its base angles are equal (∠A = ∠B and ∠C = ∠D), and its diagonals are equal.

example.q: In trapezium ABCD, AB ∥ DC and ∠A = 65°. Find ∠D.
steps: ∠A and ∠D are on the same slanting side
They are co-interior angles, so they add to 180°

learn.reallife: Many bridges and the sides of a handbag are trapeziums; festival kites are, of course, kites!

games.title: Kite or trapezium?
items: Two pairs of equal neighbouring sides
One diagonal is the perpendicular bisector of the other
One pair of opposite angles equal (between unequal sides)
At least one pair of parallel sides
Angles on a slanting side add to 180°
Isosceles type has equal base angles

quiz.q: In trapezium ABCD, AB ∥ DC and ∠A = 65°. What is ∠D?
quiz.explain: ∠A and ∠D are co-interior angles between the parallel sides, so ∠D = 180° − 65° = 115°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the angles on a slanting side are equal

quiz.q: In isosceles trapezium PQRS, PQ ∥ SR and ∠P = 70°. What is ∠R?
quiz.explain: Base angles are equal, so ∠Q = 70°. ∠Q and ∠R are on the same slanting side, so ∠R = 180° − 70° = 110°.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all four angles are equal

quiz.q: In kite ABCD, AB = AD and CB = CD. If ∠B = 100°, what is ∠D?
quiz.explain: In a kite the angles between the unequal sides are equal: ∠B = ∠D = 100°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks opposite angles of a kite add to 180°

quiz.q: In kite ABCD (AB = AD, CB = CD), the diagonals meet at O and BD = 12 cm. How long is BO?
quiz.explain: Diagonal AC is the perpendicular bisector of BD, so BO = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm.
quiz.mistake: Forgets which diagonal is bisected

quiz.q: In kite ABCD, ∠A = 60° and ∠B = ∠D = 110°. What is ∠C?
quiz.mistake: Thinks ∠A and ∠C must be equal

quiz.q: Which diagonal of kite ABCD (with AB = AD and CB = CD) is cut into two equal halves?
options: AC, the diagonal joining the corners where equal sides meet
BD, the diagonal joining the corners between unequal sides
quiz.explain: AC is the line of symmetry; it cuts BD in half at right angles. AC itself is usually not bisected.
steps: AC is the line of symmetry
quiz.mistake: Thinks a kite's diagonals bisect each other like a parallelogram's

quiz.q: In trapezium ABCD, AB ∥ DC and ∠B is twice ∠C. What is ∠C?
quiz.mistake: Forgets that co-interior angles add to 180°

quiz.q: An isosceles trapezium has parallel sides of 10 cm and 4 cm, and each slanting side is 5 cm. What is its perimeter?
quiz.explain: Both slanting sides are 5 cm: 10 + 4 + 5 + 5 = 24 cm.
quiz.mistake: Counts the equal slanting side only once

teach.ask: Gappu is flying a kite with two short sides and two long sides. What special things are true about its diagonals?
teach.praise: So one diagonal is the line of symmetry and cuts the other in half at 90°. My kite flies better already!
teach.nudge: Do the diagonals of a kite meet at a right angle? Which one gets cut in half?

learn.hook: Is a square a kite? Is a rhombus a parallelogram? Quadrilaterals have a family tree, and some shapes belong to many families at once!
points: Family links: every square is a rectangle and a rhombus; every rectangle and every rhombus is a parallelogram; every rhombus (so every square) is also a kite.
In a Venn diagram, the squares sit where the rectangles and rhombuses overlap, all inside the parallelograms; the rhombuses also sit inside the kites.

Judge by diagonals: bisect each other → parallelogram; equal and bisect each other → rectangle; bisect each other at 90° → rhombus; both → square; one is the perpendicular bisector of the other → kite.
If both pairs of opposite angles are equal, the shape is a parallelogram. Perpendicular diagonals alone do NOT make a rhombus — a kite has them too.

Proof: if AB = CD and BC = DA, draw diagonal AC. Triangles ABC and CDA are congruent (SSS), so ∠BAC = ∠DCA. These are alternate angles, so AB ∥ DC; in the same way AD ∥ BC. So the shape is a parallelogram.

example.q: A rectangle has two neighbouring sides equal. What is it?
steps: A rectangle has 4 right angles and opposite sides equal
Neighbouring sides equal → all four sides equal
4 equal sides and 4 right angles → square

learn.reallife: Sorting shapes into families is like sorting cousins and siblings in a family tree at a wedding!

games.title: Always a parallelogram?
items: Square
Rectangle
Rhombus
Quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides equal
Kite
Trapezium
Quadrilateral with perpendicular diagonals
Quadrilateral with one pair of equal sides

games.title: Family facts
items: Every rhombus is a kite.
Its neighbouring sides are equal in pairs (in fact all four are equal).
Every kite is a rhombus.
A kite can have sides 3, 3, 5, 5.
Equal diagonals that bisect each other always give a rectangle.
That is the rectangle's diagonal property.
Perpendicular diagonals always give a rhombus.
A kite also has perpendicular diagonals.
A square belongs to the rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram and kite families.
It has every one of their properties.

quiz.q: Which family statement is true?
quiz.explain: A rhombus has two pairs of equal neighbouring sides, so it is a kite. The others fail for some shapes.
steps: So AB = AD and CB = CD → kite
quiz.mistake: Reverses a family link

quiz.q: A quadrilateral's diagonals are equal and bisect each other. What must it be?
quiz.explain: Equal diagonals that bisect each other are the mark of a rectangle (a square is a special case).
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the rectangle and rhombus diagonal properties

quiz.q: A quadrilateral's diagonals are perpendicular but do NOT bisect each other. What could it be?
quiz.explain: Rhombuses and squares have diagonals that bisect each other. A kite has perpendicular diagonals where only one is bisected.
quiz.mistake: Thinks perpendicular diagonals must give a rhombus

quiz.q: Both pairs of opposite angles of a quadrilateral are equal. What must it be?
options: A trapezium that is not a parallelogram
quiz.explain: If ∠A = ∠C and ∠B = ∠D, then ∠A + ∠B = 180°, so the opposite sides are parallel — a parallelogram.
quiz.mistake: Does not use the 360° angle sum

quiz.q: To prove that a quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides equal is a parallelogram, which congruence rule is used?
quiz.explain: Diagonal AC gives triangles with AB = CD, BC = DA and AC common — all three sides equal, so SSS.
steps: AB = CD, BC = DA, AC = AC
quiz.mistake: Picks a rule that does not fit the known facts

quiz.q: In the Venn diagram of quadrilaterals, which shapes are in both the rectangle circle and the rhombus circle?
quiz.explain: A shape with 4 right angles and 4 equal sides is a square.
quiz.mistake: Thinks rectangles and rhombuses never overlap

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT always a parallelogram?
quiz.explain: A kite such as one with sides 3, 3, 5, 5 has no parallel sides. The others always have both pairs of opposite sides parallel.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every symmetric shape is a parallelogram

quiz.q: A rectangle is also a kite. What must it be?
options: A rhombus that is not a square
A rectangle that is not a square
quiz.explain: Being a kite means two neighbouring sides are equal. A rectangle with neighbouring sides equal has all sides equal — a square.
quiz.mistake: Does not combine the two sets of properties

teach.ask: Gappu thinks a square can belong to only one family. How many families does a square really belong to?
teach.praise: A square is a rectangle, a rhombus, a parallelogram AND a kite — it belongs to every family!
teach.nudge: Does a square have all the properties of a rectangle? Of a rhombus?

learn.hook: 15 = 7 + 8 = 4 + 5 + 6 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5. Three ways! But try as hard as you like — you can never do it for 16.
points: Many numbers can be written as a sum of two or more consecutive natural numbers: 9 = 4 + 5 = 2 + 3 + 4, and 15 has three such ways.
Every odd number above 1 works with two terms: 2k + 1 = k + (k + 1). Powers of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, ...) can never be written this way.
Algebra for consecutive numbers: n, n + 1, n + 2 add to 3n + 3 = 3(n + 1). If the greatest is m, the three numbers are m − 2, m − 1, m, with sum 3m − 3.
Putting + or − between 1, 2, 3, ..., k: changing a + to a − changes the total by an even amount, so every result has the same parity (odd or even) as 1 + 2 + ... + k.

example.q: Write 18 as a sum of consecutive numbers in two ways.

learn.reallife: Seating rows in a stadium often grow by one seat each row — totals of such rows are sums of consecutive numbers.

items.text: If the greatest of 3 consecutive numbers is m, their sum is 3m − ___

quiz.q: How can 21 be written as a sum of 3 consecutive numbers?
quiz.explain: The middle number is 21 ÷ 3 = 7, so the numbers are 6, 7 and 8.
quiz.mistake: Uses equal or non-consecutive numbers

quiz.q: Which of these can NOT be written as a sum of consecutive natural numbers?
quiz.explain: 16 is a power of 2, and powers of 2 can never be written this way. 15 = 7 + 8, 18 = 5 + 6 + 7, 21 = 10 + 11.
steps: Powers of 2 have no odd factor > 1
quiz.mistake: Thinks even numbers can never be split this way

quiz.q: In how many ways can 15 be written as a sum of two or more consecutive natural numbers?
quiz.mistake: Stops after finding one or two ways

quiz.q: Five consecutive numbers add up to 100. What is the largest of them?
quiz.explain: The middle number is 100 ÷ 5 = 20, so the numbers are 18, 19, 20, 21, 22.
quiz.mistake: Gives the middle number instead of the largest

quiz.q: What is the sum of the 4 consecutive numbers n, n + 1, n + 2, n + 3?
quiz.mistake: Adds the extra 1, 2, 3 wrongly

quiz.q: Signs + or − go in the gaps of 1 _ 2 _ 3 _ 4 _ 5. Which of these results is possible?
quiz.explain: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15 is odd, and changing signs changes the total by even amounts, so every result is odd. For example 1 − 2 + 3 − 4 + 5 = 3.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice that the results all share one parity

quiz.q: Kavya says 32 can be written as a sum of consecutive numbers. Is she right?
quiz.explain: 32 = 2⁵ is a power of 2, so it cannot be a sum of consecutive numbers. 15 + 17 and 16 + 16 are not consecutive.
quiz.mistake: Accepts numbers that are not consecutive

quiz.q: The greatest of three consecutive numbers is m. What is their sum?
quiz.explain: The numbers are m − 2, m − 1 and m, so the sum is 3m − 3.
quiz.mistake: Writes the numbers going up from m instead of down

teach.ask: Gappu tried for an hour to write 8 as a sum of consecutive numbers. Should he keep trying? Explain!
teach.praise: Phew, I can stop! 8 is a power of 2, and those can never be split into consecutive numbers.
teach.nudge: What kind of number is 8? Is there something special about 1, 2, 4, 8, 16?

learn.hook: Pick any 2-digit number, reverse its digits and subtract the smaller from the larger. Your friend can bet the answer is in the 9 times table, every single time!
points: Parity means odd or even. Even + even = even, odd + odd = even, odd + even = odd, odd × odd = odd.
The sum of any 3 consecutive numbers is 3 times the middle one: (n − 1) + n + (n + 1) = 3n.
Triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, ... are sums 1 + 2 + ... + n, and equal n(n + 1) ÷ 2.
The reverse-and-subtract trick: (10a + b) − (10b + a) = 9(a − b), so the answer is always a multiple of 9.
In a cryptarithm, letters stand for digits. Use carries, last digits and parity to crack it.

example.q: In the puzzle A + A + A = BA, each letter is a different digit. Find A and B.
steps: 3 × A ends in the digit A, so 2 × A must end in 0
A = 0 gives 0 + 0 + 0 = 0, which is not a 2-digit number

learn.reallife: Puzzle pages in newspapers, Sudoku and magic tricks at a Diwali party all use these number patterns.

games.title: Odd or even result?
items: odd + odd
even + even
odd × odd
even + odd
even × odd
odd + odd + odd
sum of two consecutive numbers
product of two consecutive numbers

items.q: 3 consecutive numbers add to 45. Middle one?

quiz.q: Three consecutive numbers add up to 72. What is the largest of them?
quiz.explain: The sum is 3 times the middle number, so the middle is 72 ÷ 3 = 24. The numbers are 23, 24, 25, so the largest is 25.
quiz.mistake: Gives the middle number instead of the largest

quiz.q: Is the sum of 13 odd numbers odd or even?
options: It depends on which odd numbers
quiz.explain: Two odd numbers make an even sum. 13 odd numbers make 6 pairs (even) plus one odd number left over, so the total is odd.
quiz.mistake: Thinks adding odd numbers always gives an even answer

quiz.q: Harpreet adds all the numbers from 1 to 50. What total does she get?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by 2 (gets 2550)

quiz.q: Joseph takes any 2-digit number, reverses its digits and subtracts the smaller from the larger. The answer is always a multiple of which number?
quiz.explain: (10a + b) − (10b + a) = 9a − 9b = 9(a − b). For example, 41 − 14 = 27 = 9 × 3, which is not a multiple of 2, 4 or 5.
quiz.mistake: Generalises from one example such as 82 − 28 = 54, which is also even

quiz.q: In the sum 4A + A4 = 99, A stands for one digit. What is A?
quiz.explain: 4A means 40 + A and A4 means 10A + 4. So 44 + 11A = 99, giving 11A = 55 and A = 5. Check: 45 + 54 = 99.
quiz.mistake: Treats 4A as 4 × A instead of a 2-digit number

quiz.q: Is (odd × even) + odd always odd or always even?
quiz.explain: Odd × even is even. Then even + odd is odd. For example, 3 × 4 + 5 = 17.
quiz.mistake: Thinks multiplying by an odd number keeps a number odd

quiz.q: The 7th triangular number is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7. What is it?
quiz.explain: 7 × 8 ÷ 2 = 28. You can stack 28 dots into a triangle with rows of 1, 2, ..., 7.
quiz.mistake: Gives the 6th triangular number (21) or the square 7² = 49

quiz.q: Aisha says the sum of any 4 consecutive numbers is a multiple of 4. She tests 1 + 2 + 3 + 4. What does she find?
options: The sum is 10, so she is right
The sum is 10, so she is wrong
The sum is 12, so she is right
The sum is 8, so she is right
quiz.explain: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10, and 10 is not a multiple of 4. One counter-example is enough to show the claim is false.
quiz.mistake: Mixes this up with the true rule for 3 consecutive numbers

teach.ask: Gappu asks: Why is the sum of three numbers in a row, like 7 + 8 + 9, always in the 3 times table?
teach.praise: The first is one less and the last is one more than the middle, so they balance out. 3 times the middle! Brilliant!
teach.nudge: Compare the first and last numbers with the middle one. What happens when you add them?

topics.title: Parity puzzles: always, sometimes or never

learn.hook: Can five odd numbers add up to 30? Before you try 100 combinations, parity tells you the answer in one line.
points: 2n is always even and 2n + 1 is always odd. n² has the same parity as n.
n(n + 1) is always even, because one of two consecutive numbers is even. So n² + n is always even.
An odd count of odd numbers always adds to an odd number; an even count adds to an even number. So five odd numbers can never make 30.

Pairs to make fours: split even numbers into multiples of 4 (4, 8, 12, ...) and the rest (2, 6, 10, ..., which leave remainder 2). Two from the same group always add to a multiple of 4 (8 + 12 = 20, 6 + 10 = 16); one from each group never does (4 + 6 = 10). The same remainder idea pairs 1 to 8 so every pair adds to a multiple of 4: (1, 3), (5, 7), (2, 6), (4, 8) — and (1, 7), (3, 5) also works.
Always, sometimes or never? 'odd + odd is even' is always; 'n² + 1 is even' is sometimes (n = 3 yes, n = 2 no); 'three odd numbers add to an even number' is never.

example.q: Is 7n + 4 even or odd when n is odd?

learn.reallife: Seat-pairing, team-pairing and partner games all hide parity and remainder puzzles.

games.title: Always, sometimes or never?
items: odd + odd is even
n(n + 1) is even
n² + 1 is even
3n is odd
Three odd numbers add to an even number
2n + 1 is even

games.title: Parity check
items: 2n + 1 is odd for every whole number n.
It is 1 more than an even number.
Seven odd numbers can add up to 50.
An odd count of odd numbers is odd, but 50 is even.
n² + n is always even.
n² + n = n(n + 1), a product of consecutive numbers.
The numbers 1 to 8 can be paired so each pair adds to a multiple of 4.
A multiple of 4 plus an even number that is not a multiple of 4 is never a multiple of 4.
The remainders are 0 and 2, so the sum leaves remainder 2, e.g. 4 + 6 = 10.

quiz.q: Is n(n + 1) even or odd?
options: Even only when n is even
Odd only when n is odd
quiz.explain: One of n and n + 1 is even, so their product is always even.
steps: One of two consecutive numbers is even
quiz.mistake: Checks only one value of n

quiz.q: Which pair of even numbers adds up to a multiple of 4?
quiz.explain: 6 and 10 both leave remainder 2 on division by 4, and 2 + 2 = 4, so 6 + 10 = 16 is a multiple of 4. The others mix a multiple of 4 with a number leaving remainder 2: 10, 10 and 26.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any two even numbers add to a multiple of 4

quiz.q: If n is odd, is 5n + 3 even or odd?
quiz.explain: 5 × odd = odd, and odd + 3 = odd + odd = even.
quiz.mistake: Adds the parities wrongly

quiz.q: Can five odd numbers add up to 30?
options: No — five odd numbers always add to an odd number
Only if one of them is 1
quiz.explain: Five is an odd count, and an odd count of odd numbers is odd. 30 is even. (10 and 6 are not odd.)
quiz.mistake: Uses even numbers in the example

quiz.q: Which pair from 1 to 8 adds up to a multiple of 4?
quiz.explain: 5 + 7 = 12, a multiple of 4. The others give 6, 7 and 3.
quiz.mistake: Picks two numbers that are only even

quiz.q: Which statement is ALWAYS true?
quiz.explain: n² + n = n(n + 1), a product of consecutive numbers, so it is always even. The others depend on n.
quiz.mistake: Tests just one example and stops

quiz.q: '3n is odd.' Is this always, sometimes or never true?
quiz.explain: 3 × 3 = 9 is odd but 3 × 2 = 6 is even.
quiz.mistake: Thinks multiplying by an odd number always gives odd

quiz.q: Ishaan adds 7 odd numbers and 1 even number. Is the total even or odd?
quiz.explain: 7 odd numbers give an odd total; adding an even number keeps it odd.
quiz.mistake: Counts all 8 numbers as if they were odd

teach.ask: Gappu's friend says she added 9 odd numbers and got 100. Gappu believes her. Should he?
teach.praise: No way! 9 odd numbers always make an odd total, and 100 is even. Parity caught the trick!
teach.nudge: Is the sum of an odd count of odd numbers even or odd?

learn.hook: Diya's number leaves remainder 3 when divided by 5, and Om's leaves 4. What remainder does their sum leave? You don't even need the numbers!
points: If a and b are both multiples of k, then a + b and a − b are multiples of k too: 35 and 21 are multiples of 7, so 56 and 14 are as well.
If a is a multiple of k, then a × b is a multiple of k for every b. But a + b need not be (6 is a multiple of 3; 6 + 4 = 10 is not).
Remainders can be added: if a leaves 3 and b leaves 4 when divided by 5, a + b leaves 3 + 4 = 7, which is 1 five and 2 — remainder 2.
Remainders can be multiplied: a × b leaves the remainder of 3 × 4 = 12, which is 2. For a − b, use 3 − 4 = −1, then add 5 to get 4.

example.q: a leaves remainder 5 and b leaves remainder 4 when divided by 6. What remainder does a + b leave?

learn.reallife: Calendars work with remainders: if today is Monday, 100 days later is a Wednesday because 100 leaves remainder 2 when divided by 7.

quiz.q: a leaves remainder 2 and b leaves remainder 4 when divided by 7. What remainder does a + b leave?
quiz.explain: 2 + 4 = 6, which is less than 7, so the remainder is 6.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the remainders instead of adding

quiz.q: a leaves remainder 3 and b leaves remainder 4 when divided by 5. What remainder does a × b leave?
quiz.explain: 3 × 4 = 12 = 2 × 5 + 2, so the remainder is 2.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to take the remainder of 12

quiz.q: 47 and 29 each leave remainder 5 when divided by 6. What remainder does 47 + 29 leave?
quiz.explain: 5 + 5 = 10 = 6 + 4, so the remainder is 4. Check: 76 = 12 × 6 + 4.
quiz.mistake: Stops at 10, which is bigger than 6

quiz.q: Both 91 and 35 are multiples of 7. What can you say about 91 + 35?
options: It is never a multiple of 7
quiz.explain: The sum of two multiples of 7 is a multiple of 7: 91 + 35 = 126 = 18 × 7.
quiz.mistake: Thinks adding multiples can break divisibility

quiz.q: a is a multiple of 6. Which of these must also be a multiple of 6?
quiz.explain: Multiplying a multiple of 6 by any whole number gives a multiple of 6. Adding 5 or 3, or halving, can break it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks adding any number keeps divisibility

quiz.q: What is the remainder when 100 × 101 is divided by 9?
quiz.explain: 100 leaves 1 and 101 leaves 2 when divided by 9. So the product leaves 1 × 2 = 2.
quiz.mistake: Adds the remainders instead of multiplying

quiz.q: a leaves remainder 5 and b leaves remainder 7 when divided by 8. If a > b, what remainder does a − b leave?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the remainders the other way round
