quiz.mistake: Divides by 4 instead of the total 5

quiz.q: A biscuit label says wheat 60%, sugar 25%, oil 12%, and the rest is salt and flavours. What percentage is the rest?
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the parts must total 100%

quiz.q: A 200 g pack of dal says protein is 12%. How many grams of protein does it contain?
quiz.mistake: Reads 12% as 12 g

quiz.q: Which claim about a class of 30 students could be exactly true?
quiz.explain: 40% of 30 = 12, so 12 boys fits. 35% of 30 = 10.5 and 25% of 30 = 7.5 are not whole numbers of students.
quiz.mistake: Does not check that a percentage of people gives a whole number

quiz.q: Two friends share sweets in the ratio 7 : 13. What percentage does the first friend get?
quiz.explain: 7 out of 20 parts: 7/20 = 35%.
quiz.mistake: Takes the second share or uses 7/13

teach.ask: Gappu scored 18 out of 20, and Pari scored 40 out of 50. Pari says she won because 40 is bigger. Is she right?
teach.praise: My 18/20 is 90%, Pari's 40/50 is 80%. I did better! Percentages make it fair.
teach.nudge: Are the two tests out of the same total? How can you make them fair to compare?

learn.hook: A priest needed a fire altar with exactly twice the area of a square one. Doubling the side gave 4 times the area! Baudhayana found the clever fix.
points: Doubling the side does not double a square: a square of side 2a has area 4a², four times as big.
Baudhayana's Śulba-sūtra method: the square drawn on the diagonal of a square has exactly double its area.
Why: the two diagonals cut the square into 4 congruent right triangles. The square on the diagonal is made of 8 of the same triangles — twice as many.
Paper version: cut two equal squares along their diagonals into 8 triangles, and arrange all 8 into one big square — double the area.
Halving a square: join the midpoints of its sides. The four corner triangles are congruent to the four triangles inside the new square, so the new square has half the area.

example.q: A square has side 3 cm. Make a square with double its area.
steps: Draw the square on its diagonal
(Its side is the diagonal, about 4.24 cm, not 6 cm)
example.answer: Square on the diagonal, area 18 cm²

learn.reallife: Ancient Indian altar builders used rope and pegs to double squares exactly, long before calculators.

games.title: Double or not?
items: Doubling the side of a square doubles its area.
It makes the area 4 times.
The square on the diagonal of a square has twice its area.
It is made of 8 triangles instead of 4.
Joining the midpoints of a square's sides gives a square with half the area.
The corner triangles match the inner triangles.
The two diagonals cut a square into 4 congruent triangles.
They are equal isosceles right triangles.

items.q: Triangles in the square on the diagonal

quiz.q: The side of a 5 cm square is doubled to 10 cm. What is the new area?
quiz.explain: 10 × 10 = 100 cm², which is 4 times the old 25 cm², not 2 times.
quiz.mistake: Thinks doubling the side doubles the area

quiz.q: When the side of a square is doubled, how many times bigger does its area become?
quiz.explain: (2a)² = 4a², so the area becomes 4 times as big.
quiz.mistake: Doubles the area along with the side

quiz.q: The two diagonals of a square cut it into how many congruent triangles?
quiz.explain: The diagonals cross at the centre and make 4 equal isosceles right triangles.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the triangles made by one diagonal

quiz.q: Baudhayana's square on the diagonal is made of how many of those small triangles?
quiz.explain: It contains 8 such triangles, twice the 4 in the original square — so it has double the area.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the new square has the same number of triangles

quiz.q: Two squares, each of area 9 cm², are cut along their diagonals and rearranged into one big square. What is its area?
quiz.explain: Cutting and rearranging does not change area: 9 + 9 = 18 cm².
quiz.mistake: Squares the side instead of adding the areas

quiz.q: A square has side 3 cm. What is the area of the square drawn on its diagonal?
quiz.explain: The square on the diagonal has double the area: 2 × 9 = 18 cm².
quiz.mistake: Doubles the side instead of the area

quiz.q: The midpoints of the sides of a 12 cm × 12 cm square tile are joined. What is the area of the inner square?
quiz.explain: The inner square has half the area: 144 ÷ 2 = 72 cm².
quiz.mistake: Takes a quarter instead of half

quiz.q: Why does the midpoint square have exactly half the area?
options: Because its side is half as long
The 4 corner triangles are congruent to the 4 triangles inside it
Because all squares are the same
quiz.explain: Fold the corners in: each corner triangle exactly covers one inner triangle, so inside and outside have equal area.
quiz.mistake: Thinks halving the side halves the area

teach.ask: Gappu wants a square nest twice as big as his old one. He plans to double each side. Will that work?
teach.praise: Doubling the side makes it 4 times bigger! I should build on the diagonal instead — Baudhayana's trick.
teach.nudge: What happens to the area when the side doubles? Which line should the new side be?

learn.hook: Draw a triangle with two sides of 1 cm and a right angle between them. The third side is √2 cm — a number whose decimals never end and never repeat!
points: An isosceles right triangle with legs 1 has hypotenuse c with c² = 1² + 1² = 2, so c = √2.
√2 has no terminating decimal: a decimal with k decimal places, squared, has 2k decimal places ending in a non-zero digit, so it can never equal exactly 2.
√2 is not a fraction p/q: if it were (in lowest terms), then p² = 2q², so p is even; then q² = 2 × (p/2)², so q is even too — impossible for lowest terms. √2 is irrational.
For legs a, the hypotenuse is a√2. Legs 5 give hypotenuse √50 ≈ 7.07, between 7 and 8 since 49 < 50 < 64.

example.q: Between which two numbers with 2 decimal places does √2 lie?

learn.reallife: A4 paper is cut so that its long side ÷ short side ≈ √2 — fold it in half and the shape stays the same!

games.title: √2 facts
items: √2 is about 1.414.
1.414² = 1.999396, very close to 2.
√2 can be written as a fraction of two whole numbers.
The even–even argument shows it cannot.
√2 has a decimal that ends after some digits.
Squaring a terminating decimal can never give exactly 2.
The hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle with legs 1 is √2.

quiz.q: What is the hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle with both legs 1 cm?
quiz.mistake: Adds the legs instead of using squares

quiz.q: What is 1.41²?
quiz.mistake: Squares each digit separately or misplaces the decimal

quiz.q: Which pair of numbers traps √2 between them?
quiz.mistake: Picks a pair whose squares are both above or both below 2

quiz.q: An isosceles right triangle has legs of 7 cm. What is the square of its hypotenuse?
quiz.mistake: Squares just one leg or adds the legs

quiz.q: An isosceles right triangle has a hypotenuse of 10 cm. What is the square of each equal leg?
quiz.explain: a² + a² = 100, so 2a² = 100 and a² = 50. Each leg is √50 ≈ 7.07 cm.
quiz.mistake: Halves the hypotenuse instead of halving its square

quiz.q: Why can √2 not be a terminating decimal like 1.414?
options: Squaring a decimal with k places gives 2k places ending in a non-zero digit, never exactly 2
quiz.explain: If the last digit is non-zero, so is the last digit of its square, so the square still has decimal places — it cannot be exactly 2.000...
quiz.mistake: Thinks enough digits will eventually give exactly 2

quiz.q: In the proof that √2 is not a fraction, p² = 2q². What does this tell us about p?
quiz.explain: p² is 2 times something, so p² is even, and only even numbers have even squares. So p is even.
steps: odd² is odd, so p must be even
quiz.mistake: Thinks an even square can come from an odd number

quiz.q: An isosceles right triangle has legs of 5 cm. Between which two whole numbers is its hypotenuse?
quiz.mistake: Adds the legs to get 10

teach.ask: Gappu thinks √2 is exactly 1.4. Can you show him why it isn't, and how close we can get?
teach.praise: 1.4² is only 1.96! √2 ≈ 1.414..., and its decimals never end. What a mysterious number!
teach.nudge: What do you get if you square 1.4? Is it exactly 2?

learn.hook: More than 2500 years ago, the Indian mathematician Baudhayana wrote down a rule for building fire altars that we still use to find distances today!
points: A right triangle has one angle of 90°. The side opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse, and it is the longest side.
The Baudhayana–Pythagoras theorem: if the legs are a and b and the hypotenuse is c, then a² + b² = c².
In Baudhayana's words (roughly): the diagonal of a rectangle makes a square as big as the squares on its length and breadth put together.
To find the hypotenuse: c = √(a² + b²). To find a leg: a = √(c² − b²).
Converse: if the sides of a triangle satisfy a² + b² = c², then the angle opposite c is a right angle.

example.q: A 13 m ladder leans against a wall. Its foot is 5 m from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?
steps: The ladder is the hypotenuse: c = 13
One leg is 5, let the height be h

learn.reallife: Firefighters placing ladders, TV makers measuring screen size along the diagonal, and pilots finding straight-line distances all use this theorem.

items.text: In a right triangle, the longest side is called the ___
If the legs are 6 and 8, then hypotenuse² = ___
The hypotenuse is opposite the ___ angle
If c² = a² + b², the angle opposite c is ___

quiz.q: The two shorter sides of a right triangle are 6 cm and 8 cm. How long is the hypotenuse?
quiz.mistake: Adds the sides (14) instead of their squares, or forgets the square root (100)

quiz.q: A 13 m ladder leans on a wall with its foot 5 m away from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?
quiz.explain: The ladder is the hypotenuse. Height² = 13² − 5² = 169 − 25 = 144, so the height is 12 m.
quiz.mistake: Adds the squares instead of subtracting, or forgets the square root

quiz.q: Which side of a right triangle is always the longest?
options: Any side can be the longest
quiz.explain: c² = a² + b² is bigger than a² and bigger than b², so c is longer than both legs.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the side drawn at the bottom (base) is always the longest

quiz.q: Riya walks 9 m east and then 12 m north. How far is she from her starting point in a straight line?
quiz.explain: East and north make a right angle. Distance² = 9² + 12² = 81 + 144 = 225, so the distance is 15 m.
quiz.mistake: Adds the two distances walked (21 m)

quiz.q: A TV screen is 80 cm wide and 60 cm tall. How long is its diagonal?
quiz.explain: Diagonal² = 80² + 60² = 6400 + 3600 = 10,000, so the diagonal is 100 cm.
quiz.mistake: Adds the width and height instead of using squares

quiz.q: A right triangle has a hypotenuse of 25 cm and one leg of 24 cm. How long is the other leg?
quiz.explain: Other leg² = 25² − 24² = 625 − 576 = 49, so it is 7 cm.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the sides (25 − 24 = 1) instead of their squares

quiz.q: The squares on the two legs of a right triangle have areas 36 cm² and 64 cm². What is the area of the square on the hypotenuse?
quiz.explain: The theorem says the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the legs: 36 + 64 = 100 cm².
quiz.mistake: Gives the side length (10) instead of the area, or subtracts

quiz.q: In triangle PQR, ∠Q = 90°. Which equation is correct?
quiz.explain: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle at Q, so it is PR. Then PR² = PQ² + QR².
quiz.mistake: Does not find the side opposite the right angle first

teach.ask: Gappu asks: A right triangle has legs 3 and 4. How do I find the long side?
teach.praise: Square the legs: 9 and 16. Add: 25. Square root: 5! Baudhayana would be proud!
teach.nudge: What do you do to 3 and 4 first? And after adding, how do you get back to a length?

topics.title: Proof ideas and using the converse

learn.hook: Can you prove a² + b² = c² with just four paper triangles and a square? Yes, with a cut-and-arrange trick!
points: Area proof: draw a big square of side (a + b). Put 4 copies of the right triangle in its corners. The space left in the middle is a tilted square of side c.
Big square area = 4 triangles + middle square: (a + b)² = 4 × ½ab + c². So a² + 2ab + b² = 2ab + c², which gives a² + b² = c².
Rearrangement: slide the same 4 triangles into a different position in the big square, and the space left is two squares, a² and b². Same leftover area, so a² + b² = c².
Baudhayana used the diagonal to double a square: the square on the diagonal of a square has twice its area.
Converse in action: if the longest side c gives a² + b² = c², the triangle is right-angled. If a² + b² > c² it is acute; if a² + b² < c² it is obtuse.

example.q: Use the area proof with a = 3 and b = 4 to find c.

learn.reallife: Masons mark a perfect right angle for a house corner with a knotted rope stretched into a 3-4-5 triangle.

games.title: Build the proof
games.prompt: Put the steps of the area proof in order
items: Draw a big square of side a + b
Place four copies of the right triangle in its corners
The middle space is a tilted square of side c
Big square = 4 triangles + middle square: (a + b)² = 2ab + c²
Expand: a² + 2ab + b² = 2ab + c², so a² + b² = c²

games.title: Right or not?
items: A triangle with sides 6, 8 and 10 has a right angle.
A triangle with sides 4, 5 and 6 has a right angle.
16 + 25 = 41, but 6² = 36. It is an acute triangle.
The diagonal of a square with side 1 has length √2.
In every triangle, a² + b² = c².
This is true only for right triangles.
A knotted rope with sides 3, 4 and 5 units can be used to mark a right angle.
3² + 4² = 5², so by the converse the angle between 3 and 4 is 90°.
If both legs of a right triangle are doubled, the hypotenuse also doubles.

quiz.q: In the area proof, a big square of side (a + b) holds 4 right triangles with legs a and b, and a middle square of side c. If a = 3 and b = 4, what is the area of the middle square?
quiz.explain: Big square = 7² = 49. Four triangles = 4 × 6 = 24. Middle square = 49 − 24 = 25, so c = 5.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract the triangles, or uses only one triangle

quiz.q: A triangle has sides 5 cm, 6 cm and 8 cm. What kind of triangle is it?
quiz.explain: 5² + 6² = 61, which is less than 8² = 64. When the two smaller squares add to less than the largest square, the triangle is obtuse.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any triangle with whole-number sides is right-angled

quiz.q: What is the diagonal of a square of side 5 cm? (Use √2 ≈ 1.41.)
quiz.mistake: Adds the two sides (10 cm) instead of using the theorem

quiz.q: Baudhayana's idea: a square is drawn on the diagonal of a square of side 6 cm. What is the area of the new square?
quiz.explain: Diagonal² = 6² + 6² = 72. The new square's area is diagonal², which is 72 cm², twice the original 36 cm².
quiz.mistake: Doubles the side (12 cm), which makes 144 cm², four times the area

quiz.q: Why do masons use a knotted rope with sides 3, 4 and 5 units?
options: Because 3² + 4² = 5², so the triangle has a right angle for making square corners
Because it makes an equilateral triangle
Because ropes cannot make other shapes
quiz.explain: By the converse of the theorem, sides 3, 4, 5 must make a right angle between the 3 and 4 sides.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the converse of the theorem to real right angles

quiz.q: A triangle has sides 9, 10 and 12. Is it acute, right or obtuse?
quiz.explain: 9² + 10² = 181, which is more than 12² = 144. When the two smaller squares add to more than the largest, all angles are acute.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up which way the inequality points to acute or obtuse

quiz.q: A right triangle has legs 5 and 12. If both legs are doubled, what is the new hypotenuse?
quiz.explain: The old hypotenuse is 13. Doubling both legs doubles the hypotenuse: 26. Check: 10² + 24² = 676 = 26².
quiz.mistake: Thinks the hypotenuse stays the same or becomes 4 times bigger

quiz.q: In the rearrangement proof, the four triangles are moved inside the same big square so that two squares are left uncovered. What are their areas?
quiz.explain: The leftover space is a square of side a and a square of side b. Before the move it was one square of side c, so a² + b² = c².
quiz.mistake: Confuses the triangles' areas (½ab) with the leftover squares

teach.ask: Gappu asks: How does putting 4 triangles inside a big square prove a² + b² = c²?
teach.praise: The leftover space is c² in one arrangement and a² + b² in the other. Same space, so they are equal. Mind blown!
teach.nudge: What is left uncovered in the middle? And what is left after you move the triangles?

topics.title: Combining squares and drawing squares of any area

learn.hook: Can you cut a 3 × 3 and a 4 × 4 square of paper and rebuild them into ONE square? Yes — a 5 × 5 one! That's the theorem in your hands.
points: Two squares with sides a and b can be cut and rearranged into one square of side c, where c² = a² + b². For 3 and 4, c = 5.
To draw a square with 5 times the area of a unit square: draw a right triangle with legs 1 and 2. Its hypotenuse is √5, so the square on it has area 5.
For 3 times the area: use legs 1 and √2 (the diagonal of the unit square). The hypotenuse is √3.
On a square dot grid, a tilted square whose side goes 'a across and b up' has area a² + b². So areas 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10 ... are possible, but area 3 is not (3 is not a sum of two squares).

example.q: Draw a square of area 5 on a dot grid.
steps: Draw a side going 2 across and 1 up
Turn 90° and repeat to make the other sides

learn.reallife: Tile setters and quilt makers combine and tilt squares to fit odd-sized floors and patterns.

games.title: Tilted squares on a dot grid
Possible as a square area on a dot grid?

quiz.q: Squares of side 6 cm and 8 cm are cut and rearranged into one square. What is its side?
quiz.mistake: Adds the sides instead of the areas

quiz.q: Paper squares of area 9 cm² and 16 cm² are combined into one square. What is its area?
quiz.explain: Cutting and rearranging keeps the total area: 9 + 16 = 25 cm².
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the areas

quiz.q: To draw a square with area 5 square units, what legs should the right triangle have?
quiz.explain: 1² + 2² = 5, so the hypotenuse is √5 and the square on it has area 5.
quiz.mistake: Uses legs whose sum (not sum of squares) is 5

quiz.q: To draw a square with 3 times the area of a unit square, which right triangle works?
quiz.explain: 1² + (√2)² = 1 + 2 = 3, so the hypotenuse is √3.
quiz.mistake: Uses the number 3 directly as a leg

quiz.q: A tilted square on a dot grid has corners (0,0), (1,1), (0,2) and (−1,1). What is its area?
quiz.explain: Each side goes 1 across and 1 up, so the area is 1² + 1² = 2.
quiz.mistake: Counts only whole small squares

quiz.q: One side of a tilted square on a dot grid goes from (0,0) to (2,1). What is its area?
quiz.explain: The side goes 2 across and 1 up, so the area is 2² + 1² = 5.
quiz.mistake: Adds 2 + 1

quiz.q: Which square area can NOT be drawn with corners on a square dot grid?
quiz.explain: Grid squares have area a² + b². 2 = 1 + 1, 5 = 4 + 1, 8 = 4 + 4, but 3 is not a sum of two squares.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every whole number area is possible

quiz.q: A tilted square's side goes 3 across and 1 up on a dot grid. What is its area?
quiz.explain: Area = 3² + 1² = 10.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square the steps

teach.ask: Gappu wants to draw a square of area 10 on dotted paper. Every square he draws has area 1, 4 or 9. Help him!
teach.praise: Tilt it! A side that goes 3 across and 1 up gives 9 + 1 = 10. My square is ready!
teach.nudge: Must the sides go straight along the grid lines? What if a side slants?

learn.hook: 3, 4, 5 is a magic trio: 9 + 16 = 25. Are there more such trios? Infinitely many!
points: A Pythagorean triple is three whole numbers a, b, c with a² + b² = c². The smallest is (3, 4, 5).
Multiply a triple by any whole number to get another: (6, 8, 10), (9, 12, 15), (30, 40, 50).
Some triples are not multiples of smaller ones: (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17), (7, 24, 25), (20, 21, 29).
A recipe: for any whole number m > 1, the numbers 2m, m² − 1 and m² + 1 form a triple. For m = 4: 8, 15, 17.
To test a triple, square the two smaller numbers, add them, and compare with the square of the largest.

example.q: Is (20, 21, 29) a Pythagorean triple?

learn.reallife: Carpenters and tile layers use triples like 6-8-10 to check that corners are truly square.

quiz.q: Which of these is a Pythagorean triple?
quiz.mistake: Picks numbers that just look close together

quiz.q: Complete the Pythagorean triple (9, 40, __).
quiz.mistake: Adds 9 and 40 instead of their squares

quiz.q: Using 2m, m² − 1 and m² + 1 with m = 7, what is the largest number of the triple?
quiz.mistake: Uses m² (49) without adding 1

quiz.q: (3, 4, 5) is a triple. Which of these is also a triple made by multiplying it?
quiz.explain: (15, 20, 25) = 5 × (3, 4, 5). Multiplying every number by the same amount keeps a² + b² = c².
quiz.mistake: Adds the same number to each, or multiplies only some of the numbers

quiz.q: A right triangle has legs 10 cm and 24 cm. How long is the hypotenuse?
quiz.mistake: Uses the triple (5, 12, 13) but forgets to double 13

quiz.q: Harpreet's triangle has sides 7 cm, 24 cm and 25 cm. Is it a right triangle?
options: Yes, because 25 is the longest side
quiz.explain: 49 + 576 = 625 = 25². By the converse of the theorem, the triangle has a right angle.
quiz.mistake: Adds the sides instead of their squares

quiz.q: In the Pythagorean triple (20, 21, x), what is x?
How many Pythagorean triples are there?
quiz.explain: Multiplying (3, 4, 5) by 2, 3, 4, ... gives a new triple every time, and that never ends.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only the few famous triples exist

teach.ask: Gappu asks: How do I check if 5, 12, 13 is a Pythagorean triple?
teach.praise: 25 + 144 = 169 = 13². The two small squares add up to the big square. It is a triple!
teach.nudge: What do you do with 5 and 12? Then what do you compare the answer with?

topics.title: Primitive triples and Fermat's famous puzzle

learn.hook: a² + b² = c² has endless whole-number answers. But try a³ + b³ = c³ — there are NONE. It took 350 years to prove!
points: A triple is primitive if its three numbers share no common factor bigger than 1: (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17). (6, 8, 10) is not primitive — it is 2 × (3, 4, 5).
Odd-number recipe: n² = 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n − 1). If the last odd number 2n − 1 is itself a square k², then n² = (n − 1)² + k².
Examples: 2n − 1 = 9 gives n = 5 and 5² = 4² + 3²; 2n − 1 = 25 gives 13² = 12² + 5²; 2n − 1 = 49 gives 25² = 24² + 7².
Fermat's Last Theorem: there are no positive whole numbers x, y, z with xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ when n is bigger than 2.
Pierre de Fermat wrote this in the margin of a book (around 1637), saying the margin was too small for his proof. Andrew Wiles finally proved it in 1994.

example.q: Use the odd-number recipe with the odd square 81.

learn.reallife: Mathematicians worked on Fermat's puzzle for over 350 years — proof that some questions are worth a lifetime!

quiz.q: Which of these is a primitive triple?
quiz.explain: 8, 15 and 17 have no common factor above 1. The others are multiples of (3, 4, 5) or (5, 12, 13).
quiz.mistake: Thinks every triple is primitive

quiz.q: (12, 16, 20) is a triple. Dividing by the HCF of its numbers gives which primitive triple?
quiz.mistake: Divides by 2 only

quiz.q: In the odd-number recipe, the odd square 2n − 1 = 25. What is n?
quiz.explain: 2n − 1 = 25 gives n = 13, and then 13² = 12² + 5².
quiz.mistake: Takes the square root of 25 instead

quiz.q: Which triple does the odd square 49 give in the recipe?
quiz.explain: 2n − 1 = 49 gives n = 25, so 25² = 24² + 7²: the triple is (7, 24, 25).
quiz.mistake: Uses 49 itself as a side

quiz.q: The odd square 81 gives a triple. What is its largest number?
quiz.explain: 2n − 1 = 81 gives n = 41, and 41² = 40² + 9².
quiz.mistake: Gives n − 1 instead of n

quiz.q: How many solutions in positive whole numbers does x³ + y³ = z³ have?
quiz.explain: Fermat's Last Theorem (proved by Wiles) says there are none for any power bigger than 2.
quiz.mistake: Assumes it works like a² + b² = c²

quiz.q: Who proved Fermat's Last Theorem in 1994?
quiz.explain: Fermat only claimed a proof; Andrew Wiles proved it in 1994.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Fermat himself proved it

quiz.q: Where did Fermat write his famous claim?
options: In the margin of a book
quiz.explain: He wrote it in the margin of his copy of an old maths book and said the margin was too small for the proof.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Fermat with older mathematicians

teach.ask: Gappu found (30, 40, 50) and wants to know if it is a 'new' triple. Is it primitive?
teach.praise: (30, 40, 50) is just 10 × (3, 4, 5) — not primitive. I need a triple with no common factor!
teach.nudge: Do 30, 40 and 50 share a factor? What do you get if you divide by it?

topics.title: More uses: lotus, rhombus, triangles and a box puzzle

learn.hook: In Bhaskara's Lilavati, a lotus sways in the wind until its flower touches the water. From that, you can find how deep the lake is!
points: Lotus problem: a lotus stands h above the water; the wind pushes it until the flower touches the water a distance s away. If the depth is d, the stem is d + h, so d² + s² = (d + h)².
With h = 10 cm and s = 30 cm: d² + 900 = d² + 20d + 100, so 20d = 800 and d = 40 cm.
A rhombus's diagonals bisect each other at right angles, so side² = (half of one diagonal)² + (half of the other)². Diagonals 16 and 12 give side √(8² + 6²) = 10.
An equilateral triangle of side a has altitude h with h² + (a/2)² = a², so h = (√3/2)a. Area = ½ × a × h. For a = 10 cm: h ≈ 8.66 cm and area ≈ 43.3 cm².
Logic puzzle: three boxes are labelled Red, Blue and Mixed, but every label is wrong. Pick one ball from the box labelled Mixed — it can only be all one colour — and you can then work out every box.

example.q: A lotus flower is 10 cm above the water. Pushed by the wind, it touches the water 30 cm away. How deep is the water?

learn.reallife: Engineers use the same theorem to find heights, depths and diagonal braces in buildings and bridges.

games.title: Solve the box puzzle
items: All three labels are wrong
Take one ball from the box labelled Mixed
That box holds only that ball's colour
The box labelled with the other colour must be Mixed
The last box gets the remaining colour

quiz.q: A lotus flower is 10 cm above the water. The wind pushes it until it touches the water 30 cm away. How deep is the water?
quiz.mistake: Takes the stem length (50 cm) as the depth

quiz.q: A lotus flower is 20 cm above the water and touches the water 60 cm away when pushed. How deep is the water?
quiz.mistake: Gives the stem length instead of the depth

quiz.q: A rhombus has diagonals 16 cm and 12 cm. How long is each side?
quiz.explain: Half-diagonals are 8 and 6, and they meet at 90°. Side = √(64 + 36) = 10 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses the full diagonals in the theorem

quiz.q: A rhombus has diagonals 10 cm and 24 cm. What is its perimeter?
quiz.explain: Side = √(5² + 12²) = 13 cm, so the perimeter is 4 × 13 = 52 cm.
quiz.mistake: Stops at one side

quiz.q: An equilateral triangle has side 10 cm. Using √3 ≈ 1.732, how long is its altitude?
quiz.mistake: Uses half the side as the altitude

quiz.q: Using an altitude of 8.66 cm, what is the area of an equilateral triangle with side 10 cm?
quiz.explain: Area = ½ × base × height = ½ × 10 × 8.66 = 43.3 cm².
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½

quiz.q: Three boxes are labelled Red, Blue and Mixed, and every label is wrong. From which box should you take one ball to fix all the labels?
quiz.explain: The box labelled Mixed cannot be mixed, so one ball tells you its true colour. Then the other two follow.
steps: Mixed label is wrong → that box is one colour
quiz.mistake: Picks a box whose ball would not decide the answer

quiz.q: In the box puzzle, you take a red ball from the box labelled Mixed. What does the box labelled Blue contain?
quiz.explain: The Mixed-labelled box is Red. The Blue-labelled box is not blue (its label is wrong) and not red (taken), so it is Mixed. The Red-labelled box is Blue.
steps: Box labelled Blue → not Blue, not Red → Mixed
quiz.mistake: Forgets that every label is wrong

teach.ask: Gappu sees a reed sticking 10 cm out of a pond. When he pulls its tip sideways 30 cm, it touches the water. How can he find the pond's depth?
teach.praise: d² + 900 = (d + 10)², so d = 40 cm! Bhaskara's lotus trick works for reeds too.
teach.nudge: If the depth is d, how long is the whole reed? Which side is the hypotenuse?

learn.hook: One samosa costs ₹15, two cost ₹30, ten cost ₹150. Double the samosas and you double the bill. That is direct proportion!
points: Two quantities are in direct proportion if, when one is multiplied by a number, the other is multiplied by the same number.
In direct proportion, y ÷ x stays the same. We can write y = kx, where k is the constant.
Examples: number of pens and their cost; petrol used and distance at a steady speed; time and pay for a fixed hourly wage.
Test a table: divide each y by its x. If you always get the same number, it is direct proportion.
Not everything that grows together is in proportion. A child's age and height both grow, but height does not double when age doubles.

example.q: 5 m of cloth costs ₹350. What is the cost of 8 m?
steps: Cost ÷ length stays the same: 350 ÷ 5 = ₹70 per metre

learn.reallife: Your phone data bill, petrol pump meters and auto-rickshaw fares (after the minimum charge) grow in direct proportion.

games.title: Direct or not?
items: Number of pens and their total cost
Distance travelled at a steady speed and time taken
Litres of petrol and its cost
Laddoos made and kg of sugar used (same recipe)
A child's age and height
Number of workers and days to finish a job
Speed and time for a fixed journey
A person's age and weight

items.text: If 3 pens cost ₹36, then 6 pens cost ₹___
x and y in direct proportion: x = 2, y = 14; x = 5, y = ___
If y = 4x, then when x = 9, y = ___
In direct proportion, y ÷ x stays ___

quiz.q: 5 m of cloth costs ₹350. What is the cost of 8 m?
quiz.mistake: Adds 3 to the price because 8 is 3 more than 5

quiz.q: x and y are in direct proportion. When x = 6, y = 15. What is y when x = 10?
quiz.mistake: Adds 4 to y because x went up by 4

quiz.q: Which pair of quantities is in direct proportion?
options: Number of workers and time to build a wall
Number of tickets bought and total cost
Age and height of a child
Speed of a car and time for a fixed trip
quiz.explain: Each ticket costs the same, so twice the tickets cost twice as much. The others are not direct proportion.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any two quantities that change together are directly proportional

quiz.q: A car uses 6 litres of petrol to travel 90 km. How far can it go on 10 litres?
quiz.explain: It goes 90 ÷ 6 = 15 km per litre, so on 10 litres it goes 150 km.
quiz.mistake: Adds 4 km for the 4 extra litres

quiz.q: x and y are in direct proportion. When x is 3, 5 and 8, y is 12, 20 and ?. What is the missing y?
quiz.mistake: Adds 8 to 20 instead of using the constant ratio

quiz.q: Meena types 270 words in 6 minutes at a steady speed. How many words does she type in 15 minutes?
quiz.explain: She types 270 ÷ 6 = 45 words a minute. In 15 minutes: 45 × 15 = 675 words.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 270 by 6 instead of dividing

quiz.q: A photocopier makes 80 copies in 4 minutes. How many minutes does it take to make 300 copies?
quiz.explain: It makes 80 ÷ 4 = 20 copies a minute. 300 ÷ 20 = 15 minutes.
quiz.mistake: Divides 300 by 4 instead of by the copies per minute

quiz.q: Joseph says: 'In direct proportion, when x doubles, y goes up by 2.' What is the correct statement?
options: When x doubles, y also doubles
When x doubles, y is halved
When x doubles, y goes up by 2
When x doubles, y stays the same
quiz.explain: In direct proportion y = kx. If x is multiplied by 2, y is multiplied by 2 as well.
quiz.mistake: Confuses multiplying by 2 with adding 2

teach.ask: Gappu asks: How can I tell if the cost of bananas is in direct proportion to the number of bananas?
teach.praise: Divide cost by number for each pair. If it is always the same, it is direct proportion. Banana-tastic!
teach.nudge: If you buy twice as many bananas, what happens to the cost? What stays the same?

learn.hook: On a map of India, Delhi and Jaipur are about 4 cm apart. With the right scale, that tiny gap becomes about 240 km!
points: Check a proportion a : b :: c : d by cross-multiplying: it holds exactly when a × d = b × c.
A map scale like 1 : 60,00,000 is a ratio: 1 cm on the map stands for 60,00,000 cm = 60 km on the ground.
Map to real: multiply by the scale. Real to map: change to the same unit, then divide. At 1 : 50,000, a real 4 km = 4,00,000 cm becomes 8 cm on the map.
A map gives the straight-line (geographical) distance. The road distance is usually longer, because roads bend around hills, rivers and towns.
Make your own map: measure your classroom and draw it to scale, for example 1 : 100 (1 cm for 1 m).

example.q: On a map with scale 1 : 60,00,000, two cities are 4 cm apart. How far apart are they really?

learn.reallife: Google Maps, school atlases and house plans all depend on scales.

items.q: 1 : 50,000 — 4 km is how many cm on the map?
1 : 100 — a 9 m wall is how many cm?

games.title: Maps and proportions
items: 4 : 10 :: 6 : 15 is a true proportion.
The road distance between two towns is never longer than the map's straight-line distance.
Roads bend, so road distance is usually longer.
A scale of 1 : 100 means 1 cm on the drawing is 1 m in real life.
3 : 5 :: 9 : 16 is a true proportion.

quiz.q: Are 4 : 10 and 6 : 15 in proportion?
quiz.explain: Cross-multiply: 4 × 15 = 60 and 10 × 6 = 60. They are equal, so the ratios are in proportion.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the wrong pairs or compares differences

quiz.q: A map has scale 1 : 60,00,000. Two towns are 5 cm apart on it. What is the straight-line distance between them?
quiz.explain: 1 cm = 60 km, so 5 cm = 300 km.
quiz.mistake: Gets the units wrong when changing cm into km

quiz.q: At a scale of 1 : 50,000, how long is a real distance of 4 km on the map?
quiz.mistake: Divides without first changing km into cm

quiz.q: A map says '1 cm = 25 km'. How is this written as a ratio scale?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to change km into cm

quiz.q: The map distance between two villages gives 30 km, but the bus travels 42 km. Why?
options: Buses always travel twice the distance
The road bends, so it is longer than the straight-line distance
quiz.explain: A map's scale distance is a straight line; real roads curve around obstacles.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the map shows road length

quiz.q: A classroom is 8 m long. It is drawn at a scale of 1 : 100. How long is it on the drawing?
quiz.mistake: Divides 8 m by 100 without changing units

quiz.q: A 9 m wall is drawn at a scale of 1 : 50. How long is it on the drawing?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by 50 instead of dividing

quiz.q: Are 3, 7, 12, 28 in proportion (3 : 7 :: 12 : 28)?
options: Yes, because all are whole numbers
quiz.explain: Extremes 3 × 28 = 84 and means 7 × 12 = 84 are equal.
quiz.mistake: Compares differences instead of products

teach.ask: Gappu found Pune and Mumbai 2 cm apart on a map with scale 1 : 60,00,000. How far should he fly in a straight line?
teach.praise: 2.5 × 60 = 150 km in a straight line. Flying birds don't need roads!
teach.nudge: How many km does 1 cm stand for on this map?

topics.title: Ratios with more than two terms

learn.hook: Garam masala, concrete and tie-dye paint all follow three-part (or more!) ratios. Change one part and you must change them all.
points: A ratio can have many terms, like cumin : coriander : chilli = 2 : 3 : 1. To scale it, multiply EVERY term by the same number: 4 : 6 : 2.
Mixtures: concrete is often cement : sand : gravel = 1 : 2 : 4; paints and spice mixes use ratios too.
To divide a quantity in a : b : c, add the terms, find one part, then multiply. ₹1800 in 2 : 3 : 4 → 9 parts, 1 part = ₹200 → ₹400, ₹600, ₹800.
The same method shares time, books or coins: 120 minutes in 3 : 2 : 1 gives 60, 40 and 20 minutes.

example.q: A 300 g spice mix has cumin : coriander : chilli = 2 : 3 : 1. How much coriander is in it?

learn.reallife: Masons mix cement, sand and gravel by ratio — a wrong mix makes weak walls!

quiz.q: A 300 g spice mix has cumin : coriander : chilli = 2 : 3 : 1. How many grams of coriander does it contain?
quiz.explain: 6 parts in all; 1 part = 50 g; coriander = 3 parts = 150 g.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 3 terms instead of 6 parts

quiz.q: The same 2 : 3 : 1 spice mix is made with 6 teaspoons of chilli. How many teaspoons of cumin are needed?
quiz.explain: Chilli 1 → 6 means × 6, so cumin 2 → 12.
quiz.mistake: Adds 5 to every term

quiz.q: Concrete uses cement : sand : gravel = 1 : 2 : 4. How many bags of gravel go into a 35-bag mix?
quiz.explain: 7 parts in all; 1 part = 5 bags; gravel = 4 × 5 = 20 bags.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 3 instead of the total parts

quiz.q: Paint is mixed red : white : yellow = 1 : 3 : 2. If 9 L of white is used, what is the total amount of paint?
quiz.explain: White 3 → 9 is × 3, so the mix is 3 : 9 : 6, a total of 18 L.
quiz.mistake: Adds only two of the parts

quiz.q: ₹1800 is divided in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. What is the largest share?
quiz.explain: 9 parts in all; 1 part = ₹200; largest = 4 × 200 = ₹800.
quiz.mistake: Divides into 3 equal shares

quiz.q: Diya splits 120 minutes of study between maths, science and English in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1. How long is maths?
quiz.explain: 6 parts; 1 part = 20 minutes; maths = 3 × 20 = 60 minutes.
quiz.mistake: Uses 3 out of 3 + 2 instead of all 6 parts

quiz.q: 60 books are shared among three classes in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3. How many does the middle class get?
quiz.explain: 6 parts; 1 part = 10 books; the middle share is 2 × 10 = 20.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 3

quiz.q: A purse has ₹1, ₹2 and ₹5 coins in the ratio 5 : 3 : 1 by number. The total is ₹48. How many ₹2 coins are there?
quiz.explain: One 'set' of 5, 3 and 1 coins is worth 5 + 6 + 5 = ₹16. ₹48 is 3 sets, so there are 3 × 3 = 9 ₹2 coins.
quiz.mistake: Splits the money in 5 : 3 : 1 instead of the coin counts

teach.ask: Gappu's grandma makes chai masala with ginger : cardamom : pepper = 3 : 2 : 1. He wants 60 g. How much of each?
teach.praise: 6 parts, 10 g each: 30 g ginger, 20 g cardamom and 10 g pepper. Grandma's chai, Gappu-sized!
teach.nudge: How many parts are there altogether? How much is one part?

learn.hook: Can a triangle have sides in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3? Try building it with straws — it just falls flat!
points: Angles of a triangle add to 180°. If they are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4, the 9 parts make 180°, so 1 part = 20° and the angles are 40°, 60°, 80°.
A ratio like 1 : 2 : 3 for angles gives 30°, 60°, 90° — a right triangle.
Sides in a ratio: 2 : 3 : 4 with perimeter 36 cm gives 1 part = 4 cm, so sides 8, 12 and 16 cm.
Triangle inequality: the two shorter sides must add up to MORE than the longest. 1 : 2 : 3 fails (1 + 2 = 3), so no triangle can be made. 4 : 5 : 6 works.

example.q: A triangle's angles are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. Find them.

learn.reallife: Roof trusses and bridge supports are designed with side ratios that are sure to make strong triangles.

games.title: Can these be the sides of a triangle?

quiz.q: A triangle's angles are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. What is the largest angle?
quiz.explain: 9 parts = 180°, so 1 part = 20° and the largest is 4 × 20° = 80°.
quiz.mistake: Uses 360° instead of 180°

quiz.q: A triangle's angles are in the ratio 1 : 1 : 2. What is its largest angle?
quiz.explain: 4 parts = 180°, so 1 part = 45° and the angles are 45°, 45°, 90°.
quiz.mistake: Divides 180 by 3 because there are 3 angles

quiz.q: A triangle's angles are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3. What is the smallest angle?
quiz.explain: 6 parts = 180°, so 1 part = 30°.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 3 instead of 6

quiz.q: A triangle's sides are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4 and its perimeter is 36 cm. How long is the longest side?
quiz.explain: 9 parts = 36 cm, so 1 part = 4 cm and the longest side is 4 × 4 = 16 cm.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 3 sides instead of 9 parts

quiz.q: Can a triangle have sides in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3?
options: No — the two shorter sides only equal the longest, so they lie flat
Yes — it makes a right triangle
No — the sides must all be equal
quiz.explain: For sides k, 2k, 3k: k + 2k = 3k. The shorter sides must add to MORE than the longest, so no triangle forms.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the triangle inequality

quiz.q: A triangle has sides in the ratio 3 : 4 : 5 and perimeter 24 cm. What are its sides?
quiz.explain: 12 parts = 24 cm, so 1 part = 2 cm: sides 6, 8, 10 cm (a right triangle, since 6² + 8² = 10²).
quiz.mistake: Uses the ratio numbers as lengths

quiz.q: Which ratio can be the sides of a triangle?
quiz.explain: 4 + 5 = 9 > 6, so a triangle forms. In the others the two smaller numbers add to less than the largest.
quiz.mistake: Checks only that the numbers are different

quiz.q: A triangle's angles are in the ratio 5 : 6 : 7. What is the middle-sized angle?
quiz.explain: 18 parts = 180°, so 1 part = 10° and the middle angle is 6 × 10° = 60°.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 3

teach.ask: Gappu has three twigs in the ratio 1 : 1 : 3. He wants a triangle-shaped perch. Will it work?
teach.praise: No! 1 + 1 is less than 3, so the twigs can't meet. I need the two short ones to be longer together than the long one.
teach.nudge: What must be true about the two shorter sides compared with the longest side?

topics.title: A slice of the pie: pie charts

learn.hook: A pie chart is a rotī cut fairly: each slice's angle shows its share of the whole 360°.
points: A pie chart shows parts of a whole as sectors (slices) of a circle.
Each sector's central angle is proportional to its value: angle = (value ÷ total) × 360°. All angles add to 360°.
From percentages: angle = percentage × 3.6°. So 25% gives 90° and 40% gives 144°.
To draw it: find each angle, draw a radius, measure the first angle with a protractor from it, then measure the next angle from the new line, and so on. Label each sector.
To read it: value = (angle ÷ 360°) × total. A 72° sector of 500 students is 72/360 × 500 = 100 students.

example.q: In a survey of 36 students, 12 like cricket, 9 like football and 15 like kabaddi. Find the sector angles.

learn.reallife: Budget news on TV often shows where each rupee goes using a pie chart.

games.title: Draw a pie chart
items: Find the total
Work out each angle: value ÷ total × 360°
Draw a circle and one radius
Measure each angle with a protractor, one after another
Label each sector

quiz.q: 30 out of 120 students walk to school. What is the angle of the 'walk' sector in a pie chart?
quiz.mistake: Uses the count itself as the angle

quiz.q: In a pie chart, a category makes up 40% of the total. What is its sector angle?
quiz.mistake: Uses the percentage as the angle

quiz.q: A pie chart shows 500 students. The 'music club' sector is 72°. How many students are in the music club?
quiz.mistake: Reads the angle as the number of students

quiz.q: A sector of a pie chart has an angle of 60°. What fraction of the whole does it show?
quiz.mistake: Divides by 100 instead of 360

quiz.q: In a survey of 36 students, 12 like cricket. What is the angle of the cricket sector?
quiz.mistake: Uses 100 as the whole instead of 360°

quiz.q: A family's budget of ₹30,000 is shown in a pie chart. The rent sector is 108°. How much is the rent?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the angle by 100

quiz.q: What do all the sector angles of a pie chart add up to?
quiz.explain: The sectors fill the whole circle, which is 360°.
quiz.mistake: Confuses angles with percentages

quiz.q: When drawing a pie chart with a protractor, where do you measure the second sector's angle from?
options: From the same starting radius again
From the line that ends the first sector
From the top of the page
From the centre outwards in any direction
quiz.explain: Sectors are placed side by side, so each new angle starts where the last one ended.
quiz.mistake: Measures every sector from the same starting line, so they overlap

teach.ask: Gappu asked 20 birds their favourite food: 10 said seeds, 5 worms, 5 berries. How should he draw the pie chart?
teach.praise: Seeds get 180° (half), worms 90°, berries 90°. My bird-food pie chart is ready!
teach.nudge: What fraction of the birds chose seeds? What angle is that?

learn.hook: One painter takes 12 days to paint a house. Do 3 painters also take 12 days? No, just 4 days! More hands, fewer days.
points: Two quantities are in inverse proportion if, when one is multiplied by a number, the other is divided by the same number.
In inverse proportion, x × y stays the same.
Examples: workers and days for a fixed job; speed and time for a fixed distance; number of children and laddoos each gets from a fixed box.
To solve: find the fixed product first, then divide by the new value.
Not every 'one goes up, other goes down' is inverse proportion. Check that the product stays the same.

example.q: 6 workers build a wall in 10 days. How long will 15 workers take at the same rate?

learn.reallife: More checkout counters at a shop mean shorter queues, and a faster train means a shorter journey time.

items.q: 6 workers take 10 days. 12 workers take how many days?
4 taps fill a tank in 6 hours. 8 taps take how many hours?
At 50 km/h a trip takes 4 hours. At 100 km/h, how many hours?
15 children get 8 laddoos each. With 20 children, how many each?
3 pumps empty a tank in 12 hours. 9 pumps take how many hours?

quiz.q: 6 workers build a wall in 10 days. How many days will 15 workers take, working at the same rate?
quiz.explain: Workers × days = 6 × 10 = 60. With 15 workers: 60 ÷ 15 = 4 days.
quiz.mistake: Treats it as direct proportion and gets 25 days

quiz.q: A train at 60 km/h takes 5 hours for a journey. How many hours does it take at 75 km/h?
quiz.explain: Distance = 60 × 5 = 300 km. At 75 km/h: 300 ÷ 75 = 4 hours.
quiz.mistake: Uses direct proportion and gets a longer time

quiz.q: Which pair of quantities is in inverse proportion?
options: Distance and time at a steady speed
Litres of milk and its cost
Speed and time for a fixed distance
quiz.explain: For a fixed distance, speed × time = distance stays the same. Double the speed, half the time.
quiz.mistake: Picks a direct proportion pair

quiz.q: x and y are in inverse proportion. When x = 8, y = 9. What is y when x = 12?
quiz.mistake: Uses direct proportion (gets 13.5)

quiz.q: A camp has enough food for 40 children for 15 days. If 10 more children join, how many days will the food last?
quiz.explain: Children × days = 40 × 15 = 600. With 50 children: 600 ÷ 50 = 12 days.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add the new children, or uses direct proportion

quiz.q: Riya shares a box of laddoos equally. With 8 friends, each gets 9 laddoos. How many does each get if there are 12 friends?
quiz.explain: Total laddoos = 8 × 9 = 72. With 12 friends: 72 ÷ 12 = 6 each.
quiz.mistake: Adds 4 more laddoos because there are 4 more friends

quiz.q: Which table shows x and y in inverse proportion?
quiz.explain: 2 × 12 = 4 × 6 = 8 × 3 = 24. The product stays the same, so it is inverse proportion.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any decreasing table is inverse proportion without checking products

quiz.q: 4 pipes fill a tank in 3 hours. How many such pipes are needed to fill it in 1 hour?
quiz.explain: Pipes × hours = 4 × 3 = 12. For 1 hour: 12 ÷ 1 = 12 pipes.
quiz.mistake: Thinks fewer hours means fewer pipes

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 2 birds eat a pile of seeds in 6 hours. How long will 4 birds take?
teach.praise: 2 × 6 = 12 bird-hours stays the same, so 4 birds take 12 ÷ 4 = 3 hours. More birds, less time!
teach.nudge: When the number of birds doubles, what happens to the time? What stays the same?

learn.hook: Ravi paints a wall in 6 days and Sita in 3 days. Working together, do they take 9 days? 4.5? Neither — they finish in 2!
points: Think of the rate: if Ravi takes 6 days for the whole job, he does 1/6 of it each day. Sita does 1/3 each day.
Working together, the rates add: 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2 of the job per day, so together they take 2 days.
Pipes work the same way: one fills a tank in 4 hours, another in 6 hours. Together: 1/4 + 1/6 = 5/12 per hour, so 12/5 = 2.4 hours (2 hours 24 minutes).
A drain pipe works against you, so subtract its rate: fill in 3 hours, empty in 6 hours → 1/3 − 1/6 = 1/6 per hour, so 6 hours to fill.

example.q: Ravi paints a wall in 6 days and Sita in 3 days. How long do they take together?

learn.reallife: Construction teams, kitchen staff and even two pumps in a housing society all 'work together' this way.

games.title: Together or not?
items: Two people working together always take the average of their times.
Rates add; the time is shorter than either person alone.
If A does 1/8 of a job per day, A alone takes 8 days.
8 × 1/8 = 1 whole job.
A drain pipe's rate is subtracted from a filling pipe's rate.
It removes water while the other adds.
Two equal workers who each take 10 days finish together in 5 days.

quiz.q: Ravi paints a wall in 6 days and Sita paints it in 3 days. How many days do they take together?
quiz.explain: Rates: 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2 of the wall per day, so 2 days.
quiz.mistake: Adds or averages the times

quiz.q: One pipe fills a tank in 4 hours and another in 6 hours. How long do both together take?
quiz.explain: 1/4 + 1/6 = 5/12 per hour, so 12/5 = 2.4 hours (2 h 24 min).
quiz.mistake: Averages the two times

quiz.q: A can finish a job in 10 days and B in 15 days. How many days do they take together?
quiz.mistake: Adds the days

quiz.q: A tap fills a tank in 3 hours, but a leak empties a full tank in 6 hours. With both open, how long does it take to fill?
quiz.explain: Fill rate 1/3 minus leak rate 1/6 = 1/6 per hour, so 6 hours.
quiz.mistake: Adds the leak rate instead of subtracting

quiz.q: Asha can do a job alone in 8 days. What fraction of the job does she do in one day?
quiz.explain: The whole job takes 8 days, so each day she does 1/8 of it.
quiz.mistake: Gives the number of days instead of the rate

quiz.q: Three taps fill a tank in 6, 12 and 4 hours. How long do all three take together?
quiz.mistake: Adds the times

quiz.q: Amit can finish a job in 12 days. He works 4 days and leaves; Bina finishes the rest in 6 days. How long would Bina take alone?
quiz.explain: Amit does 4/12 = 1/3. Bina does the remaining 2/3 in 6 days, so the whole job takes her 6 × 3/2 = 9 days.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Bina did the whole job in 6 days

quiz.q: Two workers who each take 10 days for a job work together. How many days do they take?
quiz.explain: 1/10 + 1/10 = 1/5 per day, so 5 days. This also fits inverse proportion: twice the workers, half the time.
quiz.mistake: Adds the days

teach.ask: Gappu builds a nest in 4 days and his friend Pari in 4 days too. Gappu thinks together they need 8 days. Help him!
teach.praise: Each of us does 1/4 a day, so together 1/2 a day — just 2 days! Teamwork is faster.
teach.nudge: How much of the nest does each bird build in one day?

learn.hook: The Vande Bharat Express can run at 160 km/h. A cheetah can sprint at over 100 km/h, but only for a few seconds. Who wins a long race? Rates tell the story!
points: A rate compares two different kinds of quantities: km per hour, ₹ per kg, words per minute, heartbeats per minute.
A unit rate is the amount for 1 unit: 300 km in 5 hours is 60 km per hour.
Speed = distance ÷ time, distance = speed × time, time = distance ÷ speed.
To change km/h to m/s, multiply by 1000/3600 = 5/18. So 72 km/h = 20 m/s.
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. It is not always the average of the two speeds.

example.q: A train goes 180 km in 2 hours and then 120 km in 2 hours. What is its average speed?

learn.reallife: Cricket commentators give run rates per over, doctors check pulse rate per minute, and shops show price per kg.

games.title: Slowest to fastest
items: Walking at 5 km/h
Cycling 3 km in 12 minutes
Auto-rickshaw: 50 km in 2 hours
Car at 20 m/s
Train: 450 km in 5 hours

games.title: Rate check
items: 36 km/h is the same as 10 m/s.
Going 60 km/h for 1 hour and then 40 km/h for 1 hour gives an average speed of 50 km/h.
Total 100 km in 2 hours = 50 km/h. The times are equal, so here it works.
Going 60 km at 60 km/h and then 60 km at 40 km/h gives an average speed of 50 km/h.
Time = 1 h + 1.5 h = 2.5 h, so average = 120 ÷ 2.5 = 48 km/h.
At ₹40 per kg, 3 kg cost ₹120.
Speed = time ÷ distance.
Speed = distance ÷ time.
A heart rate is measured in beats per minute.
It counts heartbeats in each minute.

quiz.q: A bus travels 240 km in 4 hours. What is its speed in km per hour?
quiz.explain: Speed = distance ÷ time = 240 ÷ 4 = 60 km/h.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies distance by time

quiz.q: Change 72 km/h into metres per second. What is the number of m/s?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by 3.6 instead of dividing (gets 259.2)

quiz.q: Kabir cycles at 15 km/h. How long does he take to cover 45 km?
quiz.explain: Time = distance ÷ speed = 45 ÷ 15 = 3 hours.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies distance by speed, or divides speed by distance

quiz.q: Aisha walks 2 km to school in 30 minutes. What is her speed in km/h?
quiz.explain: 30 minutes = 1/2 hour. Speed = 2 ÷ 1/2 = 4 km/h.
quiz.mistake: Divides minutes by km (30 ÷ 2 = 15) without changing to hours

quiz.q: A train travels 180 km in 2 hours and then 120 km in 2 hours. What is its average speed for the whole trip in km/h?
quiz.explain: Total distance 300 km in total time 4 hours: 300 ÷ 4 = 75 km/h.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 2 hours only, or gives total distance

quiz.q: Rice costs ₹480 for 8 kg. What is the rate per kg?
quiz.explain: Rate = ₹480 ÷ 8 kg = ₹60 per kg.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies instead of dividing

quiz.q: A heart beats 72 times a minute. How many times does it beat in one hour?
quiz.explain: 1 hour = 60 minutes. 72 × 60 = 4320 beats.
quiz.mistake: Adds 60 instead of multiplying, or multiplies by 10

quiz.q: Joseph drives 60 km at 60 km/h and then another 60 km at 30 km/h. What is his average speed for the whole trip in km/h?
quiz.explain: Time: 60 ÷ 60 = 1 h and 60 ÷ 30 = 2 h. Total 120 km in 3 hours = 40 km/h.
quiz.mistake: Averages the two speeds (45) even though the times are different

teach.ask: Gappu asks: I flew 30 km in 2 hours. How do I find my speed?
teach.praise: Distance divided by time: 30 ÷ 2 = 15 km per hour. Zoom zoom, Gappu!
teach.nudge: Which two numbers do you need, and do you multiply or divide them?

learn.hook: Look closely at a fern leaf: each little leaflet looks like a tiny copy of the whole leaf. Shapes like this are called fractals!
points: A fractal is a shape that repeats itself at smaller and smaller scales (self-similar). Ferns, cauliflower florets, lightning and coastlines are natural examples.
Sierpinski carpet: split a square into 9 equal squares and remove the middle one. Repeat with each of the 8 remaining squares. After step n there are 8ⁿ squares left.
Holes in the carpet: 1 after step 1, 1 + 8 = 9 after step 2, 1 + 8 + 64 = 73 after step 3.
Sierpinski gasket: join the midpoints of an equilateral triangle's sides to get 4 congruent triangles and remove the middle one. Repeat. After step n there are 3ⁿ triangles.
Remaining area: the carpet keeps 8/9 of its area at each step, so (8/9)ⁿ after n steps; the gasket keeps 3/4, so (3/4)ⁿ.

example.q: A Sierpinski carpet starts as an 81 cm² square. What area is left after 2 steps?
steps: Each step keeps 8/9 of the area

learn.reallife: Mobile phone antennas are sometimes shaped like fractals so they can pick up many signals in a small space.

games.title: Fractal facts
items: A fern leaf is a natural example of a fractal.
Each leaflet looks like a small copy of the whole.
Joining the midpoints of an equilateral triangle gives 4 congruent triangles.
They are all equilateral with half the side.
The Sierpinski carpet gains area at every step.
It loses 1/9 of its area at each step.
After step 3 the Sierpinski gasket has 27 triangles.

quiz.q: How many small squares remain after step 1 of the Sierpinski carpet?
quiz.explain: The square is split into 9 and the middle one is removed, leaving 8.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to remove the middle square

quiz.q: How many small squares remain after step 2 of the Sierpinski carpet?
quiz.explain: Each of the 8 squares becomes 8 smaller squares: 8 × 8 = 64.
quiz.mistake: Adds 8 instead of multiplying

quiz.q: How many holes does the Sierpinski carpet have after step 2?
quiz.explain: Step 1 makes 1 hole; step 2 makes one hole in each of the 8 squares: 1 + 8 = 9.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the new holes

quiz.q: A Sierpinski carpet starts with area 81 cm². What area remains after 2 steps?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts only one ninth, once

quiz.q: How many shaded triangles are there after step 1 of the Sierpinski gasket?
quiz.explain: Joining midpoints makes 4 triangles, and removing the middle one leaves 3.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to remove the middle triangle

quiz.q: How many shaded triangles are there after step 3 of the Sierpinski gasket?
quiz.explain: Each step triples the number of triangles: 3³ = 27.
quiz.mistake: Uses 4 instead of 3 for each step

quiz.q: What fraction of the Sierpinski gasket's original area remains after step 2?
quiz.explain: Each step keeps 3/4 of the area: (3/4)² = 9/16.
quiz.mistake: Keeps 3/4 only once

quiz.q: Which of these is a fractal found in nature?
quiz.explain: Each small part of a fern looks like a smaller copy of the whole leaf.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any natural object is a fractal

teach.ask: Gappu drew a triangle, joined the midpoints and shaded the corner triangles. What should he do next to make a fractal?
teach.praise: Repeat with every shaded triangle, again and again — 3, 9, 27 triangles! My Sierpinski gasket is growing.
teach.nudge: What do you do with each of the three shaded triangles?

topics.title: The Koch snowflake and fractals in art

learn.hook: Start with a triangle, add tiny triangles to every side again and again — the snowflake's border grows forever, yet it fits on your page!
points: Koch snowflake: start with an equilateral triangle. Split each side into 3 equal parts and build a small equilateral triangle on the middle part (removing its base). Repeat on every new side.
Each step turns every side into 4 sides, each 1/3 as long. So the number of sides goes 3, 12, 48, 192, ... = 3 × 4ⁿ.
Each step multiplies the perimeter by 4/3. A triangle of side 9 cm (perimeter 27 cm) becomes 36 cm after step 1 and 48 cm after step 2.

Fractal ideas in art and buildings: the Kandariya Mahadev temple at Khajuraho has spires made of smaller and smaller copies of the main spire; Fulani blankets from West Africa repeat diamond patterns at smaller sizes; the artist M. C. Escher drew shrinking repeated shapes.

example.q: A Koch snowflake starts as a triangle with side 9 cm. Find the perimeter after step 2.

learn.reallife: Temple spires, rangoli borders and mehendi designs often repeat a motif at smaller and smaller sizes — fractal art!

games.title: Fractals in art
items: The Kandariya Mahadev temple is at Khajuraho.
It is in Madhya Pradesh.
Fulani blankets come from West Africa.
Their patterns repeat at smaller sizes.
Each Koch step makes the perimeter smaller.
Each step multiplies it by 4/3.
The number of sides of the Koch snowflake is multiplied by 4 at each step.
Every side becomes 4 sides.

quiz.q: How many sides does the Koch snowflake have after step 1?
quiz.explain: Each of the 3 sides becomes 4 sides: 3 × 4 = 12.
quiz.mistake: Adds a side instead of multiplying by 4

quiz.q: How many sides does the Koch snowflake have after step 2?
quiz.mistake: Doubles instead of multiplying by 4

quiz.q: A Koch snowflake starts with side 9 cm. What is its perimeter after step 1?
quiz.explain: 12 sides of 3 cm = 36 cm.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the sides become one third as long

quiz.q: The same snowflake (start side 9 cm): what is its perimeter after step 2?
quiz.explain: 48 sides of 1 cm = 48 cm.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the side count by the original side

quiz.q: By what number is the Koch snowflake's perimeter multiplied at each step?
quiz.explain: Each side becomes 4 pieces, each 1/3 as long: 4 × 1/3 = 4/3.
quiz.mistake: Uses only the 4 new pieces or only the 1/3

quiz.q: Where is the Kandariya Mahadev temple, famous for its fractal-like spires?
quiz.explain: The Kandariya Mahadev temple at Khajuraho has small spires repeating the shape of the main spire.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up famous temple towns

quiz.q: Fulani blankets with repeating diamond patterns come from which region?
quiz.explain: The Fulani people of West Africa weave blankets whose diamonds repeat at smaller sizes.
quiz.mistake: Guesses without knowing the craft's home

quiz.q: What makes a design 'fractal-like'?
options: It has exactly one line of symmetry
The same shape repeats at smaller and smaller sizes
quiz.explain: Self-similarity — copies of the shape inside itself at smaller scales — is the key idea.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any pretty pattern is a fractal

teach.ask: Gappu drew a triangle and added a bump to the middle of each side. What should he do to make a Koch snowflake?
teach.praise: Split every side into thirds, add a triangle on the middle part, and repeat on all the new sides. Snowflake!
teach.nudge: How do you split each side? Which part gets the new triangle?

learn.hook: Imagine slicing one corner off a cube with a knife. How many faces, edges and corners does it have now? Close your eyes and picture it!
points: Cutting off one corner of a cube removes 1 vertex but makes a new triangular face with 3 new vertices and 3 new edges. So F = 7, V = 10, E = 15 (and 7 + 10 − 15 = 2 still).
Cut off all 8 corners and the cube has 6 + 8 = 14 faces, 8 × 3 = 24 vertices and 12 + 24 = 36 edges.
A prism has two copies of a base joined by rectangles. With an n-sided base: faces n + 2, edges 3n, vertices 2n.
A pyramid has one base and triangles meeting at a top point. With an n-sided base: faces n + 1, edges 2n, vertices n + 1.
Prisms and pyramids are named by their base: triangular prism, pentagonal pyramid, hexagonal prism ...

example.q: Count the faces, edges and vertices of a hexagonal pyramid.

learn.reallife: Gem cutters slice corners off crystals to make new faces — they must picture the result before cutting!

quiz.q: A cube has one corner sliced off. How many faces does it have now?
quiz.explain: The cut makes one new triangular face: 6 + 1 = 7.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the new face made by the cut

quiz.q: A cube has one corner sliced off. How many vertices does it have now?
quiz.explain: One vertex is removed and 3 new ones appear: 8 − 1 + 3 = 10.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the old corner disappears

quiz.q: A cube has one corner sliced off. How many edges does it have now?
quiz.explain: The new triangle adds 3 edges: 12 + 3 = 15. Check Euler: 7 + 10 − 15 = 2.
quiz.mistake: Adds only one edge

quiz.q: How many edges does a prism with an octagon (8 sides) as its base have?
quiz.explain: A prism with an n-sided base has 3n edges: 3 × 8 = 24.
quiz.mistake: Uses 2n, the pyramid rule

quiz.q: How many faces does a pentagonal pyramid have?
quiz.explain: A pyramid with an n-sided base has n + 1 faces: 5 + 1 = 6.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the base

quiz.q: A pyramid has 10 edges. What is its base?
quiz.explain: A pyramid has 2n edges, so 2n = 10 and n = 5: a pentagon.
quiz.mistake: Uses the prism rule 3n

quiz.q: A prism has 9 faces. How many vertices does it have?
quiz.explain: Faces = n + 2 = 9, so n = 7. Vertices = 2n = 14.
quiz.mistake: Uses the face count as the vertex count

quiz.q: All 8 corners of a cube are sliced off. How many faces does the new solid have?
quiz.explain: Each cut adds one face: 6 + 8 = 14.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the new triangular faces

teach.ask: Gappu sliced one corner off a cheese cube. He says it still has 8 corners. Is he right?
teach.praise: The old corner vanished but three new ones appeared, so 8 − 1 + 3 = 10 corners. Cheesy maths!
teach.nudge: What happens to the corner you cut? How many new corners does the cut make?

learn.hook: Hold a glass at eye level: it looks like a rectangle. Look down into it from above: it is a circle! Same glass, different views.
points: A solid can look different from the front, the side and the top. The top view is also called the plan.
A cylinder standing up: rectangle from the front, circle from the top. A cone on its base: triangle from the front, circle from the top. A sphere looks like a circle from every side.
A cube looks like a square from the front, side and top.
For stacks of cubes, count layer by layer. The top view shows how many columns there are.
A net is a flat pattern that folds into a solid. Cylinder: a rectangle and 2 circles. Cone: a curved sector and a circle. Square pyramid: a square and 4 triangles. Cube: 6 squares.

example.q: Arjun puts 3 cubes in a row on the floor and 1 cube on top of the middle one. Describe the front view and count the cubes.
steps: Bottom row: 3 squares side by side
Top: 1 square above the middle one
example.answer: Front view: 3 squares with 1 on top of the middle; 4 cubes

learn.reallife: Architects draw front, side and top views of buildings, and sweet-box makers cut flat nets that fold into boxes.

games.title: Top view: circle or not?
buckets: Top view is not a circle
items: Cylinder standing upright
Cone standing on its base
Sphere
Steel tumbler standing upright
Cube
Square pyramid
Brick lying flat
Triangular prism lying on a rectangular face

quiz.q: What does an upright cylinder look like from the top?
quiz.explain: Looking down, you see only the round top face, so the top view is a circle.
quiz.mistake: Gives the front view (rectangle) instead of the top view

quiz.q: What is the front view of a cone standing on its base?
quiz.explain: From the front, the cone narrows from a wide base to a point, so it looks like a triangle.
quiz.mistake: Gives the top view (circle) instead of the front view

quiz.q: Which solid looks like a circle from the front, the side and the top?
quiz.explain: A sphere is round in every direction, so every view is a circle.
quiz.mistake: Picks cylinder, whose front view is a rectangle

quiz.q: Arjun stacks cubes: 3 in a row on the floor and 1 on top of the middle one. How many cubes does he use?
quiz.explain: 3 cubes in the bottom row and 1 on top: 3 + 1 = 4.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the bottom layer

quiz.q: Which net folds into a cylinder?
options: A circle and a curved sector
quiz.explain: The rectangle rolls into the curved side, and the two circles become the top and bottom. A circle and a sector make a cone.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the cylinder's net with the cone's net

quiz.q: Which shapes make up the net of a square pyramid?
quiz.explain: The square is the base, and the 4 triangles fold up to meet at the top.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the pyramid with a prism or cube

quiz.q: A cube with edge 3 cm is unfolded into a net of 6 squares. What is the total area of the net?
quiz.explain: Each square is 3 × 3 = 9 cm². Six squares: 6 × 9 = 54 cm².
quiz.mistake: Finds the volume (27) or uses only 4 faces (36)

quiz.q: Joseph builds a 2 × 2 × 2 cube from small cubes. How many small cubes can he see from directly above?
quiz.explain: From the top you see only the top layer, which is 2 × 2 = 4 small cubes. The bottom 4 are hidden.
quiz.mistake: Counts all 8 cubes, including hidden ones

teach.ask: Gappu asks: Why does my cylinder-shaped water bottle look like a rectangle sometimes and a circle at other times?
teach.praise: From the front it looks like a rectangle, and from the top it looks like a circle. It depends on the view! Clever!
teach.nudge: Where are you looking from when it looks like a circle? And when it looks like a rectangle?

topics.title: Faces, edges, vertices and Euler's formula

learn.hook: Count the faces, corners and edges of any box, add the faces and corners, then subtract the edges. You will always get 2. Try it on a dice!
points: A solid's flat surfaces are faces, the lines where two faces meet are edges, and the corners are vertices.
A cube or cuboid has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. A square pyramid has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices.
A polyhedron is a solid whose faces are all flat polygons. Cylinders, cones and spheres have curved surfaces, so they are not polyhedra.
Euler's formula for polyhedra: F + V − E = 2. For a cube: 6 + 8 − 12 = 2.
A prism has two identical ends joined by rectangles. A pyramid has one base with triangles meeting at the top.

example.q: A pentagonal prism has 7 faces and 15 edges. How many vertices does it have?

learn.reallife: Gift boxes, tents, the pyramid-shaped roof of a temple and a cricket ball show the difference between polyhedra and curved solids.

games.title: Polyhedron or not?
items: Cube
Cuboid
Square pyramid
Triangular prism
Sphere
Cylinder
Cone
A round laddoo

quiz.q: How many edges does a cube have?
quiz.explain: A cube has 4 edges on the top, 4 on the bottom and 4 upright ones: 12 edges.
quiz.mistake: Counts faces (6) or vertices (8) instead of edges

quiz.q: A polyhedron has 8 faces and 6 vertices. How many edges does it have? (Use F + V − E = 2.)
quiz.mistake: Adds 2 instead of subtracting it

quiz.q: How many vertices does a square pyramid have?
quiz.explain: It has 4 corners at the square base and 1 at the top: 5 vertices.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the top point (apex)

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a polyhedron?
quiz.explain: A cylinder has curved surfaces. A polyhedron must have only flat polygon faces.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any solid shape is a polyhedron

quiz.q: A triangular prism has 5 faces and 6 vertices. How many edges does it have?
quiz.explain: F + V − E = 2 gives 5 + 6 − E = 2, so E = 9. Count check: 3 + 3 edges on the triangles and 3 joining them.
quiz.mistake: Adds F and V without subtracting 2

quiz.q: Meena wraps a cuboid-shaped gift box, covering every face. How many faces does she cover?
quiz.explain: A cuboid has 6 faces: top, bottom, front, back, left and right.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the side faces, or counts corners

quiz.q: A pentagonal prism has 7 faces and 15 edges. How many vertices does it have?
quiz.explain: 7 + V − 15 = 2, so V = 10. Each pentagon end has 5 corners: 5 + 5 = 10.
quiz.mistake: Gets the signs in Euler's formula mixed up

quiz.q: Can a polyhedron have 10 faces, 10 vertices and 15 edges?
options: No, because F + V − E would be 5, not 2
No, because 15 is an odd number
quiz.explain: Every polyhedron obeys F + V − E = 2. Here 10 + 10 − 15 = 5, so no such polyhedron exists.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the number of edges must be even (a triangular prism has 9)

teach.ask: Gappu asks: What is Euler's formula, and how can I check it on a cube?
teach.praise: Faces plus vertices minus edges is 2. For a cube: 6 + 8 − 12 = 2. Euler was a genius, and so are you!
teach.nudge: Which three things do you count on a cube? What do you do with them?

learn.hook: An ant wants to crawl from one corner of a box to the opposite corner along its surface. The shortest route is easy to find — if you unfold the box!
points: A net is a flat shape that folds into a solid. A cube has exactly 11 different nets, each made of 6 squares. Six squares in a 2 × 3 block is NOT a cube net.
Other nets: cuboid — 6 rectangles; tetrahedron — 4 equilateral triangles; square pyramid — 1 square and 4 triangles; triangular prism — 2 triangles and 3 rectangles; octahedron — 8 triangles.
Shortest path on a surface: unfold the faces the path crosses into a flat net. The shortest path is then a straight line, found with the Baudhayana–Pythagoras theorem.
Example: a box with a 3 cm × 3 cm base and height 8 cm. Unfold two side faces: the ant crosses a 6 cm × 8 cm rectangle, so the path is √(6² + 8²) = 10 cm.

example.q: An ant crawls on the surface of a cube with edge 1 m from one corner to the opposite corner. How long is the shortest path?
steps: Unfold two faces into a 2 m × 1 m rectangle

learn.reallife: Packaging designers draw nets to cut cardboard boxes, and engineers unfold surfaces to lay the shortest cables.

games.title: Cube net or not?
items: A cross: 4 squares in a column with one on each side of the second
A 2-2-2 staircase of squares
4 in a row with one above the 1st and one below the 4th
Six squares in a 2 × 3 block
Five squares in a row with one on top
A 2 × 2 block of squares with two more attached

quiz.q: How many different nets does a cube have?
quiz.explain: There are exactly 11 different ways to arrange 6 squares so that they fold into a cube.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the number of nets with the number of faces

quiz.q: Which arrangement of 6 squares is NOT a net of a cube?
options: A cross of 4 in a column with one square on each side
4 in a row with one square above the first and one below the last
quiz.explain: In a 2 × 3 block, folding makes squares overlap and leaves faces open, so it cannot form a cube.
steps: Try folding: two squares end up on the same face
quiz.mistake: Thinks any 6 squares make a cube

quiz.q: What is the net of a tetrahedron made of?
quiz.explain: A tetrahedron has 4 triangular faces, so its net has 4 triangles.
quiz.mistake: Mixes it up with a square pyramid

quiz.q: How many triangles are in the net of an octahedron?
quiz.explain: 'Octa' means eight: an octahedron has 8 triangular faces.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with 6 (cube faces)

quiz.q: Which shapes make the net of a triangular prism?
quiz.explain: A triangular prism has 2 triangular ends and 3 rectangular sides.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the numbers of triangles and rectangles

quiz.q: A box has a 3 cm × 3 cm base and is 8 cm tall. An ant crawls over two side faces from a bottom corner to the opposite top corner. How long is its shortest path?
quiz.explain: Unfold the two faces into a 6 cm × 8 cm rectangle. The straight path is √(36 + 64) = 10 cm.
quiz.mistake: Adds the edges instead of using the theorem

quiz.q: An ant crawls on a cube with edge 1 m from one corner to the opposite corner. What is the square of the shortest path length?
quiz.explain: Unfolding two faces gives a 2 × 1 rectangle, so path² = 2² + 1² = 5 (path ≈ 2.24 m).
quiz.mistake: Uses the diagonal through the inside of the cube (√3)

quiz.q: What is the total area of the net of a 5 cm × 4 cm × 3 cm cuboid?
quiz.explain: The net has two of each face: 2 × (20 + 15 + 12) = 94 cm².
quiz.mistake: Counts each face only once

teach.ask: Gappu wants to walk across a box from one corner to the far corner on its surface. How can a net help him find the shortest way?
teach.praise: Unfold the box flat, draw a straight line, and use the theorem. Shortest walk found!
teach.nudge: What happens to the path when the box is unfolded? What is the shortest path on a flat sheet?

topics.title: Projections, shadows and building from views

learn.hook: At noon your shadow is tiny; in the evening it is longer than you. A shadow is a projection — and it obeys some neat rules.
points: Projecting a point onto a plane means dropping it straight onto the plane. Projecting an object projects all its points.

When light falls straight down (a perpendicular projection, like the overhead noon sun), the shadow is never longer than the object: a 10 cm pencil's shadow can be anything from 0 (pencil upright) to 10 cm (pencil flat). Slanting evening light can make longer shadows.
Sunlight casts shadows that are parallel projections, so parallel rods have parallel shadows.
Matching views: a cylinder has a circle top view and a rectangle front view; a square pyramid has a square (with diagonals) top view and a triangle front view.
Building from views: if the top view of a stack of cubes is a 2 × 2 square and the front and side views each show two columns 2 cubes high, there can be up to 8 cubes, but as few as 6.

example.q: A stack's top view is a 2 × 2 square; its front and side views each show two columns, 2 cubes tall. What is the fewest number of cubes?
steps: Each of the 4 places needs at least 1 cube (top view)
Each front column and each side column needs a tower of 2
Two towers of 2 on a diagonal do both jobs

learn.reallife: Architects draw front, side and top views so builders can make exactly the right shape.

games.title: Shadow rules
items: A shadow (projection) can be longer than the object under the overhead sun.
A parallel projection is never longer than the object.
Two parallel rods in sunlight cast parallel shadows.
Parallel lines project to parallel lines.
A pencil standing straight up under the overhead sun casts almost no shadow.
It projects to a point.
A flat square tile held parallel to the ground casts a square shadow under the overhead sun.
It is projected without change.

quiz.q: Under the overhead sun, how long can the shadow of a 10 cm pencil be?
quiz.explain: A projection is never longer than the object. Upright gives a point; lying flat gives 10 cm.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a shadow can stretch longer than the object

quiz.q: A stick stands straight up under the overhead noon sun. What is its shadow?
options: A line as long as the stick
quiz.explain: Every point of the stick drops onto the same spot on the ground.
steps: Vertical stick, vertical rays → one point
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the sun is straight overhead

quiz.q: Two parallel bamboo poles stand in the sun. What can you say about their shadows?
options: The shadows meet at a point
The shadows are always equal to the poles
The shadows are at right angles
quiz.explain: Sunlight gives parallel projection, and parallel lines project to parallel lines.
quiz.mistake: Thinks shadows meet like lines from a lamp

quiz.q: A square tile is held parallel to the ground under the overhead sun. What shape is its shadow?
options: A square of the same size
quiz.explain: When the object is parallel to the ground, the overhead sun projects it without any change.
steps: Parallel to the ground → same shape and size
quiz.mistake: Thinks every shadow is distorted

quiz.q: A solid has a square top view and a triangle front view. Which solid is it?
quiz.explain: A square base seen from above and a triangle from the front fits a square pyramid.
quiz.mistake: Matches only one of the two views

quiz.q: A stack's top view is a 2 × 2 square and its front and side views each show two columns 2 cubes tall. What is the greatest number of cubes it can have?
quiz.explain: At most 2 cubes stand in each of the 4 places: 4 × 2 = 8.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the cubes seen in one view

quiz.q: For the same views (top 2 × 2, front and side each two columns 2 tall), what is the fewest number of cubes?
quiz.explain: Two towers of 2 placed on a diagonal make every front and side column 2 tall; the other 2 places need 1 cube each: 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 6.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every place must be 2 tall

quiz.q: Which solid can have a circle as its top view AND a circle as its front view?
quiz.explain: A sphere looks like a circle from every direction.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that a cylinder looks like a rectangle from the front

teach.ask: Gappu's shadow at noon is tiny but in the evening it's huge. Explain what a shadow is and why its length changes!
teach.praise: A shadow is a projection made by light. At noon the sun is overhead, so my shadow is short; in the evening the light comes at a slant!
teach.nudge: What makes a shadow? Where is the sun at noon compared with the evening?

learn.hook: Can you draw a 3D cube on flat paper so it really looks solid? Isometric dot paper makes it easy — and lets you draw impossible shapes too!
points: Isometric dot paper has dots in a triangular pattern; each dot has 6 equally spaced neighbours.
On it, vertical edges stay vertical and the other edges slope at 30° to the horizontal. Equal edges of a cube are drawn the same length.
