An isometric drawing of a cube shows 3 faces, 7 vertices and 9 edges; one vertex is hidden at the back.
Arrangements of cubes (like tetris shapes) are drawn cube by cube, starting with the front-most cubes.
The impossible triangle looks solid, but each corner joins beams that are at different depths. Each corner makes sense alone; the whole object cannot exist in 3D.

example.q: How many small cube faces can you see in an isometric drawing of a 2 × 2 × 2 cube?
steps: Each big face shows 2 × 2 = 4 small faces

learn.reallife: Video games, engineering drawings and furniture assembly guides often use isometric views.

games.title: Isometric facts
items: On isometric paper, vertical edges are drawn vertical.
Only the other two directions slope.
An isometric drawing of a cube shows all 6 faces.
It shows 3 faces.
Each dot on isometric dot paper has 6 equally spaced neighbours.
The dots form a triangular grid.
The impossible triangle can be built from three straight wooden beams.
It only works as a drawing.

items.q: Faces of a cube you can see
Vertices of a cube you can see
Edges of a cube you can see
Small faces seen on a 2 × 2 × 2 cube
Small faces seen on a 3 × 3 × 3 cube

quiz.q: On isometric dot paper, how are the vertical edges of a box drawn?
quiz.explain: Vertical edges stay vertical; only the other two sets of edges slope at 30°.
quiz.mistake: Slopes every edge

quiz.q: On isometric paper, at what angle to the horizontal are the non-vertical edges drawn?
quiz.explain: The two sloping directions make 30° with the horizontal.
quiz.mistake: Uses 45°, as in some sketches

quiz.q: How many faces of a cube can you see in an isometric drawing?
quiz.explain: Only the top and two side faces face the viewer.
quiz.mistake: Counts all the faces of the cube

quiz.q: How many vertices of a cube can you see in an isometric drawing?
quiz.explain: All 8 corners exist, but one is hidden behind the cube.
quiz.mistake: Counts the hidden vertex

quiz.q: How many small cube faces can you see in an isometric drawing of a 2 × 2 × 2 cube?
quiz.explain: 3 big faces are visible, each made of 4 small faces: 3 × 4 = 12.
quiz.mistake: Counts the small cubes instead of the visible faces

quiz.q: Why is the impossible triangle impossible?
options: Its corners join beams at different depths, so the whole shape cannot exist in 3D
quiz.explain: Each corner looks fine, but following the beams around shows they cannot all meet in real space.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the drawing breaks a rule of triangles

quiz.q: What pattern do the dots on isometric dot paper make?
options: A triangular pattern, each dot with 6 equal neighbours
quiz.explain: Isometric dots sit at the corners of equilateral triangles.
quiz.mistake: Confuses isometric paper with square dot paper

quiz.q: In an isometric drawing of a cube with edge 3 cm, how long are the drawn edges?
options: Only the vertical edges are drawn
quiz.explain: Isometric drawing keeps equal edges equal, so every edge of the cube is drawn the same length.
quiz.mistake: Thinks sloping edges must be drawn shorter

teach.ask: Gappu wants to draw a tetris-shaped stack of 4 cubes so it looks 3D. How can isometric paper help?
teach.praise: Vertical lines straight up, the rest at 30°, and draw the front cubes first. My tetris block looks real!
teach.nudge: Which edges stay vertical on isometric paper? Which cubes should you draw first?

learn.hook: With just a pencil, a ruler and a compass you can draw a perfect 60°, 30°, 90° or 45° angle, without ever looking at a protractor!
points: A compass keeps a fixed distance, so every point on an arc is the same distance from the compass point.
Perpendicular bisector of AB: draw arcs of the same radius (more than half of AB) from A and from B. Join the two points where they cross. Every point on this line is equally far from A and B.
Angle bisector: draw an arc from the vertex cutting both arms. From those two points draw equal arcs that cross. Join the crossing point to the vertex.
60°: draw an arc from the vertex, then an arc of the same radius from where it cuts the arm. This makes an equilateral triangle. Bisect 60° to get 30°; bisect 90° to get 45°.
A triangle can be drawn from three sides only if any two sides together are longer than the third.

example.q: How can you construct an angle of 45° with a ruler and compass?
steps: Draw a line and mark a point O on it
Construct a perpendicular at O to get 90°

learn.reallife: Architects, carpenters and rangoli artists use compass constructions to get exact angles and symmetric designs.

games.title: How to construct it
pairs: arc from vertex, same arc from where it cuts the arm
draw a perpendicular to a line

games.title: Compass check
items: Every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB is the same distance from A and from B.
That is exactly what makes it the perpendicular bisector.
For a perpendicular bisector, the arcs must have a radius less than half of AB.
With less than half, the arcs from A and B would not meet. The radius must be more than half.
Bisecting a 60° angle gives 30°.
A triangle can be drawn with sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm.
3 + 4 = 7, which is less than 8, so the sides cannot meet.
Bisecting 90° and then bisecting one half again gives 22.5°.
An angle bisector divides an angle into two equal parts.
Bisect means cut into two equal halves.

quiz.q: What angle do you get when you bisect a 90° angle?
quiz.explain: Bisecting cuts an angle into two equal halves: 90° ÷ 2 = 45°.
quiz.mistake: Doubles the angle instead of halving it

quiz.q: Riya draws arcs of the same radius from points A and B and joins the two points where the arcs cross. What has she drawn?
quiz.explain: The two crossing points are each equally far from A and B. The line through them cuts AB in half at 90°.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the perpendicular bisector with the angle bisector

quiz.q: Point P lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB, and PA = 7 cm. What is PB?
quiz.explain: Every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB is equally far from A and B, so PB = PA = 7 cm.
quiz.mistake: Doubles or halves PA, thinking P must be the midpoint

quiz.q: Which set of side lengths can make a triangle?
quiz.explain: 5 + 6 = 11 is more than 10, so the sides can meet. In the others, the two shorter sides add up to the longest side or less.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any three lengths can make a triangle

quiz.q: To construct 60°, you draw an arc from the vertex and then an arc of the same radius from where it cuts the arm. Why does this give 60°?
options: It makes an equilateral triangle, and each angle of that triangle is 60°
quiz.explain: The vertex, the first cut point and the crossing point are all one radius apart, forming an equilateral triangle. Each of its angles is 180° ÷ 3 = 60°.
quiz.mistake: Follows the steps without seeing the equilateral triangle behind them

quiz.q: Kabir bisects an angle of 130°. What is the size of each part?
quiz.explain: Bisecting means halving: 130° ÷ 2 = 65°.
quiz.mistake: Doubles the angle

quiz.q: Which construction gives an angle of 120°?
options: Make two 60° angles side by side
quiz.explain: 60° + 60° = 120°. Bisecting 60° gives 30°, bisecting 90° gives 45°, and a perpendicular gives 90°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks bisecting makes an angle bigger

quiz.q: Aisha bisects a 60° angle, then bisects one of the halves. What angle does she get?
quiz.mistake: Stops after the first bisection

teach.ask: Gappu asks: I have lost my protractor! How can I still draw a 30° angle?
teach.praise: Make 60° with compass arcs (an equilateral triangle), then bisect it to get 30°. No protractor needed!
teach.nudge: Which angle can you make easily with just a compass? How do you get half of it?

topics.title: The mean as a balance point

learn.hook: Put coins on a ruler at 2 cm, 4 cm and 9 cm. Where should your finger go to balance it? Exactly at the mean, 5 cm!
points: The mean (average) = sum of values ÷ number of values. It is one way to describe the centre of data.
The mean is the balance point: the total distance of values above the mean equals the total distance of values below it. For 2, 4, 9 (mean 5): below 3 + 1 = 4, above 4.
A dot plot puts one dot above a number line for each value. Imagine the line as a see-saw — it balances at the mean.
This helps find a missing value: if the mean of 4, 6 and x is 7, the values below are 3 + 1 = 4 short, so x must be 4 above: x = 11.

example.q: Show that 5 is the balance point of 2, 4 and 9.
steps: Equal totals, so 5 balances the data

learn.reallife: Cricket batting averages and average rainfall are means — single numbers that balance all the data.

items.text: Mean of 4, 6, x is 7, so x = ___

games.title: Balance point facts
items: Distances above the mean always balance distances below it.
That is why the mean is the balance point.
The mean must be one of the data values.
The mean of 1 and 2 is 1.5.
A dot plot shows one dot for each value.
So you can see every value.
The mean of 2, 4, 9 is 4.

quiz.q: What is the mean of 3, 5 and 10?
quiz.mistake: Gives the middle value (median) or the total

quiz.q: For 3, 5 and 10 (mean 6), what is the total distance of the values below the mean?
quiz.explain: 3 is 3 below and 5 is 1 below: 3 + 1 = 4. It balances 10, which is 4 above.
quiz.mistake: Counts only one value

quiz.q: The mean of 4, 6 and x is 7. What is x?
quiz.explain: Below the mean: 3 + 1 = 4. So x must be 4 above 7: x = 11. Check: 21 ÷ 3 = 7.
quiz.mistake: Averages the two known values

quiz.q: A dot plot has 2 dots at 3, 1 dot at 4 and 1 dot at 6. What is the mean?
quiz.mistake: Divides by the number of different values (3)

quiz.q: Why is the mean called the 'balance point' of data?
options: It is always the middle value
The total distance of values above it equals the total distance below it
It is the most common value
It is the largest value minus the smallest
quiz.explain: Like a see-saw, the values on each side 'weigh' the same amount of distance.
steps: Sum of distances above = sum below
quiz.mistake: Confuses the mean with the median or mode

quiz.q: The mean of 10, 12, 14 and 20 is 14. What is the total distance of the values below the mean?
quiz.explain: 10 is 4 below and 12 is 2 below: 4 + 2 = 6, which balances 20 (6 above).
quiz.mistake: Includes 14, which is not below the mean

quiz.q: 8 friends have a mean of ₹45 pocket money. What is their total?
quiz.explain: Total = mean × number = 45 × 8 = ₹360.
quiz.mistake: Adds 8 instead of multiplying

quiz.q: Where is the balance point of the data 1, 2, 3, 10?
quiz.explain: Mean = 16 ÷ 4 = 4. Below: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6; above: 10 − 4 = 6. Balanced.
quiz.mistake: Takes the middle of the list

teach.ask: Gappu put pebbles at 1, 3 and 8 on a stick. Where should he hold it to balance? Explain why!
teach.praise: At 4! The pebbles at 1 and 3 are 3 + 1 = 4 below, and 8 is 4 above. Perfect balance!
teach.nudge: What is the mean of 1, 3 and 8? How far is each pebble from it?

learn.hook: Kabir scored 12, 30, 45, 30 and 8 runs in five matches. Is he a 30-run batter or a 25-run batter? It depends on which 'average' you use!
points: Data are facts or numbers we collect. Putting them in order or in a table makes them easier to read.
Mean (the usual average) = sum of all values ÷ number of values.
Median = the middle value after arranging the data in order. If there are two middle values, take their mean.
Mode = the value that appears most often.
Range = largest value − smallest value. It tells how spread out the data are.

example.q: Kabir's runs: 12, 30, 45, 30, 8. Find the mean, median, mode and range.

learn.reallife: Cricket averages, your class's average marks, and the most popular size of school shoes all come from these ideas.

quiz.q: Kabir's scores in 5 matches are 12, 30, 45, 30 and 8. What is his mean score?
quiz.explain: Sum = 125 and there are 5 matches, so the mean is 125 ÷ 5 = 25.
quiz.mistake: Gives the total (125) or the most common score (30)

quiz.q: What is the median of 12, 30, 45, 30, 8?
quiz.explain: In order: 8, 12, 30, 30, 45. The middle (3rd) value is 30.
quiz.mistake: Picks the middle value without arranging in order (45)

quiz.q: The heights of 6 plants are 10, 14, 15, 18, 20 and 25 cm. What is the median height?
quiz.explain: With 6 values, the two middle ones are 15 and 18. Median = (15 + 18) ÷ 2 = 16.5 cm.
quiz.mistake: Picks one of the two middle values, or finds the mean (17)

quiz.q: Shoe sizes in a group: 5, 6, 6, 7, 6, 8, 5, 6. What is the mode?
quiz.explain: Size 6 appears 4 times, more than any other size.
quiz.mistake: Picks the largest value, or the first value in the list

items: Size 5
Size 6
Size 7
Size 8

quiz.q: The mean of 4 numbers is 15. Three of them are 10, 12 and 20. What is the fourth number?
quiz.explain: Total of all 4 numbers = 4 × 15 = 60. The three known numbers add to 42, so the fourth is 60 − 42 = 18.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the missing number must equal the mean (15)

quiz.q: The midday temperatures (in °C) for a week were 31, 34, 29, 35, 33, 30 and 32. What is the range in °C?
quiz.explain: Range = highest − lowest = 35 − 29 = 6.
quiz.mistake: Gives the highest value or the median instead of the spread

quiz.q: Which measure is best for finding the most popular ice-cream flavour in a class?
quiz.explain: Flavours are names, not numbers, so we cannot add or order them. The mode tells which flavour was chosen most often.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the mean is always the right average

quiz.q: Riya's mean mark in 6 tests is 70. After a 7th test her mean becomes 72. What did she score in the 7th test?
quiz.explain: Total for 6 tests = 6 × 70 = 420. Total for 7 tests = 7 × 72 = 504. So the 7th test = 504 − 420 = 84.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the new mark is just the new mean, or adds the two means

teach.ask: Gappu asks: How do I find the median of 9, 2, 7, 4, 5?
teach.praise: Put them in order: 2, 4, 5, 7, 9. The middle one is 5. That is the median!
teach.nudge: What must you do to the numbers first? Then which one do you pick?

learn.hook: A new player scoring 26 joins a team whose mean is 20. Does the mean go up, down or stay? You can tell without any calculation!
points: Adding a value above the mean raises the mean; adding one below lowers it; adding one equal to the mean keeps it the same.
Removing a value above the mean lowers the mean; removing one below raises it.
Adding a balanced pair — one value d above and one d below the mean — keeps the mean the same.
Adding the same number c to every value adds c to the mean. Multiplying every value by k multiplies the mean by k.
Fixing a wrong entry: mean 40 for 10 values, but 25 was written as 52. Correct total = 400 − 52 + 25 = 373, so the correct mean is 37.3.

example.q: 5 players have a mean score of 20. A sixth scores 26. What is the new mean?

learn.reallife: Teachers correct averages when a mark was entered wrongly — this is exactly how they do it.

games.title: What happens to the mean?
items: Add a value above the mean
Remove a value below the mean
Add 5 to every value
Add a value below the mean
Remove a value above the mean
Add a value equal to the mean
Add one value 3 above and one 3 below

quiz.q: 5 values have a mean of 20. A sixth value, 26, is added. What is the new mean?
quiz.explain: New total = 100 + 26 = 126, and 126 ÷ 6 = 21. The mean rises because 26 is above 20.
quiz.mistake: Averages 20 and 26

quiz.q: 5 values have a mean of 20. One value, 30, is removed. What is the new mean?
quiz.explain: New total = 100 − 30 = 70, and 70 ÷ 4 = 17.5. Removing a value above the mean lowers it.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 5 again instead of 4

quiz.q: Data with a mean of 20 has two new values added: 15 and 25. What is the new mean?
quiz.explain: 15 is 5 below and 25 is 5 above — a balanced pair — so the mean stays 20.
quiz.mistake: Thinks adding values always changes the mean

quiz.q: The mean of some marks is 12. Every student gets 5 bonus marks. What is the new mean?
quiz.explain: Adding 5 to every value adds 5 to the mean: 12 + 5 = 17.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by 5 instead of adding

quiz.q: The mean of some lengths is 8 cm. Every length is tripled. What is the new mean?
quiz.explain: Multiplying every value by 3 multiplies the mean by 3: 8 × 3 = 24 cm.
quiz.mistake: Adds 3 instead of multiplying

quiz.q: The mean of 10 marks was found to be 40, but one mark of 25 had been entered as 52. What is the correct mean?
quiz.explain: Wrong total = 400. Correct total = 400 − 52 + 25 = 373, so the mean is 37.3.
quiz.mistake: Adds the error instead of subtracting it

quiz.q: A value exactly equal to the mean is added to the data. What happens to the mean?
quiz.explain: The new value is 0 away from the mean, so the balance does not change.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any new value shifts the mean

quiz.q: The mean of 4 values is 50. A fifth value makes the mean 52. What is the fifth value?
quiz.explain: Old total = 200, new total = 5 × 52 = 260. Fifth value = 260 − 200 = 60.
quiz.mistake: Takes the new mean as the new value

teach.ask: Gappu's class has a mean height of 140 cm. A new student who is 150 cm joins. Gappu says the mean stays 140. Is he right?
teach.praise: No! The new student is above the mean, so the mean goes up a little. Balance tips upward!
teach.nudge: Is 150 above or below the mean? What does that do to the balance?

learn.hook: Five shopkeepers earn ₹12k, ₹14k, ₹15k, ₹16k — and one earns ₹2 lakh. Which 'average' tells the true story?
points: Adding a very large value moves the median only one step, but can drag the mean far away. 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 has mean and median 7; add 100 and the median becomes 8 but the mean jumps to 22.5.
Removing a value also shifts the median by at most a step: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 → remove 10 → median moves from 6 to 5.
The median is less affected by extreme values (outliers) than the mean.
Choose the median when there are extreme values (incomes, house prices). Choose the mean when the values are fairly even and you want to use every value.

example.q: Find the mean and median of 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 100.
steps: The single 100 pulls the mean far more than the median

learn.reallife: News reports often give the 'median income' because a few very rich people would push the mean up.

games.title: Which average fits better?
items: Salaries in a company with one very high salary
House prices in a city with a few palaces
Pocket money where one child gets ₹5000
Daily temperatures over a week
Marks of a class with no extreme scores
Heights of students in one class

quiz.q: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 has median 7. After adding 100, what is the median?
quiz.explain: Six values now: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 100. The middle two are 7 and 9, so the median is 8.
quiz.mistake: Does not re-find the middle after adding a value

quiz.q: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 has mean 7. After adding 100, what is the mean?
quiz.explain: (35 + 100) ÷ 6 = 135 ÷ 6 = 22.5. One extreme value pulls the mean up a lot.
quiz.mistake: Gives the median

quiz.q: Which measure is less affected by one extremely large value?
quiz.explain: The median depends only on the middle position, so one extreme value moves it at most one step.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the mean resists outliers

quiz.q: Monthly salaries in a small shop: ₹12,000, ₹14,000, ₹15,000, ₹16,000 and ₹2,00,000. Which value best describes a typical salary?
quiz.explain: The mean is pulled up to ₹51,400 by one large salary; the median ₹15,000 is closer to what most people earn.
quiz.mistake: Uses the mean when there is an extreme value

quiz.q: From 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 the largest value is removed. What is the new median?
quiz.explain: 2, 4, 6, 8 has middle values 4 and 6, so the median is 5.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the old median

quiz.q: What is the median of 4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42?
quiz.explain: The middle two values are 15 and 16, so the median is 15.5.
quiz.mistake: Picks one of the two middle values

quiz.q: The value 1 is added to the data 4, 6, 8. What is the new median?
quiz.explain: 1, 4, 6, 8 has middle values 4 and 6, so the median is 5.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to put the new value in order

quiz.q: When is the mean a good choice to describe data?
options: Only when there is one huge value
When the values are fairly even, with no extreme values
quiz.explain: Without outliers, the mean uses every value and gives a fair centre.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the mean is always best

teach.ask: Gappu's flock: four birds have 2 worms each and one greedy bird has 40. Gappu says the 'average bird' has 9.6 worms. Is that fair?
teach.praise: The mean is 9.6, but the median is 2 — and that's what a typical bird really has! The greedy bird pulled the mean up.
teach.nudge: What is the middle value when you put the worm counts in order?

topics.title: Mean and median from frequency tables

learn.hook: A survey of 20 families gives sizes 2, 3, 4 or 5. Instead of writing 20 numbers, we use a frequency table — and can still find the mean and median.
points: A frequency table lists each value x and how many times it occurs (frequency f).
Mean = (sum of x × f) ÷ (sum of f). Family sizes 2, 3, 4, 5 with frequencies 3, 5, 8, 4: Σxf = 6 + 15 + 32 + 20 = 73 and Σf = 20, so the mean is 3.65.
Median: find the middle position(s), then use cumulative frequency (running totals) to see which value sits there. With 20 values, look at positions 10 and 11.
Cumulative frequencies 3, 8, 16, 20 show positions 9 to 16 have size 4, so the median family size is 4.
Such tables summarise real data like family sizes, bags harvested per farmer or goals per match.

example.q: Find the mean number of goals: 0 goals in 4 matches, 1 in 6, 2 in 5, 3 in 5.

learn.reallife: Village panchayats and health workers summarise family sizes and harvests in frequency tables.

games.title: Median from a table
items: Add the frequencies to find the total n
Find the middle position(s)
Write the cumulative frequencies
See which value the middle position falls in

quiz.q: Family sizes 2, 3, 4, 5 have frequencies 3, 5, 8, 4. What is the mean family size?
quiz.mistake: Averages the four sizes without using the frequencies

quiz.q: For the same table (sizes 2, 3, 4, 5 with frequencies 3, 5, 8, 4), what is the median family size?
quiz.explain: There are 20 families, so look at positions 10 and 11. Cumulative frequencies 3, 8, 16 show both are size 4.
quiz.mistake: Takes the middle of the list of sizes

quiz.q: For the same table, how many families are there in all?
quiz.explain: Add the frequencies: 3 + 5 + 8 + 4 = 20.
quiz.mistake: Adds the sizes instead of the frequencies

quiz.q: Farmers harvested 10 bags (2 farmers), 12 bags (5 farmers) or 15 bags (3 farmers). What is the mean harvest per farmer?
quiz.explain: Σxf = 20 + 60 + 45 = 125 and Σf = 10, so the mean is 12.5 bags.
quiz.mistake: Averages 10, 12 and 15 directly

quiz.q: For the same harvest table, what is the median number of bags?
quiz.explain: 10 farmers → positions 5 and 6. Cumulative 2, 7, 10 shows both are 12 bags.
quiz.mistake: Uses the mean instead

quiz.q: For the same harvest table, what is the cumulative frequency up to 12 bags?
quiz.explain: Running total: 2 (for 10 bags) + 5 (for 12 bags) = 7.
quiz.mistake: Gives only the frequency of 12 bags

quiz.q: A team scored 0 goals in 4 matches, 1 in 6, 2 in 5 and 3 in 5. What is the mean number of goals per match?
quiz.mistake: Divides by the number of different goal values

quiz.q: For the same goals table, what is the median number of goals?
quiz.explain: 20 matches → positions 10 and 11. Cumulative 4, 10, 15: position 10 is 1 goal and position 11 is 2 goals. Median = 1.5.
quiz.mistake: Looks at only one middle position

teach.ask: Gappu counted seeds per pod: 3 seeds (2 pods), 4 seeds (5 pods), 5 seeds (3 pods). How can he find the mean?
teach.praise: 6 + 20 + 15 = 41 seeds in 10 pods, so the mean is 4.1. Frequency tables save so much writing!
teach.nudge: What do you multiply each seed count by? What do you divide by?

learn.hook: Typing 50 marks and adding them by hand is slow. A spreadsheet adds them instantly — and updates the total when a mark changes!
points: A spreadsheet is a grid of cells. Columns are named by letters (A, B, C, ...) and rows by numbers (1, 2, 3, ...). Cell C4 is in column C, row 4.
A formula starts with '='. =B2*C2 multiplies the values in B2 and C2.
=SUM(B2:B6) adds all the cells from B2 to B6 (5 cells). =AVERAGE(B2:B6) finds their mean.
If you change a value, every formula that uses it updates automatically.

example.q: Cells B2 to B6 hold 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. What do =SUM(B2:B6) and =AVERAGE(B2:B6) show?

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers, school offices and cricket scorers keep their records in spreadsheets.

games.title: Spreadsheet words
pairs: A horizontal line of cells, named by a number

games.title: Spreadsheet check
items: A spreadsheet formula starts with '='.
For example =SUM(B2:B6).
The range B2:B6 contains 4 cells.
B2, B3, B4, B5, B6 — that is 5 cells.
Changing a cell value updates the totals that use it.
Formulas recalculate automatically.
Columns in a spreadsheet are named by numbers.
Columns use letters; rows use numbers.

quiz.q: Which cell is in column D and row 7?
quiz.explain: A cell name is its column letter followed by its row number: D7.
quiz.mistake: Writes the row before the column

quiz.q: How many cells are in the range B2:B6?
quiz.explain: B2, B3, B4, B5 and B6 — five cells.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts 6 − 2 and forgets to count both ends

quiz.q: Cells B2 to B6 hold 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. What does =SUM(B2:B6) show?
quiz.explain: SUM adds all the cells: 10 + 20 + 30 + 40 + 50 = 150.
quiz.mistake: Gives the mean instead

quiz.q: Cells B2 to B6 hold 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. What does =AVERAGE(B2:B6) show?
quiz.explain: AVERAGE = 150 ÷ 5 = 30.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 6 (the last row number)

quiz.q: Which formula finds the total of cells A1 to A10?
quiz.explain: =SUM(A1:A10) adds every cell from A1 to A10. =A1+A10 adds only two cells.
quiz.mistake: Adds only the first and last cells

quiz.q: In the same sheet (10, 20, 30, 40, 50 in B2:B6), B4 is changed from 30 to 60. What does =SUM(B2:B6) show now?
quiz.explain: The total goes up by 30: 150 + 30 = 180. The formula updates by itself.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the total stays the same

quiz.q: In a spreadsheet, what is a row?
options: A vertical line of cells, named by a letter
A horizontal line of cells, named by a number
quiz.explain: Rows go across and are numbered; columns go down and are lettered.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up rows and columns

quiz.q: B2 holds 4 (number of pens) and C2 holds 15 (price in ₹). What does =B2*C2 show?
quiz.explain: The * sign means multiply: 4 × 15 = 60.
quiz.mistake: Adds the two cells

teach.ask: Gappu typed 5 marks into cells B2 to B6. He wants the class average. What formula should he type?
teach.praise: =AVERAGE(B2:B6)! The spreadsheet does the adding and dividing for me.
teach.nudge: Which function finds the mean? Which cells should it use?

topics.title: Bar graphs, dot plots and pie charts

learn.hook: A picture can tell a story faster than a long table. One glance at a graph and you know who won the class election!
points: A bar graph uses bars of equal width with gaps between them. The height (or length) shows the value.
A double bar graph puts two bars side by side for each category, for example boys and girls.
A dot plot puts one dot for every value above a number line, so clusters and gaps are easy to spot.
Always read the scale: if 1 unit = 5 students, a bar 4 units tall shows 20 students. The scale should start at 0.
A pie chart shows parts of a whole as slices. Slice angle = (part ÷ whole) × 360°.

example.q: In a survey of 120 students, 30 like cricket best. What angle should the cricket slice have in a pie chart?

learn.reallife: News channels show election results as bar graphs and pie charts, and sports apps show runs per over as bars.

items.text: If 1 unit = 5 students, a bar 6 units tall shows ___ students
A slice that is 1/4 of a pie chart has an angle of ___

games.title: Graph facts
items: In a bar graph, the width of a bar shows its value.
All bars have the same width. The height (or length) shows the value.
A dot plot shows every single data value.
There is one dot for each value.
In a pie chart, a 180° slice shows half of the data.
180° is half of 360°.
The scale on a bar graph should start at 0 so that bar heights can be compared fairly.
If the scale starts higher, small differences look huge.
A double bar graph can compare two groups side by side.
Two bars for each category make comparing easy.
If 1 unit = 10 runs, a bar 3.5 units tall shows 3.5 runs.

quiz.q: A bar graph shows books read in a class library: Mon 4, Tue 7, Wed 3, Thu 6. On which day were the most books read?
quiz.explain: Tuesday's bar is the tallest, at 7 books.
quiz.mistake: Picks the last bar or the first bar instead of the tallest

items: Mon
Tue
Wed
Thu

quiz.q: Books read: Mon 4, Tue 7, Wed 3, Thu 6. How many more books were read on Tuesday than on Wednesday?
quiz.explain: Tuesday 7 − Wednesday 3 = 4 more books.
quiz.mistake: Adds the two values instead of finding the difference

quiz.q: On a bar graph, 1 unit stands for 50 trees. A bar is 7 units tall. How many trees does it show?
quiz.explain: Each unit is 50 trees, so 7 units = 7 × 50 = 350 trees.
quiz.mistake: Reads the bar height without using the scale

quiz.q: In a class of 40, 10 students walk to school. What angle should the 'walk' slice have in a pie chart?
quiz.explain: 10 out of 40 is 1/4 of the class. 1/4 × 360° = 90°.
quiz.mistake: Uses the number of students as the angle

quiz.q: A dot plot shows goals scored by a team in its matches: 0 goals (3 dots), 1 goal (5 dots), 2 goals (2 dots), 3 goals (1 dot). How many matches did the team play?
quiz.explain: Each dot is one match. 3 + 5 + 2 + 1 = 11 matches.
quiz.mistake: Counts the number of columns (4) instead of the dots

quiz.q: Same dot plot: 0 goals (3 dots), 1 goal (5 dots), 2 goals (2 dots), 3 goals (1 dot). How many goals did the team score in all?
quiz.explain: Multiply goals by the number of matches: 0 × 3 + 1 × 5 + 2 × 2 + 3 × 1 = 0 + 5 + 4 + 3 = 12.
quiz.mistake: Counts the dots (matches) instead of the goals

quiz.q: Which graph is best for showing what share of the whole each part is, like how Meena spends her day?
quiz.explain: A pie chart shows parts of one whole as slices, so you see each part's share at a glance.
quiz.mistake: Uses a line graph, which shows change over time

quiz.q: A double bar graph shows the children who like each sport. Cricket: boys 12, girls 9. Kabaddi: boys 6, girls 8. How many children like kabaddi?
quiz.explain: Add both bars for kabaddi: 6 boys + 8 girls = 14 children.
quiz.mistake: Finds the difference between the bars, or adds the cricket bars

teach.ask: Gappu asks: A bar graph says 1 unit = 20 birds. A bar is 3 units tall. How many birds is that?
teach.praise: Each unit is 20 birds, so 3 × 20 = 60 birds. That is a big flock!
teach.nudge: What does one unit on the graph stand for? What do you do with the 3?

learn.hook: A doctor's fever chart, a share-market screen and your height on the door frame all tell stories of change. Line graphs show how things change over time.
points: A line graph plots points for values at different times and joins them with line segments.
Time usually goes on the horizontal axis and the quantity on the vertical axis.
A line going up shows an increase, going down shows a decrease, and a flat line shows no change.
A steeper line means a faster change.
In a distance–time graph, a straight sloping line means a steady speed; speed = distance ÷ time.

example.q: Temperatures: 6 am 18°C, 9 am 22°C, 12 noon 30°C, 3 pm 32°C, 6 pm 26°C. Between which two times did the temperature rise the most?
example.answer: Between 9 am and 12 noon (a rise of 8°)

learn.reallife: Weather reports, a patient's temperature chart and a city's population over the years are all shown as line graphs.

games.title: Line graph or bar graph?
buckets: Line graph is a good choice
Bar graph is a better choice

A plant's height each week
Price of petrol each month for a year

Runs scored by each player in one match

quiz.q: Temperatures: 6 am 18°C, 9 am 22°C, 12 noon 30°C, 3 pm 32°C, 6 pm 26°C. At which of these times was it hottest?
quiz.explain: The highest point on the graph is 32°C at 3 pm.
quiz.mistake: Assumes noon is always the hottest time

quiz.q: Using the same temperatures, by how many degrees did it rise from 9 am to 12 noon?
quiz.explain: 30 − 22 = 8 degrees.

quiz.q: Using the same temperatures, between which two times did the temperature fall?
quiz.explain: From 32°C at 3 pm it went down to 26°C at 6 pm. All other parts go up.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a smaller rise with a fall

quiz.q: Harpreet's plant was 4 cm in week 1, 7 cm in week 2, 10 cm in week 3 and 13 cm in week 4. If it keeps growing the same way, how tall will it be in week 5?
quiz.explain: It grows 3 cm every week, so the line keeps the same steepness: 13 + 3 = 16 cm.
quiz.mistake: Adds 1 or doubles instead of continuing the steady +3 pattern

quiz.q: On a line graph, what does a horizontal (flat) part show?
options: The quantity did not change during that time
quiz.explain: If the line stays at the same height, the value stays the same for that time.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a flat line means the value dropped to zero

quiz.q: A cyclist's distance–time graph is a straight line from 0 km at 0 hours to 45 km at 3 hours. What is the speed in km/h?
quiz.explain: A straight line means steady speed. Speed = 45 km ÷ 3 h = 15 km/h.
quiz.mistake: Reads the final distance as the speed

quiz.q: Which data is best shown with a line graph?
options: Number of boys and girls in each class
Your weight every month for a year
Kinds of trees in a park
quiz.explain: Weight changes over time, and a line graph shows change over time. The others compare separate categories.
quiz.mistake: Uses a line graph for categories that have no order in time

quiz.q: Aisha's savings were ₹200 in January, ₹350 in February, ₹350 in March and ₹600 in April. During which period did her savings not change?
quiz.explain: Savings were ₹350 in both February and March, so the line is flat there.
quiz.mistake: Looks for the smallest bar instead of two equal readings
