teach.ask: Gappu asks: How can I tell from a line graph when something is growing fastest?
teach.praise: Where the line goes up most steeply, the growth is fastest. I can read graphs now!
teach.nudge: Look at the different parts of the line. Which part climbs the most in the same time?

learn.hook: An ad shows one bar three times taller than another — but the real difference is only 4%! Graphs can trick your eyes.
points: If the vertical axis does not start at 0, small differences look huge. Sales of 92 and 96 on an axis starting at 90 look like bars of 2 and 6 — three times as tall.
Uneven scales or stretched axes also mislead. Always read the numbers on the axes.
Infographics mix pictures and data. Doubling the height of a picture also doubles its width, so it looks 4 times as big even if the number only doubled.
Check an infographic: Are the units clear? Do the percentages of a whole add to 100%? Is the source given?
Pick the right graph: line graph for change over time; bar graph to compare categories; pie chart for parts of a whole; dot plot for a small set of values.

example.q: A graph of sales 92 and 96 has its axis starting at 90. How much bigger does the second bar look, and how much bigger is it really?
steps: Really: 96 is only 4 more than 92, about 4% more

learn.reallife: Smart readers of newspapers and social media always check the axes before believing a graph.

games.title: Best graph for the job
items: Temperature every hour of a day
A baby's weight each month
Students in each school house
Medals won by five states
How a family's budget is shared
Share of land used for each crop

games.title: Spot the trick
items: A bar graph whose axis starts at 90 can make small differences look big.
The bars show only the part above 90.
If a picture's height and width are both doubled, it looks twice as big.
Its area becomes 4 times as big.
Percentages in a pie infographic should add up to 100%.
They are parts of one whole.
A good graph shows its scale and units.
Otherwise readers cannot judge the numbers.

quiz.q: A bar graph of sales 92 and 96 starts its axis at 90. How many times taller does the 96 bar look than the 92 bar?
quiz.explain: The visible bars are 96 − 90 = 6 and 92 − 90 = 2 tall, so one looks 3 times the other.
quiz.mistake: Compares the actual values instead of the visible bar heights

quiz.q: In the same graph, how much bigger are sales of 96 than 92 really?
quiz.explain: 96 − 92 = 4, and 4 is about 4% of 92. The graph exaggerates the difference.
quiz.mistake: Trusts the bar heights without reading the axis

quiz.q: What is the most common trick that makes a bar graph misleading?
options: The vertical axis does not start at 0
quiz.explain: Starting the axis above 0 cuts off the bottom of every bar and exaggerates differences.
quiz.mistake: Blames harmless features like colour

quiz.q: An infographic shows a coin icon for 2023 and one twice as tall and twice as wide for 2024. By how many times does the 2024 icon's area grow?
quiz.explain: Area grows by 2 × 2 = 4, so the picture looks 4 times as big even if the money only doubled.
quiz.mistake: Thinks doubling height and width doubles the area

quiz.q: A pie infographic shows 45%, 30%, 20% and 10% for the four parts of one whole. What is wrong?
options: Percentages cannot be shown in a pie
quiz.explain: 45 + 30 + 20 + 10 = 105. The parts of one whole must total 100%.
quiz.mistake: Does not add the percentages

quiz.q: Which graph is best for showing the temperature every hour through a day?
quiz.explain: A line graph shows how a quantity changes over time.
quiz.mistake: Uses a pie chart for change over time

quiz.q: Which graph is best for comparing the number of students in each school house?
quiz.explain: Bars make it easy to compare separate categories side by side.
quiz.mistake: Uses a line graph for categories that are not in time order

quiz.q: An infographic says '3 out of 4 students love maths' but gives no source or sample size. What should a careful reader ask?
options: How many students were asked, and who did the survey?
quiz.explain: Without the source and sample size, you cannot tell if the claim is reliable (it might be just 4 students!).
quiz.mistake: Believes any number shown in a picture

teach.ask: Gappu saw a graph where one bar looks 5 times taller than another. He is shocked! What should he check first?
teach.praise: The axis started at 80, not 0! The real difference is tiny. I won't be fooled again.
teach.nudge: Where does the vertical axis start? What do the numbers actually say?

learn.hook: A pen costs ₹p and a notebook ₹n. Without knowing the prices, you can still write the bill for 3 pens and 2 notebooks: 3p + 2n. That is the power of algebra!
points: An algebraic expression uses numbers, letters (variables) and operations, like 3x + 5y − 2.
Terms are the parts joined by + or −. In the term −5y, the coefficient is −5.
Like terms have the same letters with the same powers: 3x² and −5x² are like terms, but 3x and 3x² are not.
We can add or subtract only like terms: 4a + 3b + 2a = 6a + 3b.
To evaluate an expression, put in (substitute) the value of each letter: if x = 3, then 2x² + 1 = 2 × 9 + 1 = 19.

example.q: Simplify (5x + 3y − 2) − (2x − y + 4).
steps: Remove the brackets; the minus changes every sign in the second bracket: 5x + 3y − 2 − 2x + y − 4

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers, coders and scientists all use letters to write rules that work for any number, like total cost = price × quantity.

games.title: Like 4x or not?
items: x
4x²
4y
xy

quiz.q: Simplify 4a + 3b + 2a − b.
quiz.explain: Add like terms only: 4a + 2a = 6a and 3b − b = 2b.
quiz.mistake: Adds unlike terms together into one term

quiz.q: What is the coefficient of y in 7x − 5y + 3?
quiz.explain: The term with y is −5y, so its coefficient is −5. The sign belongs to the term.
quiz.mistake: Drops the minus sign in front of the term

quiz.q: Find the value of 2x² + 1 when x = 3.
quiz.explain: x² = 9, so 2 × 9 + 1 = 19. Square x first, then multiply by 2.
quiz.mistake: Squares 2x instead of x, getting (2 × 3)² + 1 = 37

quiz.q: Which pair are like terms?
quiz.explain: Like terms have exactly the same letters with the same powers. Both 3x² and −5x² have x².
quiz.mistake: Thinks terms with the same number in front are like terms

quiz.q: Simplify (5x + 3y − 2) − (2x − y + 4).
quiz.explain: Subtracting a bracket changes every sign inside it: 5x + 3y − 2 − 2x + y − 4 = 3x + 4y − 6.
quiz.mistake: Changes only the first sign inside the second bracket

quiz.q: A pen costs ₹p and a notebook costs ₹n. Riya buys 3 pens and 2 notebooks. Which expression gives the total cost in rupees?
quiz.explain: 3 pens cost 3 × p = 3p and 2 notebooks cost 2 × n = 2n. Total = 3p + 2n.
quiz.mistake: Combines unlike terms or swaps the numbers

quiz.q: If a = 2 and b = −3, what is a² − ab?
quiz.mistake: Forgets that subtracting a negative number means adding

quiz.q: How many terms are there in 3x² − 4xy + 7y − 9?
quiz.explain: The terms are 3x², −4xy, 7y and −9. That is 4 terms.
quiz.mistake: Does not count the number term −9, or counts letters

teach.ask: Gappu asks: Can I add 3x and 2y to get 5xy?
teach.praise: Only like terms can be added. 3x and 2y have different letters, so it stays 3x + 2y. Thanks!
teach.nudge: What must two terms have in common before we can add them?

learn.hook: Think of any number. Double it, add 10, halve it, then take away the number you first thought of. Your answer is 5! Algebra explains the magic.
points: Let the secret number be n and follow each step: 2n → 2n + 10 → n + 5 → 5. The n disappears, so everyone gets 5.
Patterns can be written as rules. 5, 8, 11, 14, ... goes up by 3 each time, so the nth term is 3n + 2.
Matchstick squares in a row use 4, 7, 10, ... sticks: 3n + 1 sticks for n squares.
Calendar trick: in any 2 × 2 block of dates with top-left n, the four dates are n, n + 1, n + 7, n + 8, which add to 4n + 16.
Check a rule by testing it with the first few terms.

example.q: Matchstick squares in a row need 4, 7, 10, ... sticks. How many sticks are needed for 20 squares?

learn.reallife: Magicians, puzzle makers and computer programmers use rules like 3n + 1 to predict what comes next.

items.text: Think of n, add 3, then double. You get ___

quiz.q: Think of a number, double it, add 10, halve the result, then subtract the number you started with. What do you always get?
quiz.explain: With n: 2n, then 2n + 10, then n + 5, then n + 5 − n = 5.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that halving also halves the 10

quiz.q: Matchstick squares in a row use 4, 7, 10, ... sticks. How many sticks are needed for 20 squares?
quiz.explain: The rule is 3n + 1, so for 20 squares: 3 × 20 + 1 = 61. Neighbouring squares share a stick.
quiz.mistake: Uses 4 sticks for every square (80), forgetting that sticks are shared

quiz.q: What is the rule for the nth term of 5, 8, 11, 14, ...?
quiz.explain: The terms go up by 3, so the rule starts with 3n. For n = 1, 3n = 3, and we need 5, so add 2: 3n + 2.
quiz.mistake: Uses the first term (5) as the number added

quiz.q: On a calendar, Kabir picks a 2 × 2 block of dates whose top-left date is n. What is the sum of the four dates?
quiz.explain: The dates are n, n + 1 (next day), n + 7 (a week later) and n + 8. Sum = 4n + 16.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the date below is n + 1 instead of n + 7

quiz.q: Aisha says: think of a number, add 4, multiply by 3, then subtract 12. What is the answer always equal to?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies only n by 3 and forgets to multiply the 4

quiz.q: A pattern has the rule 4n − 1. What is its 10th term?
quiz.mistake: Adds 1 instead of subtracting

quiz.q: Which expression gives the sum of three consecutive numbers starting at n?
quiz.explain: The numbers are n, n + 1 and n + 2. Their sum is 3n + 3.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the +1 and +2, or adds 1 + 2 + 3

quiz.q: A pattern of triangles uses 3, 5, 7, 9, ... matchsticks (rule 2n + 1). Which term uses 51 matchsticks?
quiz.mistake: Puts 51 into the rule as n instead of solving for n

teach.ask: Gappu asks: Why does the 'double, add 10, halve, minus your number' trick always give 5?
teach.praise: Call the number n: 2n + 10, halved is n + 5, and taking away n leaves 5. The n cancels! Magic solved!
teach.nudge: What if you use a letter like n for the secret number? What happens to it at the end?

learn.hook: Ask a friend to do some sums with their birthday — then announce the date! Algebra is the secret behind the magic.
points: In 'think of a number' tricks, write the number as n and follow each step. If n cancels out, everyone ends with the same answer.
You can change one step to change the final answer: 'double, add 10, halve, subtract the number' gives 5; adding 14 instead of 10 gives 7. The fixed answer is half of what you add.
Birthday trick: month M, day D. Multiply M by 5, add 6, multiply by 4, add 9, multiply by 5, then add D. The result is 100M + D + 165.
Subtract 165 from your friend's answer to get 100M + D: the hundreds give the month and the last two digits give the day. 814 means month 8, day 14 — 14 August.

example.q: Show why the birthday trick works.

learn.reallife: Stage magicians use exactly this kind of algebra in 'mind-reading' tricks.

items.text: Double, add ___, halve, subtract the number → always 9

quiz.q: Think of a number n, add 3, double it, subtract 6, then halve it. What do you get?
quiz.explain: 2(n + 3) = 2n + 6; minus 6 gives 2n; halving gives n.
quiz.mistake: Loses track of a step

quiz.q: 'Double your number, add ___, halve it, subtract your number.' What should go in the gap so the answer is always 9?
quiz.explain: (2n + k) ÷ 2 − n = k ÷ 2. For the answer 9, k = 18.
quiz.mistake: Puts the answer itself in the gap

quiz.q: Multiply your number by 3, add 12, divide by 3, then subtract your number. What is the result?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide the 12 by 3

quiz.q: In the birthday trick (×5, +6, ×4, +9, ×5, + day), what final number does 14 August give?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add the 165

quiz.q: A friend's final number in the birthday trick is 1395. What is their birthday?
quiz.explain: 1395 − 165 = 1230: month 12, day 30 — 30 December.
quiz.mistake: Reads the digits without subtracting 165

quiz.q: What is 100M + D for 7 March (M = 3, D = 7)?
quiz.explain: 100 × 3 + 7 = 307: the hundreds show the month and the last two digits the day.
quiz.mistake: Writes 37, losing the place for the day

quiz.q: Why does a 'think of a number' trick give everyone the same answer?
options: Everyone secretly picks the same number
The letter for the number cancels out
quiz.explain: When written with n, the steps simplify to a plain number with no n left.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the trick depends on the number chosen

quiz.q: Add 5 to your number n, double it, subtract 10, then divide by n. What do you always get (n ≠ 0)?
quiz.mistake: Divides before simplifying

teach.ask: Gappu wants a trick that always ends in 10. 'Double, add something, halve, subtract the number.' What should he add?
teach.praise: Add 20! The n cancels and half of 20 is 10. Ta-da, Gappu the magician!
teach.nudge: What is the answer always equal to, compared with the number you add?

learn.hook: In a number pyramid, every block is the sum of the two blocks below it. Change one number at the bottom and watch the top change!
points: Rule: each block is the sum of the two blocks directly below it.
3-row pyramid with bottom a, b, c: middle row a + b and b + c, top a + 2b + c. The middle bottom number counts twice.
4-row pyramid with bottom a, b, c, d: top = a + 3b + 3c + d.
Unknown blocks: write an equation. Top 30 with bottom 4, x, 6 gives 4 + 2x + 6 = 30, so x = 10.
Build pyramids on Virahanka–Fibonacci numbers 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ...: bottom 1, 1, 2 gives top 5, and bottom 2, 3, 5 gives top 13 — Fibonacci numbers again!

example.q: A 3-row pyramid has bottom row 4, x, 6 and top 30. Find x.

learn.reallife: Spreadsheet formulas that add neighbouring cells build pyramids just like this.

games.title: Pyramid expressions
pairs: Top of 4 rows (a, b, c, d)

quiz.q: A 3-row pyramid has bottom row 3, 5, 2. What is the top?
quiz.explain: Middle row: 8 and 7. Top: 8 + 7 = 15 (= 3 + 2 × 5 + 2).
quiz.mistake: Adds the bottom numbers once each

quiz.q: A 3-row pyramid has bottom row 4, x, 6 and top 30. What is x?
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the middle number counts twice

quiz.q: A 4-row pyramid has bottom row 1, 2, 3, 4. What is the top?
quiz.mistake: Uses the 3-row rule

quiz.q: What is the top of a 3-row pyramid with bottom row a, b, c?
quiz.explain: The middle row is a + b and b + c; adding them gives a + 2b + c.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that b is used twice

quiz.q: What is the top of a 4-row pyramid with bottom row a, b, c, d?
quiz.explain: Rows: a + b, b + c, c + d → a + 2b + c, b + 2c + d → a + 3b + 3c + d.
steps: Second row up: a + 2b + c and b + 2c + d
quiz.mistake: Stops one row too early

quiz.q: A 3-row pyramid is built on the Fibonacci numbers 1, 1, 2. What is the top?
quiz.explain: 1 + 2 × 1 + 2 = 5, another Fibonacci number.
quiz.mistake: Adds 1 + 1 + 2 only once each

quiz.q: A 3-row pyramid is built on 2, 3, 5. What is the top?
quiz.explain: 2 + 2 × 3 + 5 = 13 — a Fibonacci number.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double the middle number

quiz.q: A 3-row pyramid has bottom row 7, b, 9 and top 40. What is b?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to halve

teach.ask: Gappu's pyramid has bottom 2, ?, 4 and the top says 20. How can he find the missing block?
teach.praise: 2 + 2b + 4 = 20, so b = 7! The middle block counts twice — that's the key.
teach.nudge: How many times does the middle bottom number reach the top?

learn.hook: Tell me the total of any 3 × 3 block on a calendar, and I'll tell you every date in it. Here's how the trick works!
points: 2 × 2 calendar block with top-left a: a, a + 1, a + 7, a + 8, total 4a + 16. If the total is 72, then 4a = 56 and a = 14.
Cross shape with centre c: c − 7, c − 1, c, c + 1, c + 7. They add to 5c, so the centre is the total ÷ 5.
3 × 3 block with centre c: all nine dates add to 9c. A row of three dates adds to 3 × the middle one.
Shape puzzles: if ▲ + ▲ + ■ = 14 and ▲ + ■ = 9, subtract the second from the first: ▲ = 5, then ■ = 4.

example.q: The 9 dates in a 3 × 3 calendar block add to 117. Find the dates.

learn.reallife: Puzzle books and quiz shows love these 'guess the dates' tricks — now you can do them too.

quiz.q: A 2 × 2 calendar block adds up to 72. What is its top-left date?
quiz.explain: 4a + 16 = 72, so 4a = 56 and a = 14. The dates are 14, 15, 21, 22.
quiz.mistake: Divides 72 by 4 without removing the 16

quiz.q: A 2 × 2 calendar block adds up to 100. What is its top-left date?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the +16

quiz.q: A cross shape of 5 dates (centre and its 4 neighbours) adds up to 100. What is the centre date?
quiz.mistake: Divides by 4 instead of 5

quiz.q: The 9 dates in a 3 × 3 calendar block add up to 117. What is the centre date?
quiz.explain: The nine dates pair up around the centre, so the total is 9c. c = 117 ÷ 9 = 13.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 3

quiz.q: In that 3 × 3 block with centre 13, what is the smallest date?
quiz.explain: The top-left date is 13 − 7 − 1 = 5.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts only 7

quiz.q: Three dates side by side in a row add up to 45. What is the smallest?
quiz.explain: The middle one is 45 ÷ 3 = 15, so the dates are 14, 15, 16.
quiz.mistake: Gives the middle date

quiz.explain: Subtract the second from the first: ▲ = 14 − 9 = 5.
quiz.mistake: Divides 14 by 3 shapes
Finds ★ but stops there

teach.ask: Gappu circled a cross of 5 dates on a calendar and they add up to 85. What is the middle date?
teach.praise: The five dates add to 5 × centre, so 85 ÷ 5 = 17. The cross is centred on the 17th!
teach.nudge: If the centre is c, what are the other four dates? What do they all add up to?

learn.hook: Use the digits 2, 3 and 4 once each to make a two-digit number times a one-digit number. Can you find the biggest product? It's not what most people guess!
points: With digits 2, 3, 4 the possible products include 42 × 3 = 126, 32 × 4 = 128, 43 × 2 = 86 and 23 × 4 = 92. The largest is 32 × 4 = 128.
Why? For digits a > b > c, compare (10b + c) × a with (10a + c) × b.
Expand: (10b + c)a − (10a + c)b = 10ab + ac − 10ab − bc = c(a − b), which is positive.
So the biggest digit should be the single-digit multiplier, the next biggest goes in the tens place, and the smallest in the units place. For 5, 7, 9: 75 × 9 = 675.

example.q: Find the largest product using 5, 7 and 9 once each (2-digit × 1-digit).
steps: Next, 7, in the tens place; 5 in the units

learn.reallife: Thinking with algebra instead of trying every case saves time — that's how puzzle setters work.

quiz.q: Using 2, 3 and 4 once each (2-digit × 1-digit), what is the largest product?
quiz.explain: 32 × 4 = 128 beats 42 × 3 = 126 and every other arrangement.
quiz.mistake: Puts the largest digit in the tens place

quiz.q: Which arrangement of 2, 3, 4 gives the largest product?
quiz.explain: Using the largest digit as the multiplier wins: 32 × 4 = 128.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the biggest two-digit number always wins

quiz.q: Using 5, 7 and 9 once each, what is the largest product?
quiz.explain: 75 × 9 = 675. The next best is 95 × 7 = 665.
quiz.mistake: Makes the largest two-digit number 97 or 95

quiz.q: For digits a > b > c, what is (10b + c) × a − (10a + c) × b?
quiz.explain: 10ab + ac − 10ab − bc = ac − bc = c(a − b).
quiz.mistake: Makes a sign slip when expanding

quiz.q: Using 1, 6 and 8 once each, what is the largest product?
quiz.explain: 61 × 8 = 488 and 81 × 6 = 486. The rule picks 61 × 8.
quiz.mistake: Picks 81 × 6 because 81 is bigger
Thinks the two products are equal

quiz.q: Using 2, 3 and 4 once each (2-digit × 1-digit), what is the SMALLEST product?
quiz.explain: 34 × 2 = 68 is smallest; 24 × 3 = 72 is next.
quiz.mistake: Uses the smallest two-digit number 23

quiz.q: Using 6, 7 and 8 once each, what is the largest product?
quiz.mistake: Chooses 86 × 7

teach.ask: Gappu has digit cards 3, 5 and 8. He thinks 85 × 3 makes the biggest product. Is he right?
teach.praise: 53 × 8 = 424 beats 85 × 3 = 255! The biggest digit should be the multiplier.
teach.nudge: Where should the largest digit go?

learn.hook: Write any 3-digit number twice, like 456456. It is ALWAYS divisible by 7, 11 and 13. Magic? No — algebra!
points: A two-digit number with digits a, b is 10a + b. Its reverse is 10b + a.
Difference: (10a + b) − (10b + a) = 9(a − b), always a multiple of 9. 82 − 28 = 54 = 9 × 6.
Sum: (10a + b) + (10b + a) = 11(a + b), always a multiple of 11. 47 + 74 = 121 = 11 × 11.
Cyclic sums: abc + bca + cab = 111(a + b + c) = 3 × 37 × (a + b + c), so it is divisible by 3 and 37. 123 + 231 + 312 = 666 = 37 × 18.

example.q: Why is 456456 divisible by 13?

learn.reallife: Number magicians on stage use these tricks to 'predict' answers chosen by the audience.

quiz.mistake: Adds the digits instead of subtracting them

quiz.q: What is 47 + 74?
quiz.mistake: Makes an addition slip
Makes an addition slip

quiz.q: 666 is divisible by 37. What is 666 ÷ 37?
quiz.mistake: Divides by 111 instead
Divides by 1000 instead of 1001

quiz.q: Every number of the form abcabc (like 728728) is divisible by which of these?
quiz.explain: abcabc = abc × 1001 = abc × 7 × 11 × 13.
quiz.mistake: Picks a number not in 1001's factors

quiz.q: A two-digit number plus its reverse is 143. What is the sum of its digits?
quiz.mistake: Divides by 10 instead of 11

quiz.q: For the digits 2, 5 and 7, what is 257 + 572 + 725?
quiz.mistake: Adds the three numbers carelessly

teach.ask: Gappu wrote 312312 and his friend said it must be divisible by 7. How did the friend know so fast?
teach.nudge: What do you multiply 312 by to get 312312?

learn.hook: An equation is like a balanced weighing scale at the sabzi mandi. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other, and it stays balanced!
points: An equation says two expressions are equal. Solving it means finding the value of the letter that makes it true.
Keep the balance: add, subtract, multiply or divide both sides by the same number (never divide by 0).
Letters on both sides: move the letter terms to one side and the numbers to the other. 5x − 7 = 2x + 8 → 3x = 15 → x = 5.
Brackets: expand first. Fractions: multiply both sides by the LCM of the denominators.
Always check your answer by putting it back into the original equation.

example.q: Solve 5x − 7 = 2x + 8 and check.

learn.reallife: Equations help you find unknowns, like how many ₹20 rides you can take at a mela with ₹150 after paying a ₹30 entry fee.

games.title: Solve step by step
games.prompt: Put the steps for solving 3(x − 2) = 2x + 4 in order

quiz.q: Solve 5x − 7 = 2x + 8. What is x?
quiz.mistake: Stops at 3x = 15 and gives 15

quiz.q: Solve 3(x − 2) = 2x + 4. What is x?
quiz.explain: Expand: 3x − 6 = 2x + 4. Then 3x − 2x = 4 + 6, so x = 10. Check: 3 × 8 = 24 and 20 + 4 = 24.
quiz.mistake: Writes 3x − 2 instead of 3x − 6 when expanding

quiz.q: Solve x/3 + 4 = 10. What is x?
quiz.explain: Subtract 4: x/3 = 6. Multiply by 3: x = 18.
quiz.mistake: Divides 6 by 3 instead of multiplying

quiz.q: Meena is 3 times as old as her brother. Together their ages add up to 32 years. How old is her brother?
quiz.explain: Let the brother be x. Then x + 3x = 32, so 4x = 32 and x = 8. Meena is 24.
quiz.mistake: Gives Meena's age (24) instead of her brother's

quiz.q: The sum of three consecutive numbers is 87. What is the smallest of them?
quiz.mistake: Divides 87 by 3 and gives the middle number (29)

quiz.q: Riya has ₹50 more than Arjun. Together they have ₹290. How much does Arjun have?
quiz.explain: Let Arjun have x. Then x + (x + 50) = 290, so 2x = 240 and x = ₹120. Riya has ₹170.
quiz.mistake: Splits ₹290 equally (₹145) or gives Riya's amount

quiz.q: The length of a rectangle is 4 cm more than its width. Its perimeter is 48 cm. What is the width?
quiz.explain: Perimeter = 2(w + w + 4) = 4w + 8 = 48. So 4w = 40 and w = 10 cm. The length is 14 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses w + (w + 4) = 48, forgetting that a perimeter has two lengths and two widths

quiz.q: Solve (2x + 1)/3 = (x + 4)/2. What is x?
quiz.explain: Multiply both sides by 6: 2(2x + 1) = 3(x + 4). So 4x + 2 = 3x + 12, and x = 10. Check: 21/3 = 7 and 14/2 = 7.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies only one term on each side by the LCM

teach.ask: Gappu asks: How do I solve 2x + 3 = 11? Help!
teach.praise: Take 3 from both sides to get 2x = 8, then divide both sides by 2: x = 4. Balanced and solved!
teach.nudge: What can you do to both sides to get rid of the + 3? And then?

learn.hook: Two gardens both need 20 m of fencing. Do they have the same space for flowers? Not necessarily — one could be twice as big!
points: Area is the amount of surface a shape covers, measured by counting unit squares (cm², m²). A 7 cm × 4 cm rectangle covers 28 unit squares.
A square can be cut into 4 equal-area parts in many ways: 4 small squares, 4 strips, 4 triangles using both diagonals, and even odd shapes, as long as each part has a quarter of the area.
Same perimeter does not mean same area. With perimeter 20 cm: 9 × 1 = 9 cm², 8 × 2 = 16 cm², 5 × 5 = 25 cm². The square gives the most.
Scaling: doubling one side doubles the area; doubling both sides makes it 4 times; tripling both sides makes it 9 times.

example.q: Find three rectangles with perimeter 20 cm and compare their areas.

learn.reallife: When buying land or a flat, the area (not the boundary length) tells you how much space you get.

games.title: Perimeter 20 cm: which areas?
items: 9 cm × 1 cm
8 cm × 2 cm
7 cm × 3 cm
6 cm × 4 cm
5 cm × 5 cm

games.title: Area ideas
items: Two rectangles with the same perimeter always have the same area.
9 × 1 and 5 × 5 both have perimeter 20 but areas 9 and 25.
Doubling both sides of a rectangle makes its area 4 times.
A square can be split into 4 equal-area parts in only one way.
Strips, small squares, triangles and more all work.
Area is measured in square units.
Like cm² or m².

quiz.q: Of all rectangles with a perimeter of 20 cm (whole-number sides), which area is the largest?
quiz.explain: Length + breadth = 10. The square 5 × 5 gives 25 cm², more than 6 × 4 = 24 cm².
quiz.mistake: Thinks all rectangles with the same perimeter have equal area

quiz.q: A 9 cm × 1 cm rectangle has the same perimeter as a 5 cm square. What is its area?
quiz.explain: 9 × 1 = 9 cm², much less than the square's 25 cm², even though both perimeters are 20 cm.
quiz.mistake: Gives the perimeter instead of the area

quiz.q: Which statement about area and perimeter is true?
options: Same perimeter always means same area
A longer perimeter always means a bigger area
Area and perimeter are the same thing
Shapes with the same perimeter can have different areas
quiz.explain: 9 × 1 and 5 × 5 rectangles share a perimeter of 20 cm but have areas 9 and 25 cm².
quiz.mistake: Links perimeter and area too closely

quiz.q: A square of side 6 cm has its side doubled. What is the new area?
quiz.explain: New side 12 cm, so area = 144 cm² — 4 times the old 36 cm².
quiz.mistake: Doubles the area

quiz.q: A 4 cm × 3 cm rectangle has both sides tripled. What is its new area?
quiz.explain: 12 × 9 = 108 cm², which is 9 times the old 12 cm².
quiz.mistake: Triples the area instead of multiplying by 9

quiz.q: A 5 m × 3 m carpet has only its length doubled. What is its new area?
quiz.explain: 10 × 3 = 30 m² — doubling one side doubles the area.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the area by 4

quiz.q: In how many ways can a square be divided into 4 parts of equal area?
options: Many ways — strips, small squares, triangles and more
quiz.explain: Any split where each part has a quarter of the area works, so there are endless ways.
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal area means the same shape

quiz.q: How many 1 cm unit squares cover a 7 cm × 4 cm rectangle?
quiz.explain: 7 rows of 4 (or 4 rows of 7) = 28 unit squares, so the area is 28 cm².
quiz.mistake: Adds the sides or finds the perimeter

teach.ask: Gappu thinks a 10 m × 2 m field and a 6 m × 6 m field are the same size because both fences are about the same. Explain!
teach.praise: The fences are 24 m each, but the areas are 20 m² and 36 m². Perimeter doesn't decide area!
teach.nudge: What is the area of each field? What is the length of each fence?

learn.hook: Your school wants a 2 m path around its garden. How much area will the path cover? Cut, add and subtract shapes to find out!
points: A composite shape is made of simpler shapes. Split it into rectangles, triangles or trapeziums and add their areas.
Or start with a big shape and subtract the missing part: area left = big area − cut-out area.
Path outside a rectangle: path area = outer rectangle − inner rectangle. A path of width w adds 2w to the length and to the breadth.
Two paths crossing in the middle: add the two strips and subtract the small square where they overlap, so it is not counted twice.
Put all lengths in the same unit before working out areas.

example.q: A garden is 20 m × 15 m. A path 2 m wide runs all around it on the outside. Find the area of the path.
steps: Outer rectangle: (20 + 4) m × (15 + 4) m = 24 m × 19 m = 456 m²

learn.reallife: Tile shops, painters and gardeners use composite areas to work out how many tiles, how much paint or how much grass seed to buy.

items.q: 10 × 10 square with a 4 × 4 square cut out
Two 1 m crossing paths on a 10 × 6 lawn. Path area?
9 × 4 rectangle with a 2 × 2 square cut out

games.title: Composite checks
items: To find the area of a path around a garden, subtract the garden's area from the outer area.
Outer area − inner area = path area.
A 1 m path outside a 10 m × 8 m garden makes the outer size 11 m × 9 m.
The path is on both sides, so the outer size is 12 m × 10 m.
When two crossing paths are added as strips, the middle square is counted twice.
So subtract the overlap once.
Before adding areas, all lengths should be in the same unit.
Mixing cm and m gives wrong answers.
An L-shape can be split into two rectangles.
Draw one line to separate the two arms.
The area of any composite shape is its perimeter × 2.
Area and perimeter measure different things.

quiz.q: An L-shaped room is made of a 6 m × 4 m rectangle and a 3 m × 2 m rectangle. What is its total area?
quiz.mistake: Finds only the bigger rectangle, or multiplies the two areas

quiz.q: A garden 20 m × 15 m has a path 2 m wide all around it on the outside. What is the area of the path?
quiz.explain: Outer rectangle = 24 × 19 = 456 m². Garden = 300 m². Path = 456 − 300 = 156 m².
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the garden's perimeter by the width (140), missing the four corner squares

quiz.q: A 10 m × 6 m lawn has two paths, each 1 m wide, crossing in the middle and parallel to the sides. What is the total area of the paths?
quiz.explain: Strips: 10 × 1 = 10 and 6 × 1 = 6. The 1 m × 1 m centre is in both, so 10 + 6 − 1 = 15 m².
quiz.mistake: Counts the middle square twice (gets 16)

quiz.q: A square tile 30 cm × 30 cm has a 10 cm × 10 cm square cut out of the middle. What area is left?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the side lengths first: (30 − 10)² = 400

quiz.q: The front of a hut is a rectangle 8 m wide and 5 m tall, with a triangular roof of base 8 m and height 3 m on top. What is the total area?
quiz.explain: Rectangle = 8 × 5 = 40. Triangle = ½ × 8 × 3 = 12. Total = 52 m².
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ for the triangle (gets 64)

quiz.q: A photo 12 cm × 8 cm has a frame 1 cm wide around it on the outside. What is the area of the frame?
quiz.explain: Outer size = 14 cm × 10 cm = 140 cm². Photo = 96 cm². Frame = 140 − 96 = 44 cm².
quiz.mistake: Uses perimeter × width (40), missing the corners

quiz.q: A floor 5 m × 4 m is to be covered with square tiles of side 50 cm. How many tiles are needed?
quiz.explain: Each tile is 0.5 m × 0.5 m = 0.25 m². Floor = 20 m². 20 ÷ 0.25 = 80 tiles. (Or 10 tiles along by 8 tiles across.)
quiz.mistake: Divides 20 m² by 0.5 m instead of by the tile's area (gets 40)

quiz.q: A trapezium-shaped flower bed has parallel sides 6 m and 10 m and a height of 4 m. A 2 m × 2 m square fountain sits inside it. What area is left for flowers?
quiz.explain: Trapezium = ½ × (6 + 10) × 4 = 32 m². Fountain = 4 m². Flowers = 32 − 4 = 28 m².
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract the fountain, or forgets the ½

teach.ask: Gappu asks: A garden has a path all around it. How do I find just the path's area?
teach.praise: Find the big outer rectangle, subtract the inner garden, and what is left is the path. Smart!
teach.nudge: Which two rectangles can you see? What do you do with their areas?

learn.hook: Cut a rectangle along its diagonal. Two identical triangles fall out — so each triangle is exactly half the rectangle!
points: A diagonal splits a rectangle into two congruent triangles, each with half the rectangle's area.
Area of a triangle = ½ × base × height. Any side can be the base; the height is the perpendicular distance from the opposite vertex to that base.
Different bases give different heights, but the same area: a triangle with area 24 cm² has height 6 cm on a base of 8 cm, and height 8 cm on a base of 6 cm.
In an obtuse triangle, the height for some bases falls outside the triangle: extend the base and drop the perpendicular to the extended line. The formula still works.

example.q: A triangle has base 14 cm and height 5 cm. Find its area.

learn.reallife: Roof painters, sail makers and kite designers all work out triangle areas.

games.title: Triangle facts
items: A diagonal cuts a rectangle into two triangles of equal area.
They are congruent.
Only the bottom side of a triangle can be its base.
Any side can be the base, with its own height.
The height of a triangle can lie outside it.
This happens in obtuse triangles.
The area of a triangle is base × height.
It is ½ × base × height.

quiz.q: A 10 cm × 6 cm rectangle is cut along a diagonal. What is the area of each triangle?
quiz.explain: The rectangle is 60 cm², and the two congruent triangles each get half: 30 cm².
quiz.mistake: Forgets to halve

quiz.q: A triangle has base 14 cm and height 5 cm. What is its area?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½

quiz.q: A triangle has area 24 cm². With the 8 cm side as base, what is its height?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double the area first

quiz.q: The same triangle (area 24 cm²) uses its 6 cm side as base. What is the height now?
quiz.explain: 48 ÷ 6 = 8 cm. A different base gives a different height but the same area.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the height stays the same

quiz.q: An obtuse triangle has base 5 cm, and its height from the opposite vertex (falling outside the triangle) is 4 cm. What is its area?
quiz.explain: The formula still works: ½ × 5 × 4 = 10 cm².
quiz.mistake: Thinks the formula fails when the height is outside

quiz.q: How is the height of a triangle measured for a chosen base?
options: The perpendicular distance from the opposite vertex to the base line
From the middle of the base to any vertex
quiz.explain: The height must be at right angles to the base (or its extension) and reach the opposite vertex.
quiz.mistake: Uses a slanting side as the height

quiz.q: A right triangle has legs 9 cm and 4 cm. What is its area?
quiz.explain: The legs are perpendicular, so one is the base and the other is the height: ½ × 9 × 4 = 18 cm².
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½

quiz.q: A triangular garden has an area of 45 m² and a height of 9 m. How long is its base?
quiz.mistake: Divides 45 by 9 without doubling

teach.ask: Gappu says a triangle's area is base × height. Show him why there should be a ½!
teach.praise: A rectangle cut along its diagonal makes two equal triangles, so each is half: ½ × base × height!
teach.nudge: What happens if you cut a rectangle along its diagonal?

learn.hook: Slide the top corner of a triangle along a line parallel to its base. The triangle leans and changes shape — but its area never changes!
points: Triangles on the same base and between the same two parallel lines have equal areas, because they share the base and the height (the gap between the lines).
A triangle and a parallelogram on the same base and between the same parallels: the triangle has half the parallelogram's area.
A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. It splits the triangle into two triangles of equal area (equal bases, same height).
The three medians split a triangle into 6 small triangles of equal area.
Joining the midpoints of the three sides makes 4 congruent triangles, each with ¼ of the area.

example.q: Triangle ABC has area 60 cm². D is the midpoint of BC and E is the midpoint of AD. Find the area of triangle ABE.
steps: AD is a median → area ABD = 60 ÷ 2 = 30
BE is a median of triangle ABD → area ABE = 30 ÷ 2 = 15

learn.reallife: Farmers splitting a triangular field fairly between two children can use a median — each gets equal land.

games.title: Area fractions of a triangle of area 48
pairs: One of the 6 triangles made by all medians
Another triangle on the same base, between the same parallels

games.title: Same area?
items: Moving the top vertex along a line parallel to the base keeps the area the same.
The base and height do not change.
A median always splits a triangle into two congruent triangles.
Equal area, but usually different shapes.
A triangle on the same base as a parallelogram, between the same parallels, has half its area.
½ × b × h vs b × h.
Joining the midpoints of the sides gives 4 triangles of equal area.
They are all congruent.

quiz.q: Two triangles stand on the same base and between the same two parallel lines. How do their areas compare?
options: The more slanted one is smaller
quiz.explain: Both have the same base and the same height (the distance between the parallels), so ½ × b × h is the same.
steps: Same base, same height → same area
quiz.mistake: Judges area by how the triangles look

quiz.q: A triangle has a base of 10 cm, and its top vertex lies on a line parallel to the base 6 cm away. What is its area?
quiz.explain: Height = 6 cm (the gap between the lines), so area = ½ × 10 × 6 = 30 cm².
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½

quiz.q: A median is drawn in a triangle of area 40 cm². What is the area of each part?
quiz.explain: A median makes two triangles with equal bases and the same height, so each has half: 20 cm².
quiz.mistake: Thinks the parts are unequal

quiz.q: The midpoints of the sides of a triangle with area 48 cm² are joined. What is the area of each small triangle?
quiz.explain: Joining the midpoints makes 4 congruent triangles: 48 ÷ 4 = 12 cm².
quiz.mistake: Divides by 3

quiz.q: Triangle ABC has area 60 cm². D is the midpoint of BC and E is the midpoint of AD. What is the area of triangle ABE?
quiz.explain: AD halves the area: ABD = 30. Then BE is a median of ABD and halves it again: ABE = 15 cm².
quiz.mistake: Halves only once

quiz.q: A parallelogram of area 50 cm² and a triangle share a base and lie between the same parallels. What is the triangle's area?
quiz.explain: Triangle = ½ × b × h and parallelogram = b × h, so the triangle has half: 25 cm².
quiz.mistake: Thinks they have equal areas

quiz.q: What happens to a triangle's area if its top vertex slides along a line parallel to its base?
quiz.explain: The base and the height (the distance to the parallel line) do not change, so neither does the area.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a leaning triangle loses area

quiz.q: All three medians of a triangle of area 36 cm² are drawn. They make 6 small triangles. What is the area of each?
quiz.explain: The three medians cut the triangle into 6 triangles of equal area: 36 ÷ 6 = 6 cm².
quiz.mistake: Divides by 3 medians

teach.ask: Gappu's grandma wants to split a triangular field equally between two grandchildren with one straight fence from a corner. Where should it go?
teach.praise: From a corner to the midpoint of the opposite side — a median! Both parts have the same base and height, so equal area.
teach.nudge: Which point on the opposite side makes the two bases equal?

learn.hook: Many fields near rivers and many window panes are trapezium-shaped. How can a farmer find the area of a field that is not a neat rectangle?
points: Area of a trapezium = ½ × (sum of the parallel sides) × height, or ½ × (a + b) × h.
The height is the perpendicular distance between the two parallel sides, not the slanting side.
Why it works: two copies of the trapezium, one turned upside down, fit together to make a parallelogram with base (a + b) and height h. Our trapezium is half of it.
Another way: a diagonal splits the trapezium into two triangles with areas ½ × a × h and ½ × b × h.
Remember: parallelogram = base × height, triangle = ½ × base × height. Area is measured in square units like cm² and m².

example.q: A trapezium has parallel sides 10 cm and 6 cm. The distance between them is 5 cm. Find its area.

learn.reallife: Farmers, architects and painters use the trapezium formula for fields, roof panels, staircase sides and window glass.

quiz.q: A trapezium has parallel sides 10 cm and 6 cm, and the distance between them is 5 cm. What is its area?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ (gets 80 cm²)

quiz.q: A field is a trapezium with parallel sides 30 m and 50 m and a height of 20 m. What is its area?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to halve, or adds all the lengths

quiz.q: A trapezium has an area of 60 cm² and a height of 6 cm. One parallel side is 8 cm. How long is the other parallel side?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ in the formula (gets 2 cm), or stops at 8 + b = 20

quiz.q: Why is the area of a trapezium ½ × (a + b) × h?
options: Two copies fit together to make a parallelogram with base (a + b) and height h
A trapezium is always half of a square
Its parallel sides a and b are always equal
quiz.explain: Turn a copy upside down and join it to the first. You get a parallelogram of area (a + b) × h, and one trapezium is half of it.
quiz.mistake: Memorises the formula without the picture behind it

quiz.q: A trapezium-shaped window has parallel sides 1.2 m and 0.8 m, and a height of 1 m. What is its area?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the parallel sides (1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96) instead of adding them

quiz.q: Which length is the 'height' of a trapezium?
options: The length of a slanting side
The perpendicular distance between the parallel sides
quiz.explain: The height must be measured at right angles to the parallel sides. A slanting side is longer than the height.
quiz.mistake: Uses a slanting side as the height

quiz.q: A parallelogram has a base of 14 cm and a height of 9 cm. What is its area?
quiz.explain: Area of a parallelogram = base × height = 14 × 9 = 126 cm².
quiz.mistake: Uses ½ as for a triangle (63), or finds the perimeter (46)

quiz.q: Joseph's trapezium has parallel sides 9 cm and 15 cm, and a height of 8 cm. He splits it with a diagonal into two triangles. What is the total area?
quiz.explain: Triangle 1: ½ × 9 × 8 = 36. Triangle 2: ½ × 15 × 8 = 60. Total 96 cm², the same as ½ × (9 + 15) × 8.
quiz.mistake: Finds only one triangle, or forgets the ½

teach.ask: Gappu asks: How do I find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 7 and 5 and height 4?
teach.praise: Add the parallel sides (12), multiply by the height (48), then halve: 24 square units. Wonderful!
teach.nudge: Which two sides do you add? What do you do with the height, and is there a half?

topics.title: Area of rhombuses, quadrilaterals and polygons

learn.hook: A rangoli rhombus, a kite for Uttarayan and a hexagonal tile: all can be measured using their diagonals or by cutting them into triangles!
points: Area of a rhombus = ½ × d₁ × d₂, where d₁ and d₂ are the diagonals. This works because the diagonals are perpendicular.
A kite also has perpendicular diagonals, so its area is ½ × d₁ × d₂ too.
Any quadrilateral: take a diagonal d and the perpendiculars h₁ and h₂ to it from the other two corners. Area = ½ × d × (h₁ + h₂).
A rhombus is a parallelogram, so its area is also base × height.
Any polygon can be split into triangles, rectangles and trapeziums. Find each area and add.

example.q: A rhombus has diagonals 10 cm and 8 cm. Find its area.

learn.reallife: Surveyors find the area of oddly shaped plots by splitting them into triangles along a long diagonal.

items.text: A rhombus with diagonals 6 cm and 4 cm has an area of ___
A quadrilateral with diagonal 10 cm and perpendiculars 3 cm and 5 cm has an area of ___
The area of a kite is ½ × d₁ × ___
From its centre, a regular hexagon can be split into ___ equal triangles

games.title: Area truths
items: The area of a rhombus is half the product of its diagonals.
The diagonals are perpendicular, so the area is ½ × d₁ × d₂.
Every rhombus with side 5 cm has an area of 25 cm².
Only the square one does. A leaning rhombus with side 5 cm has a smaller height, so less area.
Any polygon can be split into triangles to find its area.
Joining one corner to the others cuts a polygon into triangles.
A square with a diagonal of 10 cm has an area of 50 cm².
A square is a rhombus: ½ × 10 × 10 = 50.
The area of a quadrilateral is d × (h₁ + h₂).
It is half of that: ½ × d × (h₁ + h₂).
A rhombus is a parallelogram, so its area is also base × height.
Both formulas give the same area.

quiz.q: A rhombus has diagonals 10 cm and 8 cm. What is its area?
quiz.explain: Area = ½ × 10 × 8 = 40 cm².
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ (gets 80) or adds the diagonals

quiz.q: In quadrilateral ABCD, diagonal AC = 12 cm. The perpendiculars from B and D to AC are 4 cm and 6 cm. What is the area of ABCD?
quiz.explain: Area = ½ × d × (h₁ + h₂) = ½ × 12 × 10 = 60 cm². It is two triangles: 24 + 36.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ (gets 120 cm²)

quiz.q: A rhombus has an area of 96 cm² and one diagonal of 16 cm. How long is the other diagonal?
quiz.explain: ½ × 16 × d = 96, so 8d = 96 and d = 12 cm.
quiz.mistake: Divides 96 by 16 and forgets the ½ (gets 6)

quiz.q: A square has a diagonal of 6 cm. What is its area?
quiz.explain: A square is a rhombus with equal diagonals: ½ × 6 × 6 = 18 cm².
quiz.mistake: Treats the diagonal as the side (gets 36 cm²)

quiz.q: Aisha's rangoli is a regular hexagon split into 6 equal triangles, each with an area of 15 cm². What is the area of the hexagon?
quiz.explain: 6 triangles × 15 cm² = 90 cm².
quiz.mistake: Adds 6 and 15 instead of multiplying

quiz.q: A pentagon is split into a rectangle of area 48 cm² and a triangle of area 12 cm². What is the area of the pentagon?
quiz.explain: The parts do not overlap, so add them: 48 + 12 = 60 cm².
quiz.mistake: Subtracts or multiplies the parts

quiz.q: Kabir's paper kite has diagonals of 30 cm and 20 cm. What is its area?
quiz.explain: The diagonals of a kite are perpendicular, so area = ½ × 30 × 20 = 300 cm².
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ (gets 600 cm²)

quiz.q: A rhombus has a side of 13 cm and a height of 10 cm. What is its area?
quiz.explain: A rhombus is a parallelogram, so area = base × height = 13 × 10 = 130 cm².
quiz.mistake: Squares the side (169) as if it were a square, or finds the perimeter (52)

teach.ask: Gappu asks: How can I find the area of a rhombus if I only know its two diagonals?
teach.praise: Multiply the diagonals and take half: ½ × d₁ × d₂. A rhombus is easy now!
teach.nudge: What do you do with the two diagonals? Is the answer the whole product or part of it?

learn.hook: Ancient Indian altar builders could turn a rectangle into a square of exactly the same area — using only ropes and pegs!
points: Cutting a shape into pieces and rearranging them never changes the total area (like tangram pieces).

Śulba-sūtra idea, rectangle → square: an a × b rectangle can be rearranged into an L-shape that is a big square of side (a + b)/2 minus a small square of side (a − b)/2. Then the Baudhayana theorem turns this difference of squares into one square.
Check with 8 × 2: ((8 + 2)/2)² − ((8 − 2)/2)² = 25 − 9 = 16 = 4². So the square has side 4.
Rectangle → triangle of equal area: keep the height and double the base (6 × 4 rectangle → triangle with base 12 and height 4).

Real life: area decides the paint for a wall (minus doors and windows), the size of a rangoli, or a fair exchange of land plots. Shortest-path puzzles use the same geometry: crossing a field along its diagonal beats walking round two edges.

example.q: Turn an 8 m × 2 m rectangle into a square of the same area.
steps: Big square side (8 + 2)/2 = 5, small square side (8 − 2)/2 = 3
Right triangle with hypotenuse 5 and leg 3 has other leg 4 → square of side 4 m

learn.reallife: Sulba-sutra altar plans were geometry problems of area — some of the oldest in the world.

items.q: Square with the area of an 8 × 2 rectangle: side
Triangle with height 4 and area of a 6 × 4 rectangle: base
Square with the area of a 40 × 10 plot: side
Tangram pieces from an 8 × 8 square: total area

games.title: Area stays?
items: Cutting a shape and rearranging the pieces keeps the area the same.
No surface is added or lost.
A 9 × 4 rectangle can be changed into a 6 × 6 square of the same area.
Both are 36.
A triangle with the same base and height as a rectangle has the same area.
It has half the area.
The Śulba-sūtras were written for building fire altars.
They give rules for altar shapes and sizes.

quiz.q: A square of side 8 cm is cut into tangram pieces and rearranged into a cat shape. What is the cat's area?
quiz.explain: Rearranging pieces keeps the area: 8 × 8 = 64 cm².
quiz.mistake: Thinks a new shape has a new area

quiz.q: Asha must cross a rectangular park 40 m long and 30 m wide, from one corner to the opposite corner. Walking along two edges is 70 m. How many metres does she save by walking straight along the diagonal?
quiz.explain: The diagonal is √(40² + 30²) = √2500 = 50 m. So she saves 70 − 50 = 20 m. The straight path is the shortest.
quiz.mistake: Gives the diagonal length instead of the saving, or subtracts the sides

quiz.q: For an 8 × 2 rectangle, what is ((8 + 2)/2)² − ((8 − 2)/2)²?
quiz.explain: 5² − 3² = 25 − 9 = 16, which equals 8 × 2.
quiz.mistake: Adds the two squares

quiz.q: A 6 cm × 4 cm rectangle is turned into a triangle of the same area with height 4 cm. What is the triangle's base?
quiz.explain: Area = 24 cm². ½ × b × 4 = 24 gives b = 12 cm — double the rectangle's length.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the same base

quiz.q: A wall is 5 m × 3 m with a 2 m × 1 m door. Paint costs ₹20 per m². What does it cost to paint the wall (not the door)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract the door

quiz.q: A rangoli is made of 4 congruent triangles, each with base 0.5 m and height 0.5 m. What is its total area?
quiz.explain: Each triangle: ½ × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.125 m². Four of them: 0.5 m².
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ in the triangle formula

quiz.q: A farmer swaps a 40 m × 10 m plot for a square plot of equal area. How long is each side of the square?
quiz.mistake: Averages the sides

quiz.q: Why did the Śulba-sūtras give rules for changing shapes while keeping area?
options: To build fire altars of exact sizes in different shapes
quiz.explain: Altars had to keep a fixed area while changing shape, so builders needed area-preserving rules.
steps: Altars of fixed area, different shapes
quiz.mistake: Does not link the rules to their purpose

teach.ask: Gappu cut his square paper nest-mat into 5 pieces and rearranged them into a boat shape. Is the boat bigger or smaller?
teach.praise: Exactly the same area! Cutting and rearranging never adds or removes paper.
teach.nudge: Did any paper get added or thrown away?
